We are happy to announce our investment in Minimac Systems, a Pune-based company that is building the circular economy for India’s industrial lubricants, one machine and one factory at a time.
The oil nobody talks about
When we talk about India’s oil problem, we often mean fuel. But there is a second, quieter oil economy that keeps every factory, power plant, steel mill, and mine in the country running: lubricants. India is the world’s third-largest lubricant market, consuming over 5 million tonnes of lubricants and greases a year. Over the next five years, India alone is expected to add lubricant demand at a CAGR of 4-5%, accounting for a quarter of all global demand addition.
Here is the uncomfortable part. Every lubricant starts with base oil, and over 60 percent of India’s base oil requirement is imported! An import bill that has crossed $2.7 billion a year. And once used, an estimated 85 percent of this oil is improperly disposed of. Roughly half of all lubricants end up in the environment, burned in the open or dumped, carrying benzene, lead, cadmium, and other toxins with them. A single litre of used oil can contaminate a million litres of fresh water.
So we import the oil at great expense, use it briefly, and then pay for it again in polluted soil and water.
Oil doesn’t wear out, it just gets dirty
The absurdity of this chain becomes clear when you look at what used oil actually is. About 90% of it is still base oil, the valuable part. What degrades are the additives, the sacrificial 5 to 10 percent that protect the oil the way white blood cells protect the body—along with contaminants like metal particles, moisture, and soot that creep in during use.
The oil itself is fine. It is just dirty. Clean it, and it works again. Processing used oil takes roughly a third of the energy needed to refine virgin oil from crude, and where 100 litres of crude yields barely a litre of virgin base oil, 100 litres of used oil can yield around 70 litres of re-refined base oil.
Yet most of India’s used oil never gets this second life. The re-refining industry here is fragmented and largely runs on the outdated acid-clay process, which produces low-quality output and mountains of hazardous sludge. The advanced technologies used globally barely exist in India, and most of the country’s existing re-refining capacity sits underutilised because organised collection of used oil simply does not happen.
The cost of doing nothing shows up on factory floors, too. Industrial downtime costs India over $3 billion annually, and a large majority of it traces back to lubrication failures.
What Minimac does
Minimac’s insight is that lubricant recycling should not require shipping oil to a distant plant. It should happen where the oil lives, inside the plant. The company has spent over a decade miniaturising industrial-grade lubricant recovery technology i.e. filtration, water separation, thin film evaporation, and more into equipment that works at the customer’s doorstep.
Around this, they have built three progressive layers of circularity:
NanoCircularity extends the life of oil while it is still inside the machine through continuous in-service reconditioning.
MicroCircularity reclaims and repurposes oil that has been drained.
MacroCircularity, the next frontier, closes the loop fully through organised collection, reverse logistics, and re-refining used oil back into high-quality base oil.
This translates into a business that earns in two ways.
Minimac designs and manufactures recycling equipment as an Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM). It also runs services around that equipment, including Recycling on Wheels (RoW)—mobile units that perform doorstep purification and recycling at customer sites— and a newer Lubricant as a Service (LAAS) offering, where customers pay for reliable, managed lubrication as an outcome rather than buying oil and equipment separately. A digitally tracked waste lubricant collection network feeds the loop.
The proof is in the deployment. Since 2012, Minimac has completed over 2,000 projects and put around 2,500 machines in the field, handling everything from 10 litres per minute to 10,000 litres per minute for some of India’s largest power, steel, and manufacturing companies.
Why now
Regulation is finally catching up with physics. India’s Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) rules for used oil now require that a progressively rising share of base oil feedstock come from recycled sources, from 10 percent today to 50 percent by 2030. An industry that treated used oil as someone else’s problem now has a legal obligation to close the loop, and very little infrastructure to do it with.
Why we invested
Minimac is the kind of company we find easy to like and hard to find. Anshuman Agrawal, a gold medalist in Mechanical Engineering from IIT-ISM Dhanbad and a management graduate from IIM Indore, has spent well over a decade inside plants understanding how machines actually fail. He and his co-founder Harshit bootstrapped the company from Pune, built it profitably, and earned their expansion the slow way, project by project.
The business sits at an intersection we care deeply about. It reduces import dependence, cuts hazardous waste, extends the life of capital equipment, and pays for itself in avoided downtime. It is decarbonisation that shows up on a maintenance ledger rather than a sustainability report, with a stated ambition to abate 860 gigagrams of CO2 equivalent by 2034.
Our capital will help Minimac deepen its recycling technology, expand its doorstep services footprint, and work toward the re-refining capability that completes the circle. This is patient work, and we are glad to be along for it.
You can learn more about Minimac at minimacsystems.com .

From September 7, 2026, the way orders can be placed during the pre-open session is changing. There are also several changes to ETF trading, including Gold and Silver ETFs becoming part of the pre-open session for the first time.
Before regular trading begins at 9:15 AM, exchanges run a pre-open session from 9:00 AM to 9:15 AM.
Unlike regular market hours, where buy and sell orders are matched continuously, the pre-open session first collects orders and then matches them at a single price. The exchange looks for the price at which the maximum quantity can be bought and sold, and this becomes the opening price for the day.
The idea is to allow orders that have built up overnight, including those reacting to news and other market developments, to come together before regular trading begins. This helps in discovering a more stable opening price and reduces volatility when the market opens at 9:15 AM.
Changes to the pre-open session
Time
Currently
From September 7
9:00 AM to 9:05 AM
Market and limit orders can be placed, modified, or cancelled.
Market and limit orders can be placed, modified, or cancelled.
9:05 AM to 9:08 AM
Market and limit orders can be placed, modified, or cancelled. Order entry closes randomly between 9:07 AM and 9:08 AM.
Only limit orders can be placed, modified, or cancelled. Market orders placed earlier cannot be modified or cancelled.
9:08 AM to 9:10 AM
Orders are matched, and the opening price is determined.
The exchange will randomly close order entry during this period. Order matching starts immediately after order entry closes.
9:10 AM to 9:12 AM
Orders are matched, and the opening price is determined.
The opening price is determined, orders are matched, and trades are confirmed.
9:12 AM to 9:15 AM
The market transitions to regular trading.
The market transitions to regular trading.
There is also a change in the order in which trades are matched.
Currently, limit orders get priority over market orders during the pre-open matching process. From September 7, market orders will get priority over limit orders.
The matching will happen in this order:
Eligible market orders will first be matched with other market orders based on the time they were placed.
Any remaining market orders will then be matched with eligible limit orders. Better-priced limit orders get priority, and where the price is the same, the earlier order gets priority.
Finally, the remaining limit orders will be matched with one another using the same price-and-time priority.
All trades that are matched during the pre-open session are executed at the opening price discovered during the session.
So, the overall pre-open session will remain 9:00 AM to 9:15 AM. The key changes are:
Market orders can be placed only during the first five minutes.
Limit-order entry continues until the exchange randomly closes the order-entry period between 9:08 AM and 9:10 AM.
Order matching starts immediately once order entry closes.
Market orders will now get priority over limit orders during matching.
Special order types such as Stop Loss (SL), Immediate or Cancel (IOC), and Disclosed Quantity (DQ) orders will not be allowed during the pre-open session.
Gold and Silver ETFs to be part of the pre-open session
Currently, ETFs do not participate in the pre-open session. Equity, debt, Gold, Silver, Liquid and Overnight ETFs all start trading only when the regular market opens at 9:15 AM.
From September 7, this will change for Gold and Silver ETFs.
Gold and silver continue to trade in international markets when Indian exchanges are closed. Their prices can therefore move significantly before trading in the corresponding ETFs starts in India.
To improve price discovery at the open, Gold and Silver ETFs will now be included in the pre-open session. Orders collected during this period will be used to determine an opening price before regular trading begins at 9:15 AM.
Other ETFs, including equity, debt, Liquid and Overnight ETFs, will continue to start trading at 9:15 AM.
The base price used to set ETF price bands is changing
ETFs have upper and lower price limits that determine the range within which they can trade during the day. These limits are calculated from a reference known as the base price.
Currently, the base price for equity, debt and commodity ETFs is their NAV from two trading days earlier, or T-2 NAV.
The problem is that a two-day-old NAV can become stale when the underlying asset moves sharply.
For example, suppose an ETF has a T-2 NAV of ₹100. With a 20% price band, it can trade between ₹80 and ₹120.
If the underlying asset rises sharply and the ETF is already trading around ₹119, it has only about ₹1 of room left before reaching its upper price limit, even if the asset it tracks continues to rise. The reverse can happen when the underlying asset falls sharply, and the ETF is close to its lower price limit.
This happened with Gold and Silver ETFs during the sharp moves in commodity prices earlier this year. Price bands based on T-2 NAV became inadequate for the ETFs to keep up with movements in their underlying assets, and exchanges temporarily moved to a more recent reference price.
From September 7, the base price will instead be the ETF’s closing market price from the previous trading day, calculated using the volume-weighted average price of trades during the last 30 minutes of trading.
If the ETF does not trade during those 30 minutes, its last traded price for the day will be used. If it does not trade at all on the previous day, the latest available closing NAV will be used.
This should keep price bands closer to where the ETF is actually trading and reduce situations where an old reference price restricts normal price movement.
ETF price bands are changing too
Along with changing the base price, the exchanges are moving away from the same fixed 20% price band for most ETFs.
From September 7:
Equity and debt ETFs, except Liquid and Overnight ETFs, will start with a price range of 10% above and below the base price. If the ETF reaches one side of this range, that side can be widened by another 5 percentage points after a cooling-off period, up to a maximum of 20% from the base price.
Gold and Silver ETFs will start with a 6% range above and below the base price. If required, the range can be widened by 3 percentage points at a time after a cooling-off period. If international gold or silver prices move significantly, exchanges can widen these limits further.
Liquid and Overnight ETFs will have a fixed 5% range above and below the base price.
The cooling-off period is generally 15 minutes. Trading does not stop completely during this period and can continue within the existing price range. During the last 30 minutes of the trading day, the cooling-off period is reduced to five minutes.

Trading from a phone often means moving between the chart, order window, orders, and positions while trying to keep an eye on price movement. On a smaller screen, these extra steps can make placing and managing trades cumbersome.
We’ve now brought Trade From Charts (TFC) to TradingView charts on the Kite app.
With TFC, you can place and modify orders, manage positions, check market depth, and switch between instruments without leaving the chart. You can also place orders at specific price levels, drag pending orders to modify them, use instant order placement, reverse positions, and more.
If you’re using ChartIQ, you can switch to TradingView in the app settings to use TFC. If you’ve not updated to the latest version of the Kite app, you can do it from the Google Play Store or the Apple App Store .
Here’s a quick look at what you can do.
For a full walkthrough on TFC, you can check out this video.
You can also watch this video in Hindi here .
Place and manage orders from the chart
The Buy and Sell buttons at the top of the chart show the best available ask and bid prices and let you place orders directly from the chart.
You can also place limit and stop-loss orders at specific price levels. Long-press the level where you want to place the order and choose the order type.
Once placed, pending orders are shown at their respective price levels on the chart. You can modify or cancel an order from there, or simply drag it to a different price level to change its price.
Place orders instantly
You can enable Instant Order Placement if you want to skip the order window and confirmation step. Once enabled, you can select the quantity directly on the chart and place an order with a tap. Instant placement also works when modifying orders, exiting or reversing positions, and for other supported actions on the chart.
Since this skips the regular confirmation step, check the quantity and other order settings before placing an order.
Manage positions from the chart
Open positions can be displayed directly on the chart along with their P&L, so you can track and manage them alongside the price movement. You can exit a position from the chart or use Reverse to close the existing position and place an order for the same quantity in the opposite direction.
Reversing a position requires sufficient available margin. If the required margin isn’t available, the reverse action won’t go through, and the existing position remains unchanged.
Orders, positions, and market depth in one panel
The panel at the bottom of the chart gives you quick access to Positions, Open Orders, and live Market Depth. You can modify or cancel orders and manage positions from here without separately opening the order book or Positions page.
You can also switch between the charts of instruments in which you have an order or position without going back to your watchlist.
Control what you see on the chart
You can customise the Trade From Charts experience from the TradingView chart settings.
You can show or hide the Buy and Sell buttons, orders, positions, and executions; turn Instant Order Placement and execution sounds on or off; choose how P&L is displayed; and control whether reverse buttons and extended price lines appear on the chart.
You can also choose how orders and positions are aligned on the chart. This lets you keep the chart as detailed or as clean as you prefer while trading.
Multiple charts and Compare
You can also use multiple chart layouts on the Kite app.
For example, if you’re trading an option, you can keep the option contract and its underlying stock or index open on the same screen.
The Compare option lets you compare the relative performance of different stocks or indices on the same chart. You can also save up to 10 customised chart layouts locally.
Trading from Charts feature is also available on TradingView charts on Kite web .
The post Introducing Trade from Charts (TFC) on Kite app appeared first on Z-Connect by Zerodha .

Nifty opened with an 83-point gap up at 23,202, ahead of the key FOMC meeting, as global equities consolidated while crude oil prices remained firm above $107 per barrel. Nifty eventually closed at 23,217.60, around 16 points above its opening level, after a highly volatile but largely directionless session.

In our latest episode of I n The Money by Zerodha , we break down what market depth and order flow charts actually show you — and what they don’t.
Market depth is a book of intentions: resting orders that may never get executed. Order flow looks at trades that have already happened and tries to measure buying and selling pressure through metrics like delta and cumulative delta.
But where do these numbers come from? Especially in India, where exchanges don’t explicitly tag which side crossed the spread, some of what you see is observed, while some is inferred.
In this edition, we explain how these tools work, how the numbers are constructed, and what they can actually tell you about the market.

In our latest episode of I n The Money by Zerodha , we break down what market depth and order flow charts actually show you — and what they don’t.
Market depth is a book of intentions: resting orders that may never get executed. Order flow looks at trades that have already happened and tries to measure buying and selling pressure through metrics like delta and cumulative delta.
But where do these numbers come from? Especially in India, where exchanges don’t explicitly tag which side crossed the spread, some of what you see is observed, while some is inferred.
In this edition, we explain how these tools work, how the numbers are constructed, and what they can actually tell you about the market.

Welcome to The Climate Brief’s newsletter, where we break down India’s BIGGEST climate stories in a way that feels personal and relatable.
If you’ve visited Bengaluru, chances are the first thing you noticed was the magical BLUE SKY. A very Windows-wallpaper kind of blue that you see on most days!
Have you wondered why? Since we recently celebrated the International Day of Clean Air for Blue Skies, we’re asking - why is the sky blue and why does it look bluer in some cities than others?
Why Are Skies Blue?
Sunlight looks white to us but it’s made up of a spectrum of colours - the 7 colours in the rainbow! In fact these are 7 waves of different wavelengths . Red is the longest, while blue and violet are the shortest.
Light travels from the sun and hits our atmosphere which is full of tiny gas molecules - much smaller than these light waves. So when sunlight comes in, the longer red and yellow waves pass straight through, but the shorter blue and violet waves interact with these molecules and get scattered in EVERY direction across the sky. This phenomenon is called Rayleigh Scattering and what we see is the scattered blue waves, which is why the sky appears blue to us.
Since violet has an even shorter wavelength than blue, shouldn’t the sky look violet? Violet DOES scatter more but there’s less of it in sunlight to begin with and our eyes are more sensitive to blue.
This explains sunsets too - When the Sun goes low in the sky, its light has to travel through a much longer stretch of Earth’s atmosphere to reach you. Along the way, more of the blue light gets scattered away. So by the time the light reaches your eyes, what’s left is more of the red and orange.
If the same sunlight is falling ACROSS India, why does the sky look SO different in different cities?
Why Some Cities Have Bluer Skies Than Others
THREE big factors: Altitude, Humidity, and Air Quality. And, in Bengaluru, all three factors work in its favour!
#1 Altitude: Bengaluru sits at 3,000 feet above sea level compared to Delhi which is at 700 feet . The higher you go, the lower the atmospheric pressure, which means fewer molecules for sunlight to travel through and interact with before it reaches your eyes. Under clear conditions, less atmosphere in the way can give you that DEEP blue sky. It’s not just Bengaluru - this is one reason why our HILLY states have skies that look magical - Shimla is above 7,000 feet; Leh at 11,000!
#2 Humidity: Bengaluru is one of the few major Indian cities with a relatively cool and moderate temperature and lower humidity.
Warmer air can hold more moisture! So on a really hot day, there’s more water vapor in the air and the heat increases dust, aerosols and other tiny particles into the atmosphere. The more moisture, dust and particles there are in the air, the more all colours get scattered, making the sky look more white or pale and grey. !
There’s even a small role our eyes play - On hot and bright days, there’s simply more light flooding the sky, so our eyes adjust to that brightness and so the same sky can end up looking whiter when it’s flooded with intense light!
Which is why a cool, clear Bengaluru morning can give you that gorgeous deep blue, while a hot April afternoon can look much more washed out.
#3 Air Quality: Over the last few decades, the air in our cities has progressively gotten worse, all thanks to human activities - Cars, construction, industries and everything else we keep putting into the air. Dust, smoke, vehicle emissions, construction, industrial pollution, crop burning. All of it adds particles to the atmosphere like dust, ash, and carbon soot.
These particles are bigger than the particles naturally found in clean air and they scatter all colours of light and hence the sky appears more white or pale grey. Some of these particles like soot end up absorbing light rather than reflecting it, giving it a grey tinge. And the more particles there are , the more they interfere with sunlight, making that deep blue sky look hazy/pale/grey.
CPCB data shows that last winter, Bengaluru averaged 39 micrograms per cubic metre of PM2.5, compared to 48 of Mumbai and 163 in Delhi. That’s more than four times Bengaluru’s average!! So the skies of course look different.
But, a blue sky is not a clean-air certificate! How blue the sky looks depends on several things as we’ve discussed already. So even two cities with similar air quality can have very different-looking skies.
While Bengaluru is certainly not pollution-free, it is, in a way, blessed by its geography and climate and it has conditions that favour those beautiful blue skies. But if we keep filling the atmosphere with more and more pollution, we risk losing that advantage too.
Sept 7 is celebrated as the International Day of Blue Skies and it’s a great reminder of how beautiful blue skies are and what we risk losing if we don’t act to protect them soon enough. The pale grey skies that seem to have become the new normal are a visible warning that the air we breathe is killing us.
A blue sky should not be something we celebrate but something we and future generations should be able to take for granted.
Until next week,
The Climate Brief

Hello, readers!
If you’re ever travelled to Bengaluru, chances are you’ve passed through the Majestic bus stand - the city’s bustling transport hub. But here’s a fun fact: It was once a lake!
Yes, a lake. And no, Majestic wasn’t the only landmark built over a lake. In this week’s newsletter, we’re taking a closer look at how Bengaluru — once the City of Lakes — ended up building over them and what it’s cost us in the process.
How Bengaluru Built Over Its Lakes
Bangalore sits at an elevation of 3,000 ft and has no major perennial rivers flowing through it. For centuries, the city relied on man-made lakes to serve as stores of water.
The earliest systems date back to the 16th century when Kempe Gowda built an interconnected network of lakes engineered to take water from higher elevations to lower ground. These lakes primarily served as sources of water for irrigation and drinking.
At its peak, Bengaluru had 1,400+ lakes and water bodies, which became the city’s lifeline. But over the last few decades, the network disappeared. The number of water bodies fell from around 1,452 water bodies in the 1800s to about 285 lakes by the 1970s and 194 by 2016.
Today, BBMP data records 202 lakes, out of which only 183 are functional, while 19 disappeared altogether.
What happened, though?
#1 Rapid Expansion: Bengaluru grew massively from an industrial city to the tech capital it is today. The city’s population went up from 16 lakh people in 1971 to 1.2 crore today and the built-up area increased by 1,078% between 1973 and 2025 .
This lead to problem #2 Encroachments: As the city grew, so did its demand for water. And once pipes and pumps allowed water from the Cauvery to reach the city, , the dependence on lakes was reduced.
At the same time, as more people came in, they needed more buildings for homes and offices, bus stations, schools and what not. And lake beds (which now looked like a waste of space) became PRIME spots of construction.
Kanteerava Sports Stadium stands on the Sampangi Lake
The Majestic bus terminal was once Dharmambudhi Lake
KR Market stands on the former Siddikatte Lake
HBR Layout is built around what was once Hennur Lake
Bengaluru’s football stadium stands on the former Shoolay Lake.
Many other historic lakes were converted by the Bangalore Development Authority (BDA) into residential layouts, playgrounds, and government buildings.
Fun fact: The word ‘Sandra’ comes from the word ‘Samudra’ and refers to a large water body in Kannada. So all localities that have ‘Sandra’ in their name like Byrasandra would have been around a lake, many of which have now been built over.
Of Bengaluru’s 200 recorded lakes, around 949 acres are encroached and 19 lakes have been converted for urban infrastructure. Surveys have found how 88% of the lakes in Bengaluru Urban were encroached upon, 90% in Bengaluru Rural. Finally,
#3 Pollution: Since lakes became less important as a source of water, they became places where the city’s WASTEWATER ended up.
Today, untreated sewage, industrial effluents and other chemicals flow into many of Bengaluru’s lakes. In April 2026, the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board tested 93 of the 183 functioning lakes under GBA and found that 65% of the lakes were classified as under the ‘worst water-quality category’ due to lake pollution.
Why Lakes Are Important
#1: Flood buffers: During monsoons, lakes act as natural SPONGES, holding excess rainwater and slowing its flow into surrounding neighbourhoods. Because Bengaluru’s lakes were designed as a cascading system, water could move from higher to lower elevation via interconnected lakes and raja kaluves, or stormwater channels.
But the lake also needs SPACE to hold that water - Over time, silt, organic matter and waste accumulate at the bottom, making the lake shallow and reducing its water-holding capacity. Less storage means less space for rainwater, increasing the risk of waterlogging and flooding. Reports have already linked this to increased flooding in Bengaluru .
#2: Groundwater recharge: Lakes give rainwater somewhere to sit before it slowly seeps into the ground and replenishes aquifers. But when lakes are built over, there is concrete where the lake once was, water is not able to seep into the ground , and the aquifers don’t get recharged! This is especially important for Bengaluru where groundwater is fast depleting.
#3: Water storage: Considering the worsening water crisis in the city every summer - Some experts believe lakes can mitigate this impact. Even though they cannot fully meet the demands of a 1.2 crore population, they can reduce our dependence on Cauvery water and on borewells.
#4: Biodiversity: Healthy lakes provide habitat for flora and fauna, including fish, plants, insects and birds - including migratory species.
Kaikondrahalli Lake, for instance, supports around 70 species of migratory birds . But when sewage enters a lake, the excess nutrients can trigger algal blooms, which reduce oxygen levels in the water and can eventually cause fish to die.
News reports have already shown instances where fish kills have been reported in lakes including Kundalahalli and Seetharampalya.
#5: Livelihoods & communities: Lakes have historically supported livelihoods of communities via fishing and livestock. More importantly, they act as a public space which can be used for walking, birdwatching, and other recreational activities.
Can we Revive Bengaluru’s Lakes?
The good news is, the story of Bengaluru’s lakes is not a hopeless one. In recent years, the city corporation, government, CSOs and citizen-led groups have been working together to revive Bengaluru’s lakes.
Since April, the Greater Bengaluru Authority is taking up rejuvenation work across several lakes, including Hebbal, Nagawara and Ulsoor - which is why you’ve probably been seeing some of these lakes looking dry.
At Ulsoor, the lake has been emptied for the first time in nearly 25 years. In August, the North City Corporation announced a Rs 50-crore plan to restore 15 lakes through desilting and sewage diversion.
At Kithaganur Lake, desilting, clearing feeder channels and other restoration work has increased its water-holding capacity by 22%.
One of the main interventions is desilting, where layers of accumulated silt, waste and other material are removed from the lake bed, increasing the space available to store water. But desilting alone will not work! Here’s what will though:
#1: We need to first STOP encroaching on the Rajakaluves (stormwater drains), then restore the broken connections and work on rebuilding the channels connecting these lakes.
#2: We need to stop sewage from entering the system by identifying pollution sources and separating sewage from stormwater before it reaches the lake.
#3: We need a more tailored and science-based approach to restore the lake’s ecology, rather than simply focusing on how the lake looks. Every lake has different characteristics, so restoration should start with a detailed assessment of the lake. This also means solutions should be centred around the needs of the communities living around it.
But what can YOU do? Start with the lake closest to you, find out what’s happening to it and whether it’s polluted or encroached and join a citizen group working to revive these lakes!

Welcome to The Climate Brief’s newsletter, where we break down India’s BIGGEST climate stories in a way that feels personal and relatable.
Happy Monday, readers!
I’m sure you’ve heard of the famous Chilika Lake, one of Odisha’s iconic landscapes. Tucked away on the northern edge of this lake is Mangalajodi, a popular birdwatching destination.
But would you believe me if I said that two decades ago, Mangalajodi was known as bird poaching hotspot? Today, the wetland is a thriving ecotourism destination, attracting thousands of visitors and lakhs of migratory birds every winter. Its transformation from a poaching hotspot to a community-led conservation success story offers some important lessons about protecting India’s wetlands.
From Poachers to Protectors
The Chilika Lake is Asia’s largest coastal lagoon and India’s first Ramsar site. The area of the lake varies between 1,165 to 900 sq km depending on the time of the year and is so big that it is spread across different districts of Odisha.
One such path along the Northwestern edge of the lake is where you’ll find Mangalajodi - a nearly 1000-hectare wetland about 1.5 hours from Bhubaneswar.
Unlike the wide and open water of Chilika, Mangalajodi is made up of narrow waterways, tall grasses and shallow pools of water - all connected to the lake.
Every winter, this wetland houses over 3 lakh birds, including warblers, p acific golden plovers and bar-tailed godwits . Many fly thousands of kilometres from Siberia, Mongolia, Russia and the Himalayas to spend the winter here – making Mangalajodi a paradise for bird lovers. But 26 years ago, Mangalajodi had only 5,000 birds!
The wetland gets its name from the nearby Mangalajodi village, which is home to a large fishing community that has depended on Chilika for generations for food and livelihoods. And for many families, hunting and poaching of birds were the only source of income at one time.
By the 1990s, bird poaching became more common as there was increased demand for bird meat. In fact this was a dish served in restaurants nearby….so hunting became a commercial activity. At the same time, the wetland was facing pressure due to increased use of pesticides and pollution .
Since Mangalajodi was part of the larger Chilika ecosystem (and this became a Ramsar site in 1981), conservation efforts began! Though the Chilika Development Authority was formed in 1991, real change began only when organisations started working directly with the communities around the wetland.
So how did the wetland transform in two decades?
#1 Turning Poachers Into Protectors: Since poaching was a source of income, asking the community to merely stop hunting wouldn’t have worked. Instead, local fisherfolk and poachers were trained as naturalists and wetland patrollers because of the existing knowledge they already had and tourism offered them an alternative source of income. As visitors increased, former hunters became birding guides, boatmen and tourism organisers. This showed them that there was more benefit protecting the wetland than hunting.
By 2010, Mangalajodi was formalised as an ecotourist spot - leading to the creation of the Mangalajodi Ecotourism Trus t. In short, the wetland became a local business model around tourism supporting the livelihoods of these families. Today, more than 100 villagers are involved in conserving the wetland and its birds,
And the best way to measure the impact is in the birds who have returned! While there are no EXACT stats on Mangalajodi, bird populations within the wider Chilika ecosystem have more than tripled since 2011, while the 2025 Chilika bird census recorded 11 lakh birds across 196 species.
Why Are Wetlands So Important?
Wetlands are places where water covers the land either throughout the year or during seasons. They can be lakes, mangroves or marshes or even smaller water bodies. You’ve probably seen one without realising!
Mangalajodi is just ONE of the thousands of wetlands spread across India. As of 2024, India has over 1,300 wetlands, with 113 recognised as wetlands of national importance. But just like our rivers and lakes, wetlands across India are disappearing or being degraded.
In fact, India has lost nearly one-third of its natural wetlands over the last four decades . While some have been drained out, others have been polluted by sewage, plastic and industrial waste. And this is particularly worrying in our cities where wetlands are being treated as empty pieces of land that can be built over or used as dumping grounds!
Why does any of this matter? Beyond aesthetics, wetlands are described as the ‘ kidneys’ of the landscape because they can help regulate water and filter pollutants. But that is just the tip of the iceberg, here are 5 reasons why you need to care:
#1 Acts as a flood buffer: Think of a wetland like a giant sponge and so when there is heavy rainfall, it can hold excess water and release it slowly, reducing the amount of water rushing into surrounding areas all at once. This is why wetlands like the Pallikaranai Marshland in Chennai are so important for a city that faces floods very often.
#2 They store clean water: As water moves through a wetland, plants and sediments can trap some pollutants and excess nutrients, helping improve water quality. Wetlands can also help recharge groundwater by allowing water to slowly seep into the ground. This is important because our cities are increasingly becoming more drought prone and wetlands can come to the rescue!
#3 They support biodiversity: Like in Mangalajodi, its waters, grasses provide food and shelter to migratory birds and other species. Across India, wetlands provide important breeding, feeding and resting grounds for birds, fish, amphibians, insects and other wildlife.
#4 Supports Livelihoods & Tourism: Millions of people depend on wetlands for their livelihoods, through activities like fishing, farming and tourism.
#5 And above all, they are carbon sinks: Wetlands can store large amounts of carbon for a long period of time making them crucial in tackling the big global warming fight
But let’s go back to Mangalajodi and what it teaches us: If we want to save India’s wetlands, we need to think about the people who depend on them first.
Until Next Time,
Team Climate Brief

Welcome to The Climate Brief’s newsletter, where we break down India’s BIGGEST climate stories in a way that feels personal and relatable.
Hello, gentle readers!
Just as the weekend ends, I’m sure you’ve had a relaxed weekend with some good for, and if you’re anything like us, there’s a very good chance that RICE was part of your meal in some form or the other (Biryani? Khichdi, or perhaps, even curd rice?)
It’s fair to say that it’s impossible to picture Indian cuisine without steaming, hot rice! But would you believe me if I told you that rice is a crop that’s actually under threat? In this week’s Climate Brief, we’re discussing about RICE — a crop that is both a victim and perpetrator of climate change.
The History of Rice
Nearly 60% of India’s population eat rice as their primary cereal and it makes up 40% of our total foodgrain production. Evidence shows rice growing at Lahuradewa (present-day UP ) dating back to the 7th millennium BCE.
For most of history, rice was just one of many crops, until the 1960s and 70s, where India was struggling to produce enough food. This led to the Green Revolution and the rise of fertilisers, irrigation techniques, leading to higher yields and productivity for farmers.
Between 1969-70 and today, the area under paddy grew by over 36% , yields roughly tripled and production quadrupled. And in 2025, India produced 150 million tonnes of rice , crossing China to become the world’s LARGEST producer of rice .
But the Green Revolution also changed what kind of rice we grew. Farmers switched to high-yielding varieties, and slowly, traditional varieties begin to disappear, even though India is estimated to have 75,000 to 100,000 traditional rice varieties .
There’s Basmati from Punjab and Haryana, Gobindobhog from West Bengal and Palakkadan Matta, the red rice from Kerala, alongside modern varieties like Sona Masuri and Ponni rice. Many of these traditional varieties were better adapted to the conditions in which they were grown, making them more resilient to things like floods and droughts, while also offering higher nutritional value than some of the high-yielding varieties that are grown today.
The Climate Cost of Rice
Let’s first understand how rice is grown. Traditionally, it’s grown in two stages - Farmers first raise young rice seedlings in a nursery for 25-30 days and once the monsoon arrives , these are transplanted into fields, often by hand.
From sowing to harvest, a rice crop takes 90-120 days, depending on variety and where it’s grown. And for much of the growing season, rice grows in wet/flooded conditions as it helps control weeds.
Studies shows that 16% of India’s rice-growing land is under continuous flooding and this has FOUR big climate costs:
#1 Rice is a THIRSTY crop: Depending on where and how it’s grown, producing one kg of rice needs 3,000 to 4,000 litres of water and this comes from monsoon rains, groundwater reserves and irrigation. This becomes a problem when we grow rice in places that don’t naturally receive enough rainfall to support paddy cultivation.
For example, Punjab receives much less rainfall than needed for paddy cultivation… so farmers have been increasingly dependent on irrigation and groundwater. Years of extraction has led to groundwater depletion in the state.
# 2 Methane Emissions: When rice fields remain flooded, there’s little oxygen in the soil. This creates the perfect conditions for microbes to break down organic matter and release methane - a greenhouse gas more potent than CO2.
Irrigated paddy fields in India release around 3.9 million tonnes of methane every year, making them one of the world’s major methane hotspots, Methane in rice contributes to 23% of India’s agri emissions. Globally, GHG from paddy has nearly doubled since the 1960s.
#3 Excessive use of fertilisers: Fertilisers have played an important role in increasing rice yields, but excessive nitrogen application can also contribute to Nitrous Oxide emissions, and also contaminate soil and surrounding water bodies.
#4 Pollution: And finally , paddy stubble burning in North India causes severe seasonal air pollution by releasing toxic smoke directly into the air. Estimates suggest a total of 620 million tons of crop residue is generated annually in India.
But now comes the OTHER side of the story - Climate change is destroying RICE production.
#1 Erratic weather & Drought: Remember the 90-120 day window we spoke about? A farmer has to ensure that he completes the process - from sowing to harvesting - within the time period. In regions where the source of water is rain, the sowing can happen only after rain starts and the region has to keep getting rain regularly to ensure the fields don’t dry up.
But over the last few years, monsoon rains are much harder to predict. And this year, El Nino has MADE it worse. This kharif season, 397 of India’s 741 districts recorded below-normal rainfall and p addy sowing is down to 421.82 lakh hectares , from 438 lakh hectares last year. And states like Tamil Nadu and Karnataka are already facing the brunt of this.
#2 Too much Rain, All at Once: Instead of steady rainfall over longer periods, we’re now witnessing shorter but more intense bursts! And when this comes at the wrong time, it can flood fields and damage standing crops. During the 2025 Punjab floods, 3.47 lakh acres of paddy farms were destroyed
#3 Heat: Studies estimate that India could lose 6.6% of its rice yield for every 1°C rise in global temperature, which is more than THREE times higher than earlier projections. In fact, in Japan in 2023, El Nino significantly impacted yields and was one of the factors which led to rice price hike.
What’s The Solution?
The good news is, this is not a hopeless story. And no, the answer isn’t to stop growing rice… The question is - Can we grow in a smarter and sustainable manner?
#1 Change HOW we grow rice: The flooding problem can be tackled through methods like Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD), where farmers let the field dry out before watering it again. This cuts water use by up to 30% and methane emissions by 48%, without reducing yield.
Then there’s Direct-Seeded Rice (DSR), where instead of growing seedlings in a nursery and transplanting them into a flooded field, farmers sow seeds directly into the soil. And this again means less water, less emissions, and less labour! This uses 25-30% less water compared to traditional cultivation methods. This is already picking up in states like Punjab, Haryana, and Odisha.
#2 Reduce Fertiliser Use: While a complete ban on fertilisers may seem unrealistic at present, we can reduce usage… essentially using just the right amount that’s required for your soil. And some farmers are already going back to older methods and adopting natural farming - swapping chemicals for natural inputs like green manure and bio-fertilsers and other alternatives.
#3 Preserve Traditional Varieties: Many of them have higher nutritional value and better resilience that means better chances of surviving floods and drought. So preserving these and moving back to them is a great option! A great example is Seeraga Samba, which has higher fiber content and great nutritional value (And tastes great in Biryani too)
Now you’re probably like - “Okay, I’m not a farmer. What can I do?” You have MORE power than you think:
If traditional or local rice varieties are available and affordable in stores near you, choose them! Creating market demand is the first step in a long chain that will eventually incentivise more farmers to choose these varieties.
Look for chemical-free varieties of rice; They have better health benefits too.
And mix it up - Add millets and other grains to your plate because a diverse plate is always great to have.
Until next time,
Team Climate Brief

The rupee has spent the last year doing the one thing it is guaranteed to do eventually, and everybody has watched it do so with a specific number in mind.
It was at ₹68 eight years ago and ₹85 last year; it ran from ₹89 up to ₹97 before settling back to ₹95, and every move drew the same headline question: when does it hit ₹100?
The RBI, for its part, has fired what Ananth Narayan calls a bazooka. This includes a subsidised swap window for FCNR(B) deposits and external commercial borrowings, carrying a subsidy of roughly 3% a year, designed to pull fifty to seventy billion dollars into the system over a few months. He means the word as a description rather than a criticism. His larger point is that the number everyone is watching is the least interesting thing in the frame.
Ananth Narayan spent most of his career on the other side of the screen: a currency and rates trader, latterly at Standard Chartered, before he took what he cheerfully describes as a midlife crisis into teaching at the SP Jain Institute of Management and then into three years as a Whole Time Member at SEBI, a term that ended in October 2025. He now writes a column in Business Standard ( which we have also republished on Subtext ).
He describes himself throughout this conversation as an armchair professor, mostly as a way of noting that he no longer has to be right about anything by Monday morning. So, on a Varsity Live session with a full audience, Nithin Sasikumar and Pranav Agarwal sat down with him after an earlier session in which he had walked the room through how money is actually created in a banking system.
He opens provocatively by telling the room that the level of a currency does not matter, and then spends the next hour on the one channel through which it does.
He walks us through the concept of reflexivity (which was defined by legendary trader George Soros) and how it informs the way self-fulfilling prophecies in currency markets come true, how gross FDI hit a record in the same years that net FDI fell to nearly nothing, why India has 15 crore equity investors and almost no corporate bond market, why India is the only major country that taxes foreign investors at source, and what three years inside SEBI taught him about the two kinds of error a regulator cannot avoid simultaneously.
The chain he keeps returning to runs like this: India holds down returns on debt, savings pile into equity instead, Indian assets get priced beyond what foreign investors will pay for them. The currency number that everyone watches comes at the end of that sequence rather than the start.
The last half-hour belongs to the audience, who asked the big-picture questions: how are India’s GDP numbers really calculated, whether we can ever stop importing key components from China, and what Trump is doing to the dollar.
Some of the things he said stuck with us. We’re sharing eight of them here.
On why the level of a currency does not matter
The rupee is the most watched number in Indian macro, and it is watched almost entirely as a scoreboard — a running tally of whether the country is winning. Ananth’s starting position is that this is a category error, and he opens with it deliberately, knowing exactly how the clip will travel. A currency is not a verdict on an economy. It is an output of one, and a fairly downstream output at that.
“Truth be told, levels of currencies do not matter. I know this will excite a lot of things if you just play this part out, saying, you know, levels don’t matter. But take Japan, for instance, or take any other country, China, for instance. What ultimately matters is how our standard of living is looking like, what our per capita income is looking like, what the GDP growth is looking like, what the capital formation in the country is looking like, and therefore what the prospects for the future are looking like. The currency is simply a number which kind of navigates through all of this — capital flows, savings, trade flows, and all of that. Ultimately, what should matter is how we feel. Is our purchasing power going up? Is our wealth going up? Is our income going up? That’s what matters.”
On self-fulfilling expectations in the economy
Having said levels don’t matter, he spends the rest of the conversation explaining the one channel through which they do. If enough people believe the rupee is heading to 100, their behaviour changes in ways that push it there. Importers pull purchases forward. Exporters sitting on dollars abroad wait. Anyone thinking of bringing capital in decides to bring it in later, at a better rate. None of this is irrational, and all of it is self-confirming. The name for it comes from a legendary trader who is also quite infamous for reasons other than trading — George Soros:
“He [George Soros] calls it — I think the book was called Alchemy of Finance — and he talks about reflexivity, where we tend to think as economists and as professors of markets as being determined by fundamentals. Our inflation is here, our growth is here, our GDP prospects are the following, therefore currency should be here. So George Soros said, there is something called reflexivity, where if I push the market far enough, it will start to determine the fundamentals rather than the other way around. So reflexivity is something you cannot ignore. So if the fear becomes of an uncontrolled spiral of the rupee, it can go to a level where it impacts fundamentals, stops capital flows from coming in, hastens imports and delays exports. So managing that is extremely important.”
On when the rupee actually gets to 100
Nithin asked the question the episode is named after, twice, and got an answer that comes in two parts. The first part is arithmetic and slightly deflating: in the forward market, where prices are set almost entirely by the gap between rupee and dollar interest rates, 100 has already happened. The two-year forward is through it. The second part is about what the RBI has just signalled it is willing to spend to stop the spot rate from getting there on a schedule set by sentiment.
“So if it’s about three rupees of forward premia, give or take, one year forward is already about 98. Two year forward crosses 100. Okay? Having said that, do I think 100 is going to happen in a hurry? Personal view, again — if you make money off it, remember me. If you lose money on it, this conversation never happened. It’s all AI. I don’t think RBI will let 100 happen in a hurry. The whole point of firing this bazooka was not to see 100 happen tomorrow. Unless dollar strengthens dramatically, Asian currencies collapse, and we are going in sync with the rest of the market, then it might allow it to happen. But I think clearly this bazooka has been fired to keep a lid on dollar-rupee. So I don’t think it’ll happen in two years’ time, but maybe five years’ time, yeah, sure, it’ll probably go there.”
On the rate cuts nobody connected to the currency
This is the sharpest thing he says, and he says it to an audience question rather than to the hosts. Between them, the MPC cut 125 basis points, the RBI bought ₹10 lakh crore of bonds through open market operations, paid a large dividend to the government, and held liquidity in surplus so short-term rates stayed low. Each step was individually defensible; inflation averaged 2% through FY26. His objection is not that the rate cuts were wrong. It is that the trilemma every macro student learns in their first week — you cannot have an open capital account, a managed currency and an independent monetary policy at the same time — was never brought into the room.
“So, you know, I was often asked this question, including on TV: should RBI use interest rates as a defence of the currency, right? This was in the June policy and so on and so forth. That’s a straw man question. It’s like saying, should you use a nuclear bomb now that the war is being lost, or whatever, right? The real debate to have, and the real thing to acknowledge or have a debate about, is that I think low interest rates during the course of FY25 and definitely FY26 had a big role to play in reducing capital flows and in creating weakness in the rupee. Now, it might be perfectly the right thing to do. All I’m saying, let’s debate it. If you look at the MPC minutes, if you look at the debates that happened with the folks in the RBI, there was never a debate on: did low interest rates have an offsetting impact on capital flows and currency markets?”
On why cheap money makes Indian assets too expensive to buy
The FDI numbers look contradictory. Gross FDI hit a record ninety-one billion dollars, and net FDI has been close to zero. Ananth’s reading is that both facts have the same cause, and it isn’t foreign disinterest. Suppress returns on fixed income through low policy rates and punitive interest taxation, and Indian savings have nowhere to go but equity — listed, unlisted, AIFs, family offices, all of it. Valuations rise. Existing foreign investors get excellent exits and new ones stay away, while Indian companies with cash discover that everything abroad is cheaper. The mechanism is easiest to see in a specific set of listings.
“Similarly for FPI and FDI in the listed space as well. Take the case of some of the Korean majors which did IPOs in India of their Indian subsidiaries. They were getting valuations in India seven or eight times higher than what they were getting in their own home country, right? So you had companies where India accounted for 5% of the global sales, but after the IPO happened of their Indian subsidiary, that Indian subsidiary accounted for 40% of their market capitalisation. Of course, I will issue stock. So unfortunately, what has happened is, I think a lot of money has flowed into our equity markets, both listed as well as unlisted, which makes it easier for foreign investors to exit than come in.”
On the tax that turns foreign capital away
India taxes foreign investors on capital gains at source. Almost nobody else does — the OECD model, and the practice of the US, UK, Japan and Singapore, is to tax the investor where they live. India’s justification was that double-taxation treaties would make the investor whole.
Ananth walks through four separate ways that fails: entities with zero capital gains liability at home have nothing to offset against; a fund’s withholding provision inside a NAV is not a tax receipt any foreign revenue authority will credit; gains computed in rupees can be losses in dollars, and are taxed anyway; and every single sale needs a Big Four certificate before the money can leave. He is careful to say fixing it would not by itself bring money in.
“So in reality, this is a huge negative for India. I’m not saying that if you remove this tomorrow, money will flow in — please don’t misunderstand. But it is definitely a negative which prohibits or inhibits money coming into India. And as a country which is starved of capital, as a country which needs capital formation, we have no business turning off capital and putting off capital like this. In a competitive global world where everybody is fighting for that pie of global savings for capital formation, we cannot afford to be outliers saying, ‘Oh no, you have to play by my rules to come into my country.’ You have to make sure that you’re at least on par with the rest of the world. So one thing that I’ve been kind of screaming about and losing a lot of hair about is exactly this, which is: can we please go into a residence-based taxation model, where foreigners do not pay tax here, they pay whatever tax they’re liable to pay in the overseas market.”
On why India has no corporate bond market
He answered this one by asking the room for a show of hands. Almost everybody had equity or mutual funds in their demat account. Roughly a tenth of that number had a corporate bond. The standard reading of this gap is that Indian retail investors have not yet been educated into credit, and that the fix is more product design and more regulation. Ananth thinks the demand is missing for a much simpler reason, and he reaches for fixed maturity plans — a genuinely popular fixed-income product that existed until the 2023 tax change and then stopped existing.
“But by and large, that was a good product, which was a fixed income product, and that innovation came because people demanded it. If you suppress that market, you will not get demand for that product. It’s very similar to saying, ‘I put a price control on a product,’ and then you’re saying, ‘Why is this market not growing?’ Arey, who the hell wants to supply at that price? So if you allow the corporate market, the debt markets, to be freer, I can guarantee you it’ll grow by itself. It will not require RBI and SEBI to break their heads and come with new regulations. You yourself will come up with new products which will cater to the demand coming from the genuine retail.”
On the two errors a regulator cannot minimise at once
Pranav asked what it is like to be the person actually holding the pen — to be sitting in the capital markets regulator’s chair in the years when an avalanche of household savings arrived, and to have to decide in real time which risks are catastrophes and which are just experiments.
Ananth’s frame is borrowed from statistics. A type I error is the disaster that happens on your watch, while a type II error is the good thing that never happens because you regulated it out of existence. Statistics says you trade one for the other. Regulation, he argues, is not statistics.
“But type I errors are when a disaster happens. So when a Harshad Mehta happens, or when a massive fraud happens, or a scam of some kind happens, you know, something like a Rajesh Exports happens — that’s a type I error for a regulator. And regulators hate type I errors, because that’s the time all of you will wake up and say, ‘What the hell were you doing?’ So none of us like to hear that, right? So for us, we are petrified of any type I errors. If there is a cybersecurity breach tomorrow, and God forbid, if all the data available in the depositories is made available in the dark web tomorrow, can you imagine what kind of a type I error that would be? So that is something which keeps us awake at night, right? At the same time, in our zeal to prevent type I errors, if we come with loads of regulations — you know, hundreds of pages of regulations saying, ‘Thou shall not do this, and thou shall not do this, and thou shall do this’ — then we make life extremely difficult for the good people to do capital formation, right?”

For about three years after the pandemic, India was the trade everyone wanted. China looked impossible to invest in from a returns standpoint, the US was fighting inflation, and India was the only large economy that seemed to be compounding quietly in the background. Indian small caps doubled and foreign money poured in. The story wrote itself.
Then, sometime around September 2024, the parade began to halt.
Roughly $50 billion of foreign portfolio money has left Indian equities since, the rupee has slid, and the same commentators who called India the only game in town now talk about it as a value trap with a demographic clock running out.
Arvind Chari has spent that entire cycle on the other side of the table. He is chief investment strategist at Q India UK, an affiliate of Quantum Advisors, where he has worked since 2004 — first in macro, fixed income and credit, then building the gold ETF and the multi-asset funds, and for the last five years as chief investment officer. Most of his job now involves sitting in rooms in London, Hong Kong and Singapore with pension funds and sovereign wealth funds, arguing about how much of their money should be in India. He also writes on LinkedIn, in his Financial Express column, and on the Quantum blog.
Bhuvan has been reading him for years, and wanted to have this conversation because the noise had become deafening in both directions. They spoke about why India keeps getting slotted into investment themes it doesn’t fit, what the country’s actual growth rate has been since 1980 and why that number has barely moved through wars, assassinations, coalitions and single-party majorities, the arithmetic of the capital gains tax on foreign investors, why Indian corporates aren’t building factories, whether manufacturing can still create jobs in an age of automation, and what it would take to make a self-described India optimist give up.
We’re sharing six of the many insightful things that stuck with us.
On the themes India keeps getting slotted into
Foreign capital does not really allocate to countries. It allocates to stories, and India has been assigned a new one roughly every five years — BRIC, then Fragile Five, then TINA, then China Plus One, and now, in a market obsessed with AI, nothing at all. Each label arrives with money attached and leaves with money attached, and the round trip has very little to do with what actually happened inside the Indian economy over that period. Arvind’s point is that the damage isn’t the volatility; it’s that thematic framing makes investors put the wrong money into the wrong things at the wrong time.
“In 2003, ‘4, ‘5, India was BRIC: Brazil, Russia, India, China. You could not find four different countries put into a bucket. It felt as a good idea and a good story, but people started investing based on that theme. During that time, I wrote that it was considered India’s birthright to grow at 9%. That was what the assumption was. And when you make those assumptions, you also make wrong capital allocation decisions. You saw money coming into Indian real estate, money coming into greenfield infra, money coming into Indian small caps — foreign investor money. First time you’re allocating to India, and you’re taking the highest risk profile. And of course, when the Lehman collapse happened, investors lost capital. They forget about getting lower returns, they actually lost capital.”
On what India actually is
The most useful thing in the conversation is also the least dramatic: a number. Since 1980 — the point at which the Indian state stopped being actively hostile to the private sector — real GDP growth has averaged 6.3%. Arvind’s argument is that this number is remarkably insensitive to everything commentators spend their time arguing about. It survived the 1991 reforms, the Vajpayee years, UPA, the 2013 taper tantrum, demonetisation, GST and COVID. If you build your expectations off 6.3% rather than off whatever theme is currently in circulation, you get a return framework that is both boring and achievable — and you stop being disappointed.
“Since then, the average real GDP growth is 6.3%. And you can take any period in that — you had booms and busts, you’ve had wars and peacetime, you had high oil prices, you had low oil prices, you had political instability, you had assassinations, you had stability, you had strong governments, you had weak governments, you had coalition, you had single party. It hasn’t mattered. That average has remained that. It’s not dramatically fallen to 5%, it’s not gone above 7% on a sustainable basis. So if you assume that Indian real GDP growth will be 6.5% and nominal GDP will be 10, 11%, and typically earnings of companies will compound at one or two percentage points higher than average nominal GDP growth, and you can add another 1 or 2% alpha — your return framework is between 13 and 15%. That’s been the outcome, and that has been the expectation. And if you have that expectation, which is a fairly healthy global rate of return, you will not be disappointed.”
On the arithmetic of the capital gains tax
India charges foreign investors capital gains tax on Indian securities. Almost no other country does — you typically pay in your home jurisdiction instead. The domestic argument for keeping it is a fairness argument, and it is not a stupid one. Arvind’s case against it is not about fairness at all; it is about what the tax does to the hurdle rate. Once you stack a 20% capital gains tax on top of two to three percent of annual rupee depreciation, a healthy rupee return turns into an unremarkable dollar return, and India has to work substantially harder to clear a bar that its competitors don’t face.
“If your expected rate of return from Indian equities is, say, thirteen, fourteen percent in INR terms — typically the Indian rupee depreciates against the US dollar between two and a half and three percent. So that thirteen to fifteen percent, you reduce by another two or three percent for the rupee. You’re now left with, say, ten, eleven, twelve percent. On that, if there is a 20% capital gains tax, that takes away another one and a half to two percentage points. So you’re now in single-digit dollar returns — between seven, eight, nine percent. Now, that is available in the global world. Predictable double digits is not easily available, but predictable single-digit returns in dollar terms is available. So the required threshold rate of return for investing in Indian public equities has gone up by about one and a half, two percentage points. Instead of India getting money at 12, 13, 14% expected rate of return, India has to deliver 15, 16% to counter that capital gains tax, which is not there in any other country.”
On why Indian companies aren’t building
The standard explanation for India’s missing private capex cycle is a vibes-based one: Indian promoters have gone soft, the kids want to run family offices instead of factories. Arvind doesn’t buy it. Firms build when they can see demand and earn a return above their cost of capital, and if they aren’t building, the honest place to look is demand — domestic demand that is weaker than the headline suggests, and export demand that Indian companies have almost entirely failed to capture. The composition of world trade has shifted under India’s feet over the last decade, from resources to electronics, chips, EVs and garments, and India has close to nothing in most of those categories.
“If you look at the top five globally traded export commodities, it is no longer the resources that were there in the previous decade. When China was growing and importing all resources, the minings and the metals — those were the big drivers. In the last 10 years, it has predominantly been electronics and electronic components and consumer durables, memory and chips and semiconductors, auto including EV, ready-made apparels and garments. And take a look at Indian companies — we don’t have a single large Indian company or set of Indian companies who’ve been able to cater to that. We don’t have a large EV manufacturer or exporter. We don’t have anything in semiconductors and memory chips. We don’t have much on electronics and components. And apparel — if you look at our textile policies that we’ve had for so many years, we don’t have any major share. Vietnam and Bangladesh have taken a significant share of that. So if you’re an Indian corporate and you don’t have the confidence or the capability to compete in the global world with a product at a cost that is competitive — then how do you put capex?”
On whether manufacturing can still create the jobs
India’s manufacturing share of GDP has gone from around 18% in the 1980s to roughly 13% now, and the conventional reading is that India skipped the step every rich country climbed. Bhuvan put the harder version of the question: if the economists who spent careers arguing for manufacturing-led development are now saying that door has closed, and automation is coming for whatever is left behind it, what employs the enormous number of Indians entering the workforce every year? Arvind’s answer inverts the premise — manufacturing was never the big employer people remember it being, and the thing most at risk from automation is the factory floor, not the service desk.
“Services will actually create way more jobs than manufacturing, because the manufacturing of 25, 30 years ago and the manufacturing of today is very different. Today you have automated robotic — even in India, there are so many of these completely zero-manned, completely automated robotic manufacturing plants. And manufacturing was never a very large share of employment anyway. It could have been a large share of GDP as a value add, but not a very large share of employment, especially as we’ve become automated and technology enabled. And that’s actually going to increase. AI automation is actually going to have a big impact on manufacturing as compared with having on some services. Services will expand the opportunity. In manufacturing, it’ll expand the opportunity, but it’ll actually lessen the number of people that are used. The reason you need manufacturing is for capabilities.”
On what would turn him into a pessimist
We closed by asking what, over the next five years, would break his case for India. The answer skipped past everything that dominates market commentary. Not elections, not which party wins them, not the rupee, not the tax code he had spent half an hour arguing about. What worries him is the stuff that compounds silently over decades and that no government gets voted out for neglecting.
“I don’t really worry about which party is in power. I think any party in power will be able to deliver the 6, 6.5, 7%. My pessimism will be on if we continue to fail our public education and public healthcare system. Just the talent pool and the quality of the talent pool and the health of the talent pool that is available and is required for you to be able to grow faster is just not there. Second, not on the political side but on the governance side — how our cities are managed, how our administrative mechanisms are managed. I don’t think we’ve made any major progress in that. And third, the one reason why India can and should attract more capital is rule of law. Property rights, the freedom and liberty of doing anything that you want, saying anything that you want. Those things actually matter a lot. The reason GDP growth and market returns are a closer fit in India, and not in China or Russia or Brazil or Turkey, is essentially a function of governance.”

When you deal with an informal money lender, you enter the interaction with your guard fully up. But when you walk into a bank, decades of institutional history and RBI regulation create an implicit wall of trust. In Episode 7 of Cash & Copium , Aakanksha, Bhuvan, and Abid tear down that illusion to explain how banks routinely misuse customer trust to push toxic financial products, mis-sell to elderly citizens, and force illegal loan bundling.
If you’d rather skip to the arguments:
Banks are for banking, and nothing else. Use banks to deposit money, withdraw cash, or open a basic fixed deposit. Buying investment or insurance products from a bank branch is an open invitation to get mis-sold.
ULIPs give you the worst of both worlds. They combine inadequate life insurance cover with underperforming investment returns, all wrapped in steep, opaque commission structures.
Endowment plans rely on the “number fallacy”. Paying ₹1 lakh annually for 20 years to get ₹40 lakh sounds impressive, but the real inflation-adjusted return (IRR) is often a miserable 3–4%.
Bank Relationship Managers (RMs) face zero personal liability. Driven by intense sales targets and free of individual licensing consequences, bank RMs routinely mis-sell products and switch jobs before the fallout hits.
Loan bundling is illegal - use the “Ombudsman” defense. Banks are legally prohibited by the RBI from forcing you to buy insurance to get a home loan approved. Demanding that requirement in writing to forward to the RBI Ombudsman stops the pressure instantly.
The Illusion of Regulated Trust
Indian depositors approach banks with a high level of implicit trust, believing that strict oversight from a clean regulator like the RBI keeps their interests safe. Banks routinely exploit this credibility.
Bhuvan highlights the gap between perception and reality: “When an Indian person looks at a bank, there’s an enormous trust of-- amount of trust that is implicit, mostly because of the fact that they are governed by a largely incorruptible, clean organization like RBI. And yet, what happens in real life is they misuse all that trust and they just probably aggregate cumulative rupee value. They scam people more than anybody else in the system.”
The golden rule for dealing with any banking institution is simple: “banks are for banking. Simple. Like- don’t bloody use them for anything else. Go keep your money, withdraw it, at best use a fixed deposit or whatever it is. Nothing.”
ULIPs and Endowment Plans: The Worst of Both Worlds
When banks sell wealth products, Unit-Linked Insurance Plans (ULIPs) and endowment policies are their top choices. ULIPs claim to merge life insurance with market-linked investments, but they fail at both.
Bhuvan breaks down the fundamental flaw of ULIPs: “ULIP stands for unit-linked, uh, investment product. It promises, and promises being the operative word, to give you the best of both worlds, investments plus insurance. But the thing is, it gives you the worst of both worlds. It does neither of them better.”
A term insurance policy provides 500x to 1,000x your annual premium in life cover, whereas a ULIP offers an inadequate fraction. If you try to exit a ULIP early, your money gets moved into a discontinuation fund earning a paltry 4% for five years. Distributors push them because offline ULIPs yield blended commissions ranging from 4% to 10%.
Endowment plans, the “spiritual parents of ULIPs”, rely on investors misunderstanding compound growth and the time value of money. Paying ₹50,000 for 10 years to receive a lump sum after 20 years yields an effective return of 3% to 4%, which trails both government bonds and standard FDs.
Bhuvan points out why these plans succeed: “most endowment plans work on this simple principle that you don’t understand time value of money.” He adds a core financial principle: “In finance, complexity and suitability are always inversely proportional. More c-complex a financial product, the less suitable it is for you.”
Why You Shouldn’t Buy Mutual Funds from Banks
Banks frequently pitch mutual funds, but their recommendations are driven purely by commission margins rather than portfolio suitability.
Bhuvan explains: “A fiduciary is somebody who’s supposed to put the best interests of, uh, his customer above all. Banks are in the business of selling. Their only, only goal is to sell- the highest commission product[cite: 3, 6].” He sums up the bank strategy: “Fund commission high, we sell. Fund commission low, we don’t. End of story.”
Relationship Managers, Loan Bundling, and the “Ombudsman” Weapon
Bank Relationship Managers (RMs) face intense institutional pressure to meet sales targets. Unlike Registered Investment Advisors (RIAs) or Mutual Fund Distributors (MFDs), bank RMs do not hold personal regulatory licenses, meaning they face no personal liability if they mis-sell products to vulnerable customers.
Bhuvan shares a striking real-world example: “See, there is a, there is a documented case in India of a 90-year-old woman- so be- getting sold a policy with maturity date in 2124. I’m just saying it again, two one two four.”
When taking a home loan, bank RMs often claim that buying their in-house property or life insurance policy is mandatory for loan approval. Product bundling is explicitly prohibited by RBI guidelines.
If a bank manager tries to force an insurance policy onto your home loan, Bhuvan suggests a direct countermove: “tell him, ‘Boss, can you please put it in writing on an email saying that to get the loan, I have to take insurance from you. I want to forward that to ombudsman.’... Every time I’ve used the word ombudsman to a bank manager, they’re like, ‘Oh my God, he knows that name. I’m in trouble.’”
To fix these systemic abuses, Bhuvan advocates for individual regulatory accountability: “the regulator should make bank employees personally accountable for mis-selling. They should have a license.”
