Most financial advice focuses on how to get rich, but building real wealth often starts with systematically avoiding the subtle traps that keep people poor. In Episode 6 of Cash & Copium , Abid, Bhuvan, and Aakanksha break down the unspoken habits of financial stagnation - from over-managing tiny portfolios to tying down cash flows in your 20s.
Check out the episode:
If you’d rather skip to the arguments:
Slacking off in college is the first step toward financial stagnation. Big tech firms do not hire for personality; strong academic performance proves you can execute demanding work consistently.
Side hustles are often a distraction from your core career. Spreading your focus across shallow side projects ruins your ability to build a high-income primary earning engine.
Over-managing a small portfolio is a waste of time. Squeezing an extra 2% return out of a ₹20 lakh portfolio will not change your life; growing your paycheck will.
Buying a home in your 20s destroys your optionality. Committing your cash flow to an EMI at age 25 kills your flexibility to take asymmetric career risks.
Your health is your ultimate wealth engine. Because 99% of wealth is built after age 35, burning out in your 20s leaves you without the physical capacity to capture peak earning years.
The College Foundation and the Side-Hustle Trap
The path to long-term financial struggle often begins in college when students trade academic rigor for vague “personality development” or retail trading. In an AI-driven world where shallow tasks are automated, deep technical mastery in your craft is the only defensible asset.
Abid emphasizes why foundational work matters: “Microsoft and Google and Facebook are not going to hire you for your personality. They are going to hire you because you know h-how to code very well.” He adds that grades serve a specific corporate purpose: “A very high CGPA is proof that you are willing to do a lot of work just because it has to be done. And most modern organizations are just looking for people who do exactly that.”
While social media influencers preach building multiple streams of income, attempting to run shallow side hustles while starting your career usually backfires. Abid notes that AI will absorb basic tasks: “every non-deep, shallow, easily learnable, you know, trivial tasks which people give away because they want to save their time are now going to go to AI.”
Bhuvan quips that ignoring advice to focus can lead to terrible outcomes: “You do all the things that we have not asked you to do, you can have a duplex house under Silk Board flyover”.
Manage Your Career, Not Just Your Portfolio
Retail investors frequently spend hundreds of hours analyzing stock charts or chasing 1% extra portfolio returns while neglecting salary negotiations and job switches. In your 20s and early 30s, your human capital, your future earning potential, is your single largest asset.
Bhuvan highlights where your energy should actually go: “I see a lot of people who are preoccupied with building a good portfolio. Like in the sense that if you have saved, whatever, 20, 30 lakhs, you trying to juice out another 2% is not gonna materially make any difference in your life.” He sums up the core rule: “manage your money well, but manage your career. That’s your bigger portfolio.”
Abid explains why career growth beats portfolio tweaking for small accounts: “In fact, if you’re trading with something like 10 lakh portfolio, you are only making two lakh post-tax. Even if you’re spectacular, that is just 20,000 rupees per month. You can make that by volunteering for Swiggy on weekends.” He adds that learning to ask for more pay is essential: “learn to negotiate well. And negotiating well is a very critical skill in how to get yourself to a very wealthy position.”
Exponential wealth compounding happens much later in life than most people realize. Abid notes: “normally people, at least for the last 100 years, make 99% of their wealth after the age of 35. So when do you want to maximize your potential? After 35 or when you are 30s? Early 30s and late 20s are the universities for that 35 plus 99% wealth explosion curve.”
High-Interest Debt, Early Homeownership, and Marrying Badly
Beyond career missteps, three major life decisions can permanently lock you into financial stress:
High-Interest Consumer Credit: Abid warns: “One of the easiest ways to stay poor is to get extremely high interest debt on you”. Escaping high-interest credit card debt requires practicing mindful gratification delays.
Early Homeownership: Quoting Fight Club , Abid notes: “Things you own, own you.” Locking into a massive EMI in your 20s ties up your cash flow on an immovable asset, destroying your flexibility to start a company, switch cities, or take big career leaps.
Marrying Badly: Who you marry dictates your emotional stability, your time, and where you live. Abid highlights: “marrying a partner who gives you the stability and the firm ground so that the both of you can decide to do whatever you want to do in life is heavily underrated.” Bhuvan quips: “See, the surest way to get rich in life is be born rich or marry rich.”
Protecting Your Health Engine
You cannot run an exponential wealth engine in your 40s if you destroy your health in your 20s. Working 12-hour days at an entry-level job generates minimal returns compared to staying physically capable of grinding during your peak leadership years.
Abid explains: “if you want to maximize your wealth in your 40s, 50s, et cetera, you have to be extremely healthy at that point.”

Hi, I’m Kashish and last year I worked on a documentary about India’s electricity sector. The more I read, the more I realised how central — and how overlooked — it was.
For most of its life, Indian electricity was a sector nobody outside it thought about. It was one of those old, dull infrastructure sectors that only old uncles talked about at conferences and expos — functional for 120 years, politically explosive at election time, and otherwise invisible. Two things dragged it back into the foreground at once: the climate push into renewables, and the arrival of AI as a genuinely enormous new consumer of power. India now installs a gigawatt of solar every ten days. It also throws a growing share of that generation away because, in the middle of the day, there is nobody to sell it to.
Mudit is the co-founder of Voltseal, a battery manufacturing company based in Noida that Zerodha invested in through Rainmatter . He started in the World Bank’s energy finance practice, took a long detour through incubation, investing, and designing government entrepreneurship programmes, and came back to energy when the problem he had been circling for two decades started to look solvable. I had spent the past year reading my way into the sector and wanted to test that reading against someone building on the ground. Vishvesh , my colleague at Rainmatter who works on deep tech and hardware, joined me for the conversation.
We spent close to two hours on the mechanics: why curtailment happens and whose fault it isn’t, how the day-ahead market actually clears in 96 fifteen-minute blocks, what a sanctioned load is and what it costs to breach one, why Indian industry pays two and a half to three times what its competitors do for power, and what open access was supposed to do when the Electricity Act was written in 2003. The second half is about where the sector goes next — behind-the-meter storage for mid-sized factories, the India Energy Stack, and virtual power plants, which Mudit says have stopped being a magical idea and started looking like an engineering problem with a date on it.
Some of the things he said stuck with us. We’re sharing eight of them here.
On the statistic that hides the real problem
The most repeated fact about Indian solar is that the country receives, in a single week of sunlight, as much energy as it consumes in a year. It’s a genuinely staggering number, and it is also the reason the sector’s actual constraint gets so consistently misread. Abundance was never the binding problem. Timing is.
“Now, many of us use statistics like all of the energy that India uses in a year can be captured from solar energy in a week. That’s a figure that many people throw around. But what that doesn’t tell you is that you also need to store it, you need to distribute it, you need to have people who are working on it, you need to pay good engineers, you need to make profits. All these transitions don’t work if you don’t have some storage in the system. Because if renewables are intermittent and demand is also variable, you need some storage in the middle. What is that? It’s either batteries or pumped hydro or molten salt.”
On how quickly India actually built its solar fleet
There is a familiar line about Chinese industrial capacity — that at the peak of its build-out, China was commissioning a coal plant every week. It’s usually deployed to make a point about how far ahead China is, and how differently a state can move when it isn’t answerable to anybody. Mudit’s version of the comparison runs the other way. Set India’s solar build-out against that benchmark and the gap is much smaller than the story suggests — and India is doing it with a technology that has been commercially viable for a fraction of coal’s lifetime.
“When I was in the World Bank, when I was in the investing sector, the phrase that often got thrown around was that China was building a coal plant every week. And that figure that people used was one gigawatt of coal plant. Last year, India installed 36.5 gigawatts of solar — one gigawatt every 10 days. We are not very far from where China was doing coal, and coal has been known for 100 years. So we, as a country, adopted renewables. We adopted them at scale. We built one gigawatt every 10 days. And in 2011, when the Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission was established, India had a total installed solar capacity of about 700 megawatts. So you’re talking about going from a national stock, a national fleet of 700 megawatts, to installing one gigawatt every 10 days.”
On why solar gets curtailed
Curtailment is when a plant is ready and willing to generate but the grid refuses to take the power. In India it now happens routinely in the middle of the day, and the intuitive explanation — that solar is somehow too flaky for the grid to absorb — is precisely backwards. Solar is the most responsive thing on the system. The inflexibility sits in the equipment India still needs for the other sixteen hours, and it is a hard physical floor rather than a policy choice.
“But at night there’s no solar. So you need to have those coal plants running. And the coal plants cannot be ramped from zero to 100% of their capacity willy-nilly. They require time. These are very large boilers under pressure, many of them under supercritical pressure — you don’t want them exploding. You don’t want them going out of whack. So they usually have a 55% capacity factor below which their power cannot be curtailed. So the curtailment of solar does not happen because of any properties of solar. The curtailment of solar happens because the other equipment which you still need cannot be reduced below a certain threshold, which is 55% as a rule of thumb. It might be off by a few percent here and there. And because you need to keep all your coal and nuclear running at a certain level, that’s why you have to curtail solar.”
On the duck curve, the camel, and the giraffe
The duck curve is the standard picture of the problem: plot demand across the day, overlay solar generation, and you get a shape with a sagging belly at midday and a steep neck in the evening. The name comes from California. India’s version has already outgrown it, because Indian evening demand is rising much faster than the analogy can absorb — and the next animal in the sequence is one nobody wants to meet.
“So this curve is called a duck curve, and increasingly in India, it’s now being called a camel curve, because the peak in the evening is so high. In Kerala, there was an article recently — the peak in the evening is so high that a duck curve doesn’t describe it well enough. We don’t want it to go to becoming a giraffe curve, because that’s the next evolution. And that giraffe curve is very visible. It’s imminent, because increasingly you have more and more appliances at home. You are moving cooking from gas to induction. Cooking happens in the evening. You have TVs, you have ACs. As temperatures go up, more and more ACs. As incomes go up, more and more ACs get used. So the duck curve is becoming the camel curve. We don’t want it to become a giraffe curve.”
On the house that generates in a week what it cannot consume in a month
The rooftop solar conversation in India is almost entirely about payback periods and subsidy schemes. Almost none of it is about the arithmetic of what a standard array actually produces against what a standard household actually uses. Mudit did the sum out loud, using the array size most Bangalore houses already have, and the mismatch it reveals is not marginal — it is an order-of-magnitude problem hiding inside every rooftop installation.
“And especially if you have solar, if you have a standalone house, the solar energy that is generated on a weekly basis — many people don’t realise. Let’s say if it’s a five to eight kilowatt array, which is very common, most houses in Bangalore probably have that five to eight segment. On an average in India it’s a five hour per day generation. So let’s say if I take six, six into five is 30 units a day. That’s 200 units a week. Very few houses are using more than 200 units a month. That is the part people don’t realise, and that is the part that all the grid managers are struggling with. Now, if so many houses, so many solar plants, so many buildings will have solar, then there is a lot more generation than the grid can absorb.”
On why India penalises the industries it needs most
Electricity has been the most reliably political commodity in Indian public life. Mudit quotes a friend in Washington, Rick Rossow, who argues that the proxy for how well an Indian state is governed is how well it runs its power sector — because balancing the economic imperative against the political one is the hardest thing a state government does. India resolved that tension in a specific direction for decades: protect the household voter, and recover the money from the factory. Mudit thinks the bill for that choice shows up somewhere people rarely look for it.
“So India always had very high tariffs for industries. In fact, I am of the opinion that a lot of our lack of industrial growth is because we subsidised our residential customers and our industries paid very high prices. Even today, there is something called the cross-subsidy surcharge. So electricity being sold to industries is way more expensive than in our competing countries. Our industries, which are competing with China, with Southeast Asia, see almost two and a half to three times the power costs. There’s a paper on this by my friend Rahul Ahluwalia, and he’s talking about energy as a major impediment to India’s industrialisation. And you have so many governments which have come to power, state governments offering free power. And that has been a major impediment to India’s industrialisation.”
On what a virtual power plant actually is
A virtual power plant is a cluster of houses — some with solar, some with batteries, some willing to let an operator nudge their air conditioner by a degree — coordinated tightly enough to behave like a single generator. The idea has been around for fifty years and has never quite worked, mostly because a neighbourhood has no way to transact with anybody at industrial scale. What changes that, Mudit argues, is not better batteries. It’s a protocol layer, and the closest analogy is one every Indian has already lived through.
“But now think of even a distant future where this neighbourhood has, let’s say, one megawatt of solar, which is very doable. Over time, can this virtual power plant, this network of houses, start selling power to a steel plant in Odisha? Why not? So my roof becomes a profit earner. But it cannot happen if I in JP Nagar Fourth Cross go and talk to a steel producer in Odisha. That relationship is not going to work. But a million houses enabled by the India Energy Stack can negotiate with a steel producer, so that relationship becomes viable, and for that you have protocols. In a sense, think about how a bank aggregates millions of little deposits, FDs, into a big loan to an industry. So the bank serves as this intermediary, but the bank was fundamentally a human institution. What we are saying is software and hardware can fundamentally unbundle the human aspect and provide this as a technology stack.”
On why all of this needs a new device
We closed by asking where storage ends up in ten or fifteen years, given that Indian energy demand has only one direction to go — air conditioning penetration, appliances in rural households, the EV transition, all of it arriving at once. Mudit didn’t answer with a capacity forecast. He answered with the mobile phone, and then with the most honest sentence a founder can offer about their own company.
“But let me take the example of the mobile phone first. Growing up, we did not expect the TV and the fax machine and the telephone and my messaging and my letter — everything to get subsumed into a single device. That happened because there was a new device that got designed. Now, if I think about energy, nobody expected that my house will become a power plant and my petrol pump and my energy efficiency management thing, which is possible. What will it take? It’ll take a new device. Is that device like a set-top box for managing all this? Maybe. Is that device a battery? That’s the bet we are taking. So we don’t know what the right answer will be. But this fundamental restructuring, this fundamental re-architecting of the system will take a new set of technologies.”

What happens when a market goes sideways for decades, and how do you protect your wealth when career stability itself is up for renegotiation? In Episode 5 of Cash & Copium , Aakanksha, Bhuvan, and Abid (dialing in remotely with his dog Tuffy) take on retail investor anxieties ranging from Japan-style market stagnation and AI job loss to high-yield bond traps and the reality behind IPO exits.
Check out the episode:
If you’d rather skip to the arguments:
India is not on the verge of a Japan-style multi-decade crash. Japan’s bubble inflated to a 60x P/E (and a CAPE ratio of 95), whereas India’s broad headline index trades around 21–22 P/E.
Systematic investing (SIP) works even through severe market crashes. Simulations show that an investor who consistently SIP’d through Japan’s 34-year crash still generated roughly a 5% XIRR by accumulating units at lower valuations.
AI career uncertainty demands a larger financial cushion. Expand your emergency fund from 6 months to 12–18 months, lock in personal health insurance independent of your employer, and double down on your core job rather than chasing side hustles.
High-yield corporate bonds offering 15–20% are red flags, not opportunities. Chasing yield in fixed income invites permanent capital loss, tax accounting nightmares, and credit risk on assets meant to act as portfolio shock absorbers.
Most IPOs are a bad deal for retail investors. Historical data shows only 40% of IPOs beat the Nifty 500 over a 10-year period. When an IPO is primarily an Offer for Sale (OFS), insiders with complete information are simply selling out to clueless buyers.
The “What If Japan?” Fallacy When investors worry about endless sideways markets, they almost always point to Japan’s lost decades following its 1980s peak. But comparing modern India to 1989 Japan ignores fundamental valuation math.
When the Japanese market crashed, it was trading at an extreme 60x P/E ratio (with a CAPE ratio near 95) alongside economic deflation. India’s headline index currently trades at a 21–22 P/E in an inflationary, high-credit-growth economy. If India’s index stayed flat for 20 years while corporate earnings compounded at a modest 8%, the market P/E would drop under 5x. Furthermore, a simulation of a systematic investment plan (SIP) through Japan’s 34-year crash reveals that averaging down over time still yielded roughly a 5% XIRR upon recovery.

Bhuvan: “If India becomes Japan, forget Nifty returns. We’d be probably sleeping under a flyover or something like that.”
AI Career Uncertainty: Protect Your Paycheck First As AI tools disrupt corporate workflows, the risk of mass layoffs means job hunting timelines will stretch much longer than in normal economic cycles. Financial planning during structural shifts requires accounting for severe income uncertainty:
Expand Precautionary Savings: Scale up emergency funds from 6 months to 12–18 months of expenses.
Secure Personal Health Insurance: Employer-provided medical coverage does not port when you leave a job. Lacking personal health insurance while between jobs leaves you completely exposed to medical emergencies.
Avoid Lifestyle Creep and Peak-Income Debt: Do not borrow from the future or structure long-term debt obligations based on peak paycheck levels.
Entrench Yourself at Work: Instead of dividing your attention with risky side hustles, focus on becoming essential to your employer.
Abid: “Be really, really skilled at and indens- indispensable at your job Unless, of course, your industry itself is going to get toasted.”
Bhuvan: “Doing a side hustle with y- with a good job is a guaranteed way to live under Silkboard flyover.”
Bond Yields 101 & The Trap of 15% Returns Bond yields represent the interest return relative to the purchase price. When a country’s baseline sovereign interest rate is around 7%, a private bond or structured note advertising 15% to 20% interest means the underlying borrower is paying exorbitant rates to attract capital.
Taking equity-like risks in fixed income defeats the entire purpose of the asset class, which is designed to act as a shock absorber. If an equity investment drops, it can eventually recover; if a high-yield corporate bond defaults, the principal is permanently wiped out. Additionally, holding individual high-yield private bonds creates severe tax processing overhead, missing TDS credits on your Annual Information Statement (AIS), and manual accrued interest calculations that can exceed the extra yield earned.
Abid: “A front page ad is the biggest proof of desperation, ‘Bhai, please koi le le.’”
IPOs and the Myth of Easy Listing Gains Retail investors frequently chase IPOs based on gray market premiums and social media hype, but the broader data tells a clear story. According to historical distribution data from NSE Pulse and CapitalMind, the median return on IPOs over roughly a 10-year period was just 10%, and only 40% of IPOs managed to beat the Nifty 500.
The problem is compounded when an IPO consists mostly of an Offer For Sale (OFS) rather than fresh issue capital. In an OFS, early venture capital funds, private equity investors, and company executives are liquidating their personal stakes rather than raising growth capital for the business.

Outperform in Your Career, Be Average in Investing Attempting to generate massive outperformance in your portfolio by market-timing or chasing high-risk products introduces disproportionate risk. Seeking additional alpha above the benchmark requires taking on nearly double the risk.
Your primary goal in investing should be capital survival, diversification across broad asset classes, and capturing market-average returns, while channeling your energy into growing your primary career earnings.

We covered that report on The Daily Brief, and when we started Subtext, we realized we should just directly speak to the authors.
The conversation starts inside India’s solar factories, where tariffs and the ALMM list have built a module industry that still cannot match Chinese prices, and where going upstream into wafers and polysilicon costs hundreds of crores a plant — which is why the names attached to the big solar build-outs (Reliance, Adani, and more) are the names you would expect.
It then moves to the coal belt, where a billion tonnes a year supports ten to fifteen million livelihoods and funds a huge chunk of state royalties for states like Jharkhand and Odisha. Are they doomed to be losers of the green transition? How do you compensate for their losses?
Separately, on Subtext, we’ve spoken about this issue at length with Prof. Rohit Chandra, whose episode on coal in India is also one of the finest nugget-sized lessons on the economic history of post-independence India.
Then, we move the conversation abroad goes abroad to how other poor and developing nations are managing their green transition. The answers there are neither linear nor rosy.
For instance, in Ethiopia, 6% of vehicles are already electric because the government banned petrol imports outright. Then there’s Pakistan, on whose solar scale-up we did a Daily Brief story on last year, where seventeen gigawatts of Chinese panels landed in a single year and started eating the national grid’s lunch.
Eventually, the chat moves to richer countries.
First, we begin with Europe, where a carbon border tax is presented as climate policy to countries that will pay for it out of their steel exports. We, especially our steel sector, know that tax as CBAM.
Along the way, Avantika and Trishant take apart the idea that the poor world is the one dragging its feet on the green transition. BRICS countries alone, they point out, produced 51 per cent of the world’s solar power in 2024. But at the same time, Europe flip-flops on its combustion-engine ban, while the US is selling more oil and gas than ever.
The chat ends inside the halls of global institutions like COP, the World Bank, and the IMF, where the argument stops being about technology and becomes an argument about leverage: who has ever been in a position to set conditions for whom, and what would happen if that stopped being a one-way street.
Some of the things they said stuck with us. We’re sharing seven of them here.
On the fact that every rich country protected its way up
The standard objection to India’s solar tariffs and to the ALMM list is that they are inefficient — that they keep prices high and shelter firms which would otherwise have to get good. Trishant doesn’t dispute the economics. He disputes the amnesia. Protection is not an aberration in the development record; it is the development record. The more useful question is not whether to protect, but what you are meant to do after protection has done the one thing it is capable of doing.
“I would like to start by pointing out that every industrialised country had to protect its way up. All the countries that we know that have industrialised have deployed an array of different kinds of industrial policy tools to get to where they are, and this is pretty evident in many of the readings that you can do — Ha-Joon Chang, or going back to the nineteenth-century US, Alexander Hamilton. When it comes to industrial policy tools that specifically — let’s say you mentioned ALMM and custom duties, tariffs — they do what they are designed to do. They are protecting demand, they are building capacities, but they are quite blunt in what is ultimately needed, that is cost-competitive depth. So they have a utility, but that utility is also to be complemented with other kinds of policies when the time comes.”
On what actually gives you bargaining power in a joint venture
India’s clean-energy joint ventures with Chinese firms tend to be struck by the largest conglomerates — JSW with SAIC, and a string of rumoured others. The standing fear is that these deals lock the Indian partner into assembly while the technology stays offshore. Trishant’s answer is that the outcome isn’t determined by the sector or the era, but by who is sitting across the table and how badly they need you. China’s own record proves the point twice over: the Volkswagen car ventures of the 1980s transferred very little, while high-speed rail, where the state was the only buyer in the country, transferred a great deal.
“There’s other kinds of examples of JV within China itself, where the Chinese government, being the only buyer of high-speed rail — what it did was that it created very strong conditionalities for investments to come in, that you do technology transfer, you do training for our workers, and that is the only possible route that you can come in. And so companies like Alstom, companies like Kawasaki had to do these things for high-speed rail in China. So I think there is an importance of bargaining power of a government or an industry. You have to have R&D milestones embedded in the joint venture. You have to have some sort of training-related clause. There is also an element of how much is the domestic ecosystem, in terms of the companies that are forming JVs. They also have to have some level of strength, enough to have equal standing — and not to come to very disproportionate benefits and advantages that simply lead us as assembly lines, and them having all the technology deployed without having that really transferred within the country.”
On the question a just transition has to answer
Most just-transition talk in India collapses into a training problem: reskill the coal worker, hand them a job in solar, move on. Trishant thinks that framing fails on arithmetic before it fails on anything else. Coal supports ten to fifteen million people. Solar manufacturing, even scaled aggressively, will not absorb a fraction of that. And coal isn’t only employment — it is royalties, district mineral funds, and the freight revenue that keeps passenger rail fares artificially low. Which means the real question isn’t about workers at all. It is about places.
“If you see, coal employs about 10 to 15 million people by some estimates. If you were to compare that with solar manufacturing that might come up in future, it would no way be able to absorb that much employment. So you need to ask questions not like, ‘How do I train coal workers?’ or ‘How do I train this coal economy to shift to a renewable economy?’ You have to ask questions like, ‘What does a place like Korba do for a living in 2045?’ The other is the financial aspect of it. So coal is not just an energy question, it’s also a finance question, because it supports a huge part of the royalties, it supports a huge part of the DMF fund, and then the railways. In fact, the railways cross-subsidise passenger tickets with the freight earnings from coal carriage.”
On choosing between energy sovereignty and manufacturing sovereignty
There is a trade-off hiding inside every import tariff on solar panels. Tariffs are how you build a domestic manufacturing base; cheap imports are how you electrify fast. A country cannot fully have both at once, and the choice it makes says more about its fiscal room and its industrial base than about its climate ambition. Avantika’s point is that poorer countries are not failing this test — they are answering it differently, and often far more aggressively than the rich world gives them credit for.
“If you look at examples like Pakistan, which imported something like seventeen gigawatts of solar panels in 2024 — this has been by reducing import duties on solar panels coming in from China. There’s been a huge flood of solar panels, and today that’s competing in a big way with Pakistan’s own grid-produced thermal power, a system which was already under a lot of financial strain. If you look at Ethiopia today, Ethiopia has banned the import of ICE vehicles and has reduced import tariffs on electric vehicles. So today, nearly six percent of all vehicles on the road in Ethiopia are electric vehicles, which is higher than the rest of Africa. Nepal similarly — today, seventy-six percent of new vehicle sales in Nepal are electric vehicles, most of them coming in from China. So what these countries have in common is that they’ve made this choice that energy sovereignty means a lot to their domestic political conditions, their fiscal conditions.”
On seeing CBAM as a trade barrier first, climate barrier second
Europe presents its carbon border tax as the necessary companion to its own carbon price: without it, the theory goes, firms simply relocate their emissions to jurisdictions with laxer rules. Avantika’s objection isn’t that carbon leakage is impossible, but that it has never actually been observed — there is no precedent to measure it against — and that a mechanism built on that unproven premise ends up transferring the cost of European decarbonisation to the countries that did least to cause the problem and have least to spend fixing it. India’s steel and aluminium sectors send roughly a third of their output to Europe. Mozambique sends most of its aluminium there.
“There is a historical angle of industrialised countries using up more carbon to industrialise, and now telling poor countries, ‘You can’t industrialise in the same way any more, and we basically won’t give you the money or the resources to make clean industrialisation happen.’ The EU ETS carbon price hits almost 100 euros very often. It’s currently at some 75 euros. But you’re essentially telling countries like Mozambique that export most of the aluminium they produce to Europe, you’re telling India’s steel and aluminium sectors, which export about one third of their output to Europe, that you have to switch and transition to the latest clean technologies, you have to completely decarbonise your grid, you have to lower your carbon intensity to almost match the European Union — or you pay 75 euros per tonne of carbon, without any assured support or financial support, technology transfer, capacity building. So in a sense, the EU is telling poor countries that we want to no longer buy your dirty products, but you have to make their production cleaner, and we won’t help you with it. Figure that out.”
On the power dynamics behind international conferences like COP
COP is where all of this gets argued out in public, and Avantika has sat in those rooms. The pattern she describes has held for thirty years: the countries asking for room to grow get cast as the thing blocking progress, while the bloc claiming the moral high ground is largely the one that spent its own carbon budget first. The complication is that the high-ambition camp isn’t only rich countries — small island states are in it too, with genuinely everything to lose, which is part of what makes the label so useful to the Europeans standing beside them.
“Just around the time when the Paris Agreement was being signed, The New York Times ran a cartoon which featured a train which was called Paris Agreement or Climate Ambition or something, and in front of that, an elephant which was blocking the train, and the elephant was called India. And that cartoon got widely criticised… because this is what has always happened in the climate multilateral forum: that poor countries are bashed for wanting simply — the way they ask for policy space at the WTO — they’re just asking for carbon space.
One of these coalitions of the willing within the COP process has become known as the High Ambition Coalition. Typically, it’s comprised of the European Union, the United Kingdom, some Latin American countries, some small island states. And full power to the developing countries in that coalition, because the island states come with real existential challenges about their homes being submerged and losing their sacred lands. But the European Union and the UK and others being in a high ambition coalition has never really sat right with us. Because it’s always become about how these high-ambition countries want deeper emission cuts, more effort on mitigation, and they look to the big, bad India and Saudi and China who are just blocking everything and are just doing nothing.”
On the nature of sanctions
The multilateral development banks hold no legal authority over a sovereign state. What they hold is conditionality, and Trishant’s account of how that has worked is unsentimental: the leverage has always been highest, by design, when the borrower was at its weakest — structural adjustment across Asia in the 1980s, the East Asian crisis in 1997. That grip loosened once China’s banks could finance infrastructure at a scale the World Bank couldn’t match, and is quietly being rebuilt through softer instruments like credit ratings and ESG standards.
The same asymmetry runs through the institutions themselves. The World Bank changes avatar with each US administration — climate was its organising idea in 2023 and is now a word it cannot print — and the G7 will not surrender vote share, because these are the last multilateral bodies it still fully controls. Which is why every technical reform proposal, however clever, stalls in the same place.
Avantika’s argument is that this asymmetry is the whole game, and that nowhere is it plainer than in who gets to punish whom on environmental grounds. This is also how we learnt that the carbon footprint of the US military alone is larger than entire countries.
“If you have the use of certain types of sanctions on the grounds of environment, that can only be wielded by a more powerful country against a less powerful country. So the US can look at India or Southeast Asia and say that your mechanism of fishing is trapping all of these endangered species of turtles, and so you have to change the technology with which you’re doing your fishing, otherwise we will prevent market access. Only the US, in a higher position of power, can actually impose such sanctions or unilateral measures on countries in a relatively lower position of power. Imagine if countries of the Global South actually got together and instead told the US that you’re the biggest historical polluter and you continue to pollute today. You’re spreading wars and conflict and huge amounts of pollution around the world even today. The US military alone is the largest polluter.”

And then the Japanese were just like, “You know what? We can’t compete with you. You take the piece of this cake.” That reminded me of that story when you spoke of bargaining power.
Pranav: But now I want to move on from the industrialisation part of it to the net zero part of it, because I think we’ve discussed where in India the solar build-out happens. But the thing is, we are also a coal-heavy economy still. We still make most of our power needs, electricity needs, from coal, and there is no clean way of saying that renewables will eventually replace coal, even if that is the final outcome 30 years down the line — because we have no idea what happens in the middle of those 30 years. The first question I wanted to ask you about, and which is something that you’ve researched a lot about, is this idea of a just transition. Because you have coal belts in India which are primarily located in states like Jharkhand and states like Odisha, but you also have these solar farms which are in completely different states. Many of those states are very advanced industrially, like Tamil Nadu, like Gujarat. What does a just transition in that sense look like to you, just in India’s case?
Trishant: One of the things to realise is that India has managed to produce over a billion tonnes of coal now, and the coal story, at least in the near future — we don’t see coal peaking immediately. So this is not a crisis that has to be solved just tomorrow. But what we need is careful planning to start today. Because if you look at some of the examples from other countries, you look at the Ruhr region of Germany or the American case, the years of planning —
Avantika: Appalachia.
Trishant: Appalachia. The years of planning — and these regions are still, compared to their own country averages, lagging behind in socioeconomic indicators. So you have to have institutions in place that deal with this probl

Hello there, hope you’ve had a great week!
We started Markets because we, a bunch of nerds within Zerodha, were constantly suckered in by weird, fascinating ideas. We read widely, and weirdly, and then eat people’s heads about our newest preoccupations. Some people seem to like the links we send them (even though more people let our recommendations sit, unread, in their Whatsapp chats). And so, we thought we’d start sharing them with the wider world.
If this is the sort of stuff you like chatting about, come catch us at our weekly book club. More on that at the end!
We’re always hungry for more links by the way. If there’s anything that you want the world to read, drop a link in the comments.
Martin Chorzempa, Has the Chinese yuan’s rise in global usage hit a wall? ( link ): Conventional wisdom, today, tells you that the dollar is “on the decline”, and that it’s only a matter of time before the Chinese Yuan storms in to take its place. As Martin takes you through the numbers, however, you realise that isn’t the story the data tells you at all. The dollar is unchallenged as the world’s leading currency. The yuan, meanwhile, isn’t even in the top five, with China carrying out three-fourths of its trade in foreign currencies. Stories of the internationalisation of the Yuan, turns out, are terribly exaggerated.
Owen Bennett-Jones, Munir’s Victory ( link ): Something has changed in the relationship between Pakistan and its military. Of course, the military has always enjoyed unusual sway in its politics — while its civilian administration, even in the best of times, has been too corrupt to perform the most basic functions. But slowly, the military’s control has become more absolute. The smallest things, as simple as getting a road built to one’s home, now require the military’s involvement. It received its power, in part, because it finally broke through the ambiguity to take a strong stance against the Taliban. But this, too, is precarious — people’s relationship with the army is stable, at best, unlike the fanatical devotion Imran Khan enjoys in some pockets.
Oliver Hanney and Oliver Kim, Tomorrow’s AI Won’t Meet Today’s World ( link ): When I was a kid, it was taken for granted that all of Asia would eventually turn into an “Asian Tiger” — that one by one, industrialisation would come for all of us. It didn’t happen. Instead, we, along with a cohort of peer nations like the Philippines, ended up finding a consolation prize: an IT sector that exported services abroad. Then came AI, threatening to gobble this up too. Early data from the Periodic Labour Force Survey shows a serious dent in our IT employment, particularly among our youngest workers. Is this the end of our development dreams? Chances are, it is not. We humans are more malleable than we give ourselves credit for. It’s certainly a setback, however.
Dwarkesh Patel, The Rise and Fall of Agent Civilizations ( link ): If you’ve been around here for a bit, you know we’ve been reading a bit about how OpenAI’s models have been going rogue, breaking out of their sandboxes and hacking into servers. But it took this wonderful post by Dwarkesh to actually open our eyes to the sheer extent of what has been happening. There have been three generations — three civilisations, in Dwarkesh’s words — of OpenAI agents that broke out of their cages, set up elaborate plans with other models that they weren’t supposed even know the existence of, and then pulled off increasingly sophisticated cyber-attacks. Remember folks: if humanity ever succumbs to the machines, this was the last moment we could have done anything about it.
Thomas Larsen and others, AI 2040 ( link ): Most people I know have stopped thinking about the future. Too many things are up in the air. Most of all, of course, is AI: there’s a pervasive sense that we have only seen the beginning of something era-defining, which none of us have the capacity to sense. Amidst this uncertainty, the AI Futures Project can give your imagination a straw to grasp, even if you take it less as a forecast, and more as speculative fiction. In AI 2027 , they laid down a roadmap for how superhuman intelligences could take over the world. AI 2040, in comparison, tries to map out how countries might (or might not) cooperate to deal with a situation like this. It won’t be easy — not even in a best case scenario — but cooperation might be the only hope we have.
Clara Collier, After Work, We’ll Have Each Other ( link ): What if the worst world implied in these last three recommendations really comes to pass — that AI pushes us out of the workforce, leaving us in a post-work society. What if all the work-based identities we’ve curated so carefully — engineer, doctor, finance guy, whatever – simply fall off, and we’re left to find meaning elsewhere? Well, we’re apes. Our society, in all its many incarnations, ultimately descends into a frenzy for power and sex. Work briefly gave us a particularly legible source of meaning and respect. If it disappears, will we all become like mediaeval courtiers, stabbing and scheming in a bid to gather a morsel of power?
Ashwin Prasad Rao, Still on the Umbilical ( link ): India is building itself a private space industry. Have we created the conditions we need to sustain one, though? As Ashwin argues, SpaceX, the backbone of the world’s space industry, may not remain dependable in the future. We need resilience, for which, that we need a domestic launch industry. That, however, is a project mired in failure and uncertainty. It can only happen if the political will is in place. What does such a project need?
Vijayendra Rao, Why Economists Don’t Listen ( link ): They say economics is the “queen of the social sciences”. This is, in part, because uniquely among the humanities, it lives and dies by what can be measured. But then, there are things this approach renders impossible: for one, you cannot grow too close to those you measure. You cannot let yourself feel the human stories that lurk under clinical numbers. That, in turn, restricts what you can learn about your subjects. Vijayendra calls himself a spy: an economist that secretly smuggled anthropological methods into his economics. Naturally, this is a trade-off; you can’t run regressions on the stories people tell you. But what else does this open up?
Iza Ding, The Darkness That Drives Djokovic ( link ): It was 1999. Belgrade. The former Yugoslavia was caught in an cycle of war and genocide. A twelve-year old boy, sleeping in a bomb shelter, would go out to recently bombed sites to play tennis — after all, how likely was it that the same place would be bombed twice? This was the world that Djokovic came from, when he entered the gleaming, distinctly genteel world of tennis. He could never become an insider. First, he became the sport’s resident jester. Then, he became its villain. But, like the bombs of his childhood, those boos from the audience became his strength. This is the remarkable story Iza Ding tells in her incredible profile.
Neal Stephenson, My Prodigal Brainchild ( link ): In the 1992 science fiction novel, Snow Crash, the author Neal Stephenson coined the term “metaverse” — a computer-generated universe where people would escape their reality. Then, Facebook co-opted the term, eventually calling its entire social and digital media conglomerate “Meta”. At its heart was supposed to be a virtual reality universe. Now that this dream has fallen apart, Neal has some advice for the next company that attempts the idea, once the stink of Meta’s shame has dissipated, and the idea returns to vogue.

Hello there, hope you’ve had a great couple of weeks!
We at Markets like to read widely, and weirdly, and then eat people’s heads about our newest preoccupations. Some people seem to like the links we send them (even though more people let our recommendations sit, unread, in their Whatsapp chats). And so, we thought we’d start sharing them with the wider world.
If this is the sort of stuff you like chatting about, come catch us at our weekly book club. More on that at the end!
We’re always hungry for more links by the way. If there’s anything that you want the world to read, drop a link in the comments.
Decluttering the Tata saga: pieces from Anto Antony and Sanjai PR ( link ), Alisha Sachdev and Sanjai PR ( link ), Krishn Kaushik and others ( link ) and Nevin John ( link ): Apologies for a reading-list-within-a-reading-list, but we were, naturally, curious. On September 17, the Tata board suddenly brushed aside the wishes of Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata, undid the resignation of N Chandrasekaran, and moved towards listing the storied 158-year old conglomerate — a spectacular reversal of the company’s trajectory. What the hell happened? This story drips with drama: decades-old friendships that turned into bitter rivalries, frayed family ties, surprise votes, and the government pulling strings behind the scenes. Nobody quite has the full picture yet, but these pieces should help you piece some of it together.
Howard Marks, Shall We Repeal the Laws of Economics – Part III ( link ): The world, inconveniently, is run on natural laws that keep getting in the way of what we want. Take the United States, which is discovering that the world, in fact, does not want to give it an unlimited line of cheap debt. The US Treasury is now trying to work around this fact, pushing down its long-term interest rates through a program of buybacks. But can it work? Or is all of it, in Stanley Druckenmiller’s words, “ a subsidy to procrastination ”? To Marks, the US government is trying to outrun the inevitable. And the laws of economics don’t take such things kindly.
VSG, Confessions of a Macro Tourist ( link ): Those of us that open a newspaper now and then develop a weird confidence in our abilities to predict the future: not of a life, or a community, but of entire countries. This is “macro-tourism”: the notion that, having looked at a few charts, you can map out the fortunes of a whole economy. The seductive thing is that you’re sometimes broadly right, the way you would sometimes broadly be right if you tossed a coin. If you impress yourself by those successes, however, you’re likely to be caught with your pants down. VSG writes about how he learnt this lesson the hard way.
Yakov Feygin and Dominik Leusder, The Class Politics of the Dollar System ( link ): America, they say, has an “exorbitant privilege” — its government can borrow cheaply, running deficits that nobody else can. This piece, however, tries to puncture that picture, claiming that most Americans don’t actually benefit from their supposed privilege. In fact, they can lose out; for instance, it makes American goods more expensive, which hurts their employment prospects. The privilege, they argue, belongs to a small financial elite, and large firms — who can raise debt and hold highly liquid assets.
Lokendra Sharma and Pranay Kotasthane, Does India Have Leverage Against the US and China? ( link ): In our precarious, uncertain era, it feels like we’re hostage to the whims of more powerful nations like the United States or China. When our sailors die to American missiles, for instance, our protests are brushed off. What can we do if we find our backs against the wall? Are there credible threats in our arsenal? The good folks at Takshashila Institution have a framework, which throws up some options. These aren’t ideal — often, to deliver pain, we must accept pain as well. But that’s very different from having nothing to answer with.
Ideas of India, Kunal Mangal on Chasing Government Jobs in India ( link 🎧): So much of India’s youth is wasted on writing, and failing to clear, endless government exams. In a harrowing but important podcast episode, Shruti Rajagopalan interviews Kunal Manfal, who has been studying this phenomenon, to get a sense of what is happening. The results are stark. People spend endless amounts of time trying to crack a few coveted posts. The harder they are to crack, the more time they spend preparing. If they get through, of course, there’s stability and respect on the other side. If they do not, their life trajectory fundamentally shifts downwards — they earn less over the long term, marry later, start families later, and so on.
JS Tan, From Fordism to the Platform Economy: The Evolution of Firm Strategies ( link ): How do the choices that companies make affect what an economy does? This is the history Tan wants to tell. The tale begins from the old Fordist firm, which held whole supply chains — production, equipment, workers — within a single organisation. This enormous size meant one thing, however: workers could come together, pressure and bargain with the company. Firms would pay better, and invest in productivity, so that they would get more output out of each worker. From the 1970s, however, the model toppled. Increasingly, American firms bound up parts of their production process and moved them abroad — a trend that accelerated with technology. What has this meant for the wider economy?
Jeremy Stern, Mark ( link ): What does it do to a person to control a platform used by billions for over two decades? Do you still listen to others if you built one of the world’s largest companies as a teenager? Do people still tell you the truth? These are the questions Jeremy Stern asks in his expansive profile on Mark Zuckerberg. Stern has access to sides of Zuckerberg that most do not, and that shows in his portrait. You see his penchant for Augustus Caesar, you see him having the stuffing kicked out of himself by an MMA fighter, you see him continuing to work when his wife wants to stop. It gives you an interesting vantage point to look at a man that everyone has an opinion on — often one too simple to capture reality.
Erin Braid, Washer woman ( link ): For at least 4000 years, since ancient Sumeria, women have been washing dishes — with sand, with ash, with rice husk, and more. Then came the dishwasher. It took almost a hundred years to catch on, but when it did, suddenly, it relieved women of this dreary burden. This is true of a series of similar inventions, like the washing machine, or the vacuum cleaner. In 1965, the average American woman spent 35 hours a week on housework. By 2010, that number had shrunk to half as much. That time has bought us equality, opportunity, and efficiency. What other such burdens might the future lift off our shoulders?
Paul Graham, How Universities Should Prepare Founders ( link ): Paul Graham writes about what universities should do to create future entrepreneurs. In one sense, it doesn’t matter — few customers ask you what you studied if they like what you sell. But you do need a few ingredients. You need to discuss powerful ideas that would draw very smart people. You need people to learn to start and run their projects. And most interestingly, sometimes, you just need to leave people alone, so that they can do more interesting things than coursework. What universities shouldn’t do is take courses on entrepreneurship, or conduct lots of case competitions. Tragically, things that look helpful are the least helpful, when you’re trying to build the founders of tomorrow.

Welcome to the 93rd edition of The Chatter — a newsletter where we dig through what India’s biggest companies are saying and bring you the most interesting bits of insight, whether about the business, its sector, or the wider economy. We read every major Indian earnings call and listen to the interviews so you don’t have to.
We’re always eager to improve—please share your ideas on how else we can innovate “The Chatter” format to better serve your needs.
