Hi everyone, I’m Mridula , and welcome to the fourth edition of Weekly Tidbits.
We spend a lot of time reading interesting stories that never make it into a full Daily Brief piece. So, once a week, we pick some of the best ones and add a little context.
We sort them into EIC: Economy, Industry and Company.
We also come across a LOT of interesting global stories that don’t fit neatly into EIC. Should we add a global section too? Let us know. And should we add more news items to each section? It would make the edition longer, but if you’re game, so are we 🙂
With that said, let’s get started!
If you prefer watching the video, here’s the link:
E — Economy
[1] India’s carbon market can now lower UK import taxes
The UK has recognised India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme under its carbon border tax. The UK plans to charge a carbon price on imports such as steel and aluminium based on the emissions produced while making them.
Indian companies may already pay a carbon price at home under India’s own system. The UK will now take that payment into account when calculating what an Indian exporter owes at the border.
So an Indian company that has already paid for its emissions in India may face a smaller carbon bill in the UK. That matters as more countries use carbon taxes to shape trade. India’s domestic climate rules are now starting to influence how competitive its exports are overseas.
[2] Government reviews ₹25,000 crore export schemes after weak interest
The government is reviewing two export-promotion schemes worth around ₹25,000 crore after they attracted limited interest.
The schemes were meant to help Indian companies sell more goods overseas. But businesses have not used them as much as the government expected. The ₹25,000 crore Export Promotion Mission includes 11 schemes covering cheaper market access, certification, logistics and much more.
That matters because an export incentive works only if it solves a problem exporters actually face. Companies may care about cheaper credit, easier logistics or lower compliance costs. A scheme that does not address those bottlenecks will struggle to attract users even if the government sets aside a large amount of money.
The review gives the government a chance to see why companies stayed away and whether the schemes need to change.
[3] SEBI gives angel funds more time to meet investor rules
SEBI has given angel funds another seven months to comply with its new accredited-investor rules. Angel funds collect money from investors and use it to back young startups.
Under the new rules, investors in these funds need to qualify as accredited investors. An individual can qualify with annual income of at least ₹2 crore, or with annual income of at least ₹1 crore and a net worth of ₹5 crore.
The rule narrows the pool of people who can invest through angel funds. But shifting every existing fund to the new system immediately could disrupt fundraising and ongoing investments.
SEBI has now given funds more time to make that transition.
I — Industry
[4] TRAI removes the 12-minute TV advertising cap
TRAI has removed the rule that limited television advertising to 12 minutes in every clock hour.
That gives broadcasters more freedom over how many ads they show. TV channels earn a large part of their money by selling airtime to advertisers. The old rule limited how much advertising inventory they could create every hour.
Now they can create more. But the change comes as television competes with YouTube, streaming platforms and social media for advertising money.
So broadcasters have more space to sell. They still need advertisers willing to buy it and viewers willing to sit through it.
[5] Government plans to keep doorstep delivery of medicines
A government panel plans to retain the rule that allows medicines to be delivered to customers at home. Doorstep delivery became much more common during the pandemic. Since then, online pharmacies and other delivery platforms have made it a regular part of how many people buy medicines.
The rule came in during 2020, and the government had been considering whether to withdraw it before the panel recommended keeping it.
It also matters for traditional pharmacies. They are no longer competing only with the shop next door, but with platforms that can take orders online and deliver medicines directly to customers. So a temporary change made during the pandemic is becoming a more permanent part of India’s pharmacy market.
[6] India clears ₹20,804 crore to expand busy railway routes
The Cabinet has approved eight railway multitracking projects worth ₹20,804 crore. These projects will add extra tracks to routes that already carry a lot of passenger and freight traffic.
That matters because rail capacity is not just about running more trains. Congested routes can slow freight, limit how many passenger services can be added and make the network less reliable. We have written about this railway bottleneck before.
Source
Adding more tracks gives Indian Railways more room to move both goods and people without forcing them onto the same crowded lines.
For industries that depend on rail to move coal, steel, cement and other bulk goods, that extra capacity can make a real difference.
C — Company
[7] Swiggy turns Crew into a travel concierge
Swiggy has relaunched Crew as a dedicated travel concierge. Crew started as a broader lifestyle service that helped with errands and other personal requests. Swiggy is now narrowing it to travel. Users can ask Crew to help plan trips and handle travel-related requests through a 24/7 concierge.
That gives Swiggy a different way into the travel market. Instead of competing only on flight or hotel bookings, it is trying to handle more of the planning around the trip itself.
Swiggy is not alone. Startups such as M and Hulp are also building personal assistants that take everyday tasks off the user’s plate.
[8] Adani and NTPC apply for coal gasification incentives
India’s ₹37,500 crore coal-gasification scheme has received seven proposals from five companies. Instead of burning coal directly to make electricity, companies process it into gas. That gas can then be used to make products such as fertilisers, chemicals and synthetic fuels. We have written about coal gasification here .
Adani Enterprises has proposed three urea projects. NTPC has proposed a synthetic natural gas project. Coal gasification uses coal differently from a normal power plant.
India imports large quantities of some of these products and the raw materials used to make them. The government wants companies to use domestic coal to replace part of those imports. The applications from large companies show that the idea is starting to move from policy into actual projects.
[9] Coca-Cola avoids a price war with Campa Cola
Reliance’s Campa Cola has been using low prices to gain ground in India’s soft-drink market. Coca-Cola says it does not want to respond by simply matching those prices. The company instead plans to spend more on marketing and distribution. We have written about Campa Cola’s pricing strategy before.
Source
The two companies are taking different approaches. Campa Cola can use lower prices to persuade more customers to try its drinks. Coca-Cola is betting that its brands and distribution network can protect its position without cutting prices as aggressively.
That matters because price wars can help companies win customers quickly. They can also leave everyone earning less on each bottle sold.

Hi everyone, I’m Kulsum , and welcome to the fifth edition of Weekly Tidbits. Mridula is away collecting her degree at her convocation, so I’m filling in for her this week.
We spend a lot of time reading interesting stories that never make it into a full Daily Brief piece. So, once a week, we pick some of the best ones and add a little context.
We sort them into GEIC: Global, Economy, Industry and Company.
You asked for a global section last week, so we’ve added one. Let us know if it works or makes the edition too long.
With that said, let’s get started!
If you prefer watching the video, here’s the link:
G — Global
[1] US regulator eases rules for trading tokenised stocks
The US securities regulator has introduced a five-year exemption that will make it easier for platforms to trade “tokenised stocks”. These are digital tokens recorded on a blockchain, with each token representing ownership in a real company. To qualify, they must give investors the same basic rights as ordinary shares, including voting rights and dividends. Products that merely copy a stock’s price will not count.
Supporters say tokenisation could allow shares to trade around the clock, settle faster and be divided into smaller pieces. It could also bring crypto platforms such as Coinbase and Robinhood into closer competition with traditional exchanges and brokers.
But the experiment still has to answer basic questions: who holds the underlying share, what happens if a platform fails and whether investors can move their assets elsewhere.
[2] EU’s first full-scale carbon storage project begins operations
The European Union’s first full-scale carbon-storage project has started operating . Under the Greensand project, carbon dioxide from Danish biomethane plants will be captured, turned into liquid and transported to the Port of Esbjerg. Ships will then carry it to a depleted oilfield in the North Sea and inject it around 1,800 metres below the seabed.
The project can initially store up to 400,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, with plans to expand this to between 4 million and 8 million tonnes.
Carbon storage is meant for industries such as cement, steel and chemicals, where cutting emissions is especially difficult. The technology remains expensive and controversial, but Greensand will test whether it can move beyond pilot projects and work on an industrial scale.
[3] Gulf disruptions are pushing up South Asia’s energy costs
Disruptions to oil and gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea have pushed Asian spot LNG prices towards $30 per million BTU, from around $10 before the war. Bangladesh generates more than 40% of its electricity using imported LNG, so the price shock has led to power cuts and gas shortages that are forcing factories to slow or stop production.
A survey of Bangladeshi knitwear factories found that 55% had seen buyers reduce or cancel orders because of unreliable power and gas, while 78% had partially stopped production. Pakistan is facing the same price shock and has introduced fuel subsidies for motorcycles, rickshaws and small cars. A disruption thousands of kilometres away is now reaching factory floors and transport costs across countries that depend heavily on imported energy.
E - Economy
[4] India’s retail and wholesale inflation rose in August
India’s retail inflation rose to 4.82% in August, from 4.45% in July. Food inflation climbed to 5.95%, while rural inflation remained higher than urban inflation. Wholesale inflation, which measures prices before goods reach consumers, also rose to 9.92%, largely because fuel, food and manufactured products became more expensive.
Source
Retail inflation remains within the RBI’s tolerance range of 2–6%, so this is not yet an inflation crisis. But the direction matters. Higher food prices squeeze household budgets, while rising fuel and wholesale prices can eventually increase costs for businesses and consumers.
If inflation keeps climbing, the RBI may have to hold interest rates higher for longer or consider raising them, making loans more expensive.
[5] RBI absorbs ₹2.23 lakh crore of surplus bank liquidity
The RBI has absorbed ₹2.23 lakh crore from the banking system through a three-day variable rate reverse repo auction. Banks offered to park ₹2.226 lakh crore with the RBI against a notified amount of ₹2.25 lakh crore. The central bank accepted all the bids at a weighted average rate of 5.24%.
In plain English, banks currently have more cash than they need for day-to-day lending and payments. The RBI is borrowing some of that surplus for three days and paying banks interest on it. This temporarily removes money from circulation.
That matters because too much surplus cash can push short-term market interest rates below the RBI’s policy rate, making its monetary policy less effective. The auction lets the RBI drain the excess quickly without locking banks’ money away for long.
[6] India’s electronics production still relies on Chinese components
India’s trade deficit with China in electrical and electronic goods reached $43.1 billion in FY26, up from around $20 billion in FY19. China supplied at least 80% of India’s imports across 636 product categories, compared with 461 categories in FY19. These include integrated circuits, semiconductors, batteries, smartphone parts and display modules.
This exposes a gap in India’s manufacturing story. The country is assembling and exporting more phones and electronic products, but still imports many of the parts inside them. Domestic production can therefore grow without reducing dependence on China.
Replacing those imports will be difficult because China has spent decades building a dense supplier network. India needs more than factories that assemble finished products; it also needs companies that make the chips, batteries, displays and other components they use.
I — Industry
[7] Climate risks are raising insurance costs for Himalayan infrastructure
Roads, bridges and hydropower projects in the Himalayas have always been difficult to build. The terrain is steep, the weather can change quickly and materials often travel through narrow mountain routes.
Repeated floods, landslides and glacial-lake disasters are now making these projects costlier to insure. After the Sikkim glacial-lake flood, insurance rates for some roads and bridges reportedly rose by around 21%.
Insurance is a basic cost of building large infrastructure because banks and investors are unlikely to fund an unprotected project. As insurers treat the Himalayas as riskier, developers may have to pay higher premiums, accept more exclusions or bear a larger share of potential losses. Those costs eventually become part of the project’s total bill. Climate change is making infrastructure more expensive to finance even before anything is damaged.
[8] Counterfeit medicines are becoming harder to identify
Counterfeit medicines were once easier to spot through poor printing, spelling mistakes or unusual packaging. That is changing. Counterfeiters are getting better at copying boxes, batch numbers, holograms and QR codes. A packet can now look genuine even when the medicine inside contains the wrong ingredients, too little of the active ingredient or none at all.
India’s pharmaceutical supply chain is enormous. A medicine can pass through a distributor, stockist, wholesaler and pharmacy before reaching the patient, creating several points where a fake can enter. Factory inspections alone cannot cover the entire chain. Regulators also need ways to track medicines and verify that each packet came from an authorised source. As packaging becomes easier to copy, its appearance becomes weaker proof that the medicine is genuine.
[9] Organic farming is greener on some measures, not all
Organic farming is often seen as the obvious environmental choice because it avoids most synthetic fertilisers and pesticides. But an Our World in Data analysis shows that the comparison is more complicated. Organic farms generally cause less pesticide-related damage and support more insects, birds and plant life on the land being farmed.
The problem is yield. Organic farms usually produce less food from the same area, so making one kilogram of food can require substantially more land. When researchers measure emissions and water pollution per kilogram rather than per hectare, the environmental advantage often shrinks. Organic farming performs better on some measures, while conventional farming uses less land. What people eat, how much food they waste and how efficiently it is produced may matter more than the organic label alone.
C – Company
[10] Tata, Adani and Reliance now operate 19,000 EV charging points
Tata Power, Adani and Reliance Industries operated 19,000 EV charging points at the end of FY26. The network has more than tripled from 5,438 points in FY23. It also grew 21% over FY25 and 67% over FY24. Tata Power leads with 7,700 points, followed by Reliance with 6,200 and Adani with 5,100.
These chargers serve cars, buses and trucks across public, semi-public and private locations such as malls, offices, hotels and hospitals. A wider network can make EV ownership easier by reducing the fear of running out of charge.
But the three conglomerates do not dominate public charging yet. They operated around 24% of the public chargers tracked in FY26, while state-run oil companies held 37%. Their expansion is making the market larger, but public-sector fuel retailers still have the bigger footprint.
[11] PwC plans a joint venture for parts of its US and India businesses
PwC plans to combine large parts of its separately owned US and India operations in a new joint venture. The firm operates through a network of member businesses rather than as one centrally owned global company. That allows offices in different countries to operate independently, but can make it harder to share staff, technology and revenue across borders.
The venture would make India a bigger base for work done for PwC’s international clients. It comes as consulting firms are working out what AI means for their business. Research, documentation, data analysis and presentation-building can increasingly be assisted by AI, the same tasks that have traditionally supported large offshore teams. PwC is still betting on India, but the work done here could become more specialised.
[12] Semicon 2.0 attracts $11–12 billion in investment proposals
Electronics minister Ashwini Vaishnaw says Semicon 2.0 has attracted investment proposals worth $11–12 billion across semiconductor equipment, materials, gases, chemicals and substrates.
Applied Materials has announced a $5 billion India investment plan through 2035 to expand supply-chain capacity, research and talent. Tata Electronics announced seven partnerships on the first day of Semicon India and planned nine more, including agreements with Nexperia, Besi and Fujifilm across the chipmaking value chain. Kaynes Semicon is also considering a $1 billion OSAT project in Gujarat. OSAT facilities assemble, package and test chips after they are manufactured.
The announcements suggest India’s focus is expanding beyond large chip factories to the suppliers and services around them. But the $11–12 billion figure represents proposals, not money already spent. Some projects still need approvals and execution. The real test is how many announcements turn into operating facilities.

Hi everyone, I’m Mridula , and welcome to the sixth edition of Weekly Tidbits.
We spend a lot of time reading interesting stories that never make it into a full Daily Brief piece. So, once a week, we pick some of the best ones and add a little context.
We sort them into GEIC: Global, Economy, Industry and Company.
Let’s get started!
If you prefer watching the video, here’s the link:
G — Global
[1] Saudi Arabia’s oil backup route is hit
Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline was shut after drone attacks damaged pumping stations. The country has since signalled that it plans to restart the route. The pipeline gives Saudi Arabia another way to export crude because most of its oil normally leaves through the Persian Gulf and passes through the Strait of Hormuz.
The East-West pipeline avoids Hormuz by carrying crude from Saudi Arabia’s eastern oilfields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. That makes it an important backup whenever shipping through the Gulf becomes risky. We have written before about why the Strait of Hormuz matters so much to global energy markets.
Source
For now, the shutdown has reduced that flexibility, and some European refiners were told that October supplies from Yanbu would not arrive. Saudi Arabia can still export large volumes of crude, but an outage on one of its main alternative routes leaves it with fewer options if shipping through Hormuz also comes under pressure.
[2] US borrowing costs are near 20-year highs
US government borrowing costs have climbed to levels last seen before the 2008 financial crisis. The yield on the 10-year Treasury crossed 5% in mid-September. When investors sell bonds, their prices fall and the return a new buyer earns, called the yield, rises.
Several things are driving the sell-off. Higher energy prices are adding to inflation fears, while investors are also worried about how much debt governments are issuing. The Federal Reserve raised rates on September 16 and has signalled that more increases could follow. Companies are borrowing heavily too, including to fund data centres and other AI infrastructure, which means investors have even more debt to absorb. We wrote earlier this month about how America’s growing debt and borrowing needs are putting more pressure on the bond market.
The pressure has spread beyond America. Germany’s 10-year government bond yield reached its highest level since 2009, while Australia’s touched a 15-year high. Higher government yields can feed into mortgages, company loans and other borrowing, making money more expensive.
[3] China is investigating Meituan and Alibaba
Chinese regulators are investigating Meituan and Alibaba units for suspected violations of unfair competition laws. Meituan is one of China’s largest local-services platforms, spanning food delivery, hotel bookings and other services that connect consumers with businesses.
Platforms like Meituan become stronger as more merchants and users join them. More restaurants attract more customers, while more customers make the platform more important to restaurants. Once that loop becomes large enough, businesses can find it difficult to stay away even if they dislike the terms.
Chinese industry groups have raised concerns around commissions, search rankings and promotional programmes used by online platforms. Regulators are now looking at how companies use the bargaining power that comes with scale, especially when restaurants, hotels and other merchants depend heavily on them for customers.
E — Economy
[4] Bangladesh is buying Indian wheat again
Bangladesh has started buying Indian wheat again after a gap of four years. Traders have already booked more than 200,000 tonnes as disruption around the Black Sea makes supplies from Russia and Ukraine less dependable.
Bangladesh normally imports a large share of its wheat from the Black Sea region. But attacks on ports, ships and grain infrastructure have made that route riskier and more expensive. At the same time, high rice prices at home are pushing more people towards wheat, which is increasing demand just as imported supplies become harder to secure.
India suddenly has an advantage. It lifted the wheat export ban imposed in May 2022 after a strong harvest improved domestic supplies, and its proximity to Bangladesh keeps transport costs much lower than wheat coming from Australia or North America. The Black Sea war is now shaping where Bangladesh buys one of its basic staples, and India is the nearest beneficiary.
[5] GST collections are recovering
India overhauled the Goods and Services Tax last September . Four major slabs were reduced to two main rates of 5% and 18%, while a new 40% rate was introduced for some sin and luxury goods. Taxes were also cut across several categories.
Lower rates make products cheaper, but they also reduce the tax collected on every sale. Net GST collections, which means revenue after refunds, stayed subdued through the end of 2025 before beginning to recover. In August, net collections reached about ₹1.68 lakh crore, 8.3% higher than a year earlier. The comparison needs some care because GST 2.0 also changed the compensation cess on several products.
Source
When the reforms were announced, we wrote about this trade-off . Lower prices could support consumption, while simpler slabs could improve compliance and reduce classification disputes. The recent recovery suggests that at least part of the initial revenue hit is narrowing, although one year is still too early to say the tax cuts have paid for themselves.
[6] India may create a ₹20,000 crore AI fund
The government is considering putting ₹15,000–20,000 crore into a proposed National Frontier AI & Compute Fund. The fund is still under discussion, but it could provide long-term capital to Indian AI companies and finance GPU clusters, specialised data centres and other computing infrastructure.
Advanced AI models need large amounts of computing power. That means thousands of specialised chips, along with the electricity, cooling systems and high-speed networks needed to run them. Global technology companies can finance this infrastructure themselves, while an Indian startup may have the talent and the model idea but still lack enough computing power to train it at scale.
India already has the IndiaAI Mission, which is also trying to expand access to computing capacity. The new proposal appears to add a dedicated pool of long-term capital for frontier AI and infrastructure. What is still unclear is how much of it would be new support and how much would overlap with programmes the government is already building.
I — Industry
[7] India may change how DAP subsidies work
The government is considering different subsidy rates for diammonium phosphate, or DAP, depending on how companies produce it. DAP is one of India’s main fertilisers and receives support under the Nutrient Based Subsidy scheme, which helps keep the price paid by farmers under control.
Some companies import finished DAP, while others manufacture it in India using inputs such as rock phosphate and phosphoric acid. Those routes do not face the same costs. Sulphur prices have risen sharply as supply disruptions around Russia and West Asia tightened the market. Sulphur is used to make sulphuric acid, which is needed to produce phosphate fertilisers, so domestic producers feel that increase more directly.
India also wants to reduce its dependence on finished fertiliser imports. If the subsidy does not reflect the higher cost of making DAP locally, importing the finished product can become more attractive than producing it in India. Differential subsidies would try to keep fertiliser affordable without weakening that localisation push.
[8] India’s e-bus boom faces a financing problem
Electric-bus sales in India reached 5,412 units in FY26, around 35% more than the previous year. Much of that growth comes from buses operating under government-backed contracts with state transport undertakings.
Private companies often run these buses under Gross Cost Contracts. They buy and operate the vehicles, while the transport authority pays them a fixed amount for every kilometre travelled. That predictable payment stream makes financing easier. Operators running intercity, staff or other private services have a harder time because they carry the passenger and revenue risk themselves. We wrote about this model earlier , when India’s e-bus push was still largely being driven by government contracts and payment guarantees.
An electric bus can cost around ₹90 lakh to ₹1.2 crore, compared with roughly ₹43–45 lakh for a diesel or CNG bus. Lower fuel and maintenance costs can make up part of that difference over time, but shorter loan tenures leave operators with large repayments before those savings add up. The harder task is making the economics work for operators without a government contract behind them.
[9] Europe may stop sending metal scrap to India
India could lose direct access to some European metal scrap from May 2027. The European Union is changing its rules for shipping waste to countries outside the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, or OECD. India has applied for continued access but is not currently included for some metal-waste categories in the proposed list.
For Indian metal companies, scrap is a raw material. Aluminium scrap can be melted and reused, using far less energy than producing fresh aluminium from ore. India is also a major buyer of European aluminium scrap.
If those shipments are restricted, recyclers will have to source more material from other countries. Higher scrap prices would raise production costs, while using more primary metal would increase energy use. Europe wants to make sure its waste is processed safely after leaving the bloc, but the same environmental rule could change where Indian factories source their raw material and what they pay for it.
C — Company
[10] Nykaa and L’Oréal will invest in beauty startups
Nykaa and L’Oréal’s venture arm BOLD are teaming up to invest in Indian beauty, personal-care and wellness brands. BOLD stands for Business Opportunities for L’Oréal Development. The two companies plan to take minority stakes while founders continue to run their businesses.
Nykaa brings a large Indian retail platform, which gives it a view into what consumers search for, what sells and which young brands are gaining traction. L’Oréal brings capital, product expertise and decades of experience scaling beauty brands.
The partnership also pushes Nykaa further into a dual role. It already sells other companies’ products while owning brands of its own, including Nykaa Cosmetics and Dot & Key. That could make rival brands on its platform wonder how neutral it can remain as it invests in more brands itself. For startups, the attraction is simpler: Nykaa and L’Oréal can provide capital, distribution and expertise when the challenge shifts from launching a good product to building a much larger business.
[11] Apple Pay is preparing to enter India
Apple is preparing to launch Apple Pay in India, beginning with Axis Bank credit cards. It is also talking to other large banks.
The reported launch is about cards, not UPI. Apple Pay stores a tokenised version of a card on an iPhone or Apple Watch. When a user taps the device at a compatible payment terminal, the transaction still runs through the card network behind that card. UPI works differently because it moves money directly between bank accounts.
Source
Apple therefore does not need to build another payment network. It can use existing card rails and compete for the interface customers use to pay. India is overwhelmingly a UPI market and Apple has a much smaller handset share than Android, so the initial audience is likely to be narrower and more affluent than the average Indian digital-payments user.
[12] A tax dispute is holding up the JSW–Volkswagen deal
JSW Group wants Volkswagen to remain responsible for a potential tax liability of $1.4 billion, roughly ₹13,160 crore at ₹94 to the dollar, as the two companies negotiate a partnership involving Skoda Auto Volkswagen India.
The dispute goes back to vehicle parts imported between 2012 and 2024. Indian authorities say Volkswagen brought in what were effectively complete knocked-down vehicle kits but classified the parts separately. Complete kits attract a higher import duty, while individual components can attract lower rates. Volkswagen denies the allegation and is challenging the demand in a Mumbai court.
The old case now affects the valuation of the new deal. JSW does not want the liability to move into the business it is buying if Volkswagen eventually loses the case. The group is already expanding in automobiles through its partnership with MG Motor India, and a Volkswagen deal would take that push further. Before that happens, both sides need to agree on who carries this risk from the past.
That’s it for this week.
A few of these stories are still developing, so we’ll be keeping an eye on them. But if there’s one you’d like us to write about properly, let us know in the comments.

There is a line commonly attributed to Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard: “Life can only be understood backwards, but it must be lived forwards.”
Meaning, we usually understand things better after they happen. But while they are happening, we still have to deal with them without knowing what comes next.
If you have been investing in Indian equities over the last two years, you know what the second half of that quote feels like.
For the first time since the COVID crash, two-year returns on the Nifty 50 have gone negative this year. If you put money into a Nifty 50 index fund around September 2024, your annual return today, including dividends, is -1.9%.
Nifty 50 Chart
The midcap index did a bit better at +3.7% CAGR. Smallcap index managed +1.3% CAGR. Positive returns, technically, but we tend to compare this with FD returns, though we inherently know that we shouldn’t.
One bad year feels like a blip. Two years of going nowhere is when the doubt sets in.
Would SIPs have done any better? A monthly SIP of ₹10,000 on the Nifty 50 over this period gave you a negative 2.9%, actually worse than the point-to-point return of about negative 2%.
What about actively managed mutual funds, the ones that carefully pick stocks to dodge exactly this kind of fall?
To their defense, most actively managed large-cap funds technically “beat the benchmark,” but when the benchmark gave a minus 2%, barely beating that negative number is little consolation.
Now, remember the first half of that quote: life can only be understood backward.
So let’s look backward. To see if it can help us make a little more sense of where we are today.
Exercise 1: How frequently has this happened before?
When you look at data from mid-1999 to September 2026 of the Nifty 50 TRI (Total Return Index) and calculate the two-year return for each day, you will notice that earning a negative 2-year return from equity wasn’t that uncommon.
About 1,034 days out of roughly 6,250 showed a negative number. That is 16.5% of all trading days. When you dig deeper, you see where those days fall on a timeline.
They are not scattered across the calendar. They bunch up. Before the current period, every single one of those negative periods belonged to just five distinct episodes in 25 years.
See the table below:
How is this time different? In most past episodes, you could name the crisis. Financial Crisis in 2008. A pandemic shut the world down in 2020. Demonetization was announced in 2016. This time, there is no single trigger. Of course, if you want to name a few obvious ones like global trade tensions, valuation corrections, sector-specific issues like IT slowdown, all of them together, but none like a crisis time that we have seen in the past, typically.
Exercise 2: How long did negative returns last?
A negative two-year return is one thing. Living with it for months is another. So the next thing we wanted to know was: how long have such periods lasted in the past?
The dot-com bust was the longest: nearly two years, where anyone looking at their portfolio would have seen red. Other episodes took about six months to a year to see a positive 2-year return.
How is this time different? The current episode started around July 2026, about 50 days ago. The worst reading so far is -1.9%.
At first glance, the closest parallel in our data looks like 2011-13. Unlike the GFC or COVID, which was not one sharp crash but a drawn-out weak period that lasted about 19 months with a worst reading of -4.6%.
But the experience was not quite the same. In 2011-13, the market had already dipped and was moving upwards during much of that period. The two-year return was still negative on paper, but the investor could feel the recovery happening. That is a very different kind of waiting from what we have now, where the market has simply not moved.
If you go further back using price return data (which goes to 1990, before the total return index was available), there is another episode worth noting: 1995-97. No global crisis triggered it. The economy was dealing with high inflation, political instability — three prime ministers in two years — and the growing pains of higher interest rates. The market just drifted. That one feels more like what we are in today.
Currently, we are 50 days in. How long this one lasts, nobody knows.
Exercise 3: What helped in the past?
But in every past episode where equity went negative for two years, other asset classes were doing their own thing, often in the opposite direction.
Check the last column in the above image that shows returns from a simple balanced portfolio of a 60:30:10 portfolio (equity, debt, gold).
It did not always stay positive, but it took a much smaller hit every time. During the GFC, pure equity fell 14% while the blended portfolio fell about 4%. That’s the benefit of diversification.
This time around, gold did the heavy lifting. At roughly 46% CAGR return, gold more than compensated for equity’s losses. While debt grew by around 7%.
The returns from the diversified portfolio may not be starkly different, but at least you have one asset class cushioning other asset classes’ fall, which will come to your rescue if you suddenly need money during these times.
Key Takeaway
We looked at two-year returns because that is the period we are most uncomfortable with right now. And as the usual lecture goes, two years in equities is not long enough.
Negative two-year returns are not something we see every few years. But when they do appear, they can stick around for months, sometimes close to two years.
But the bigger takeaway from this exercise is to look at your portfolio as a whole (as we did above), rather than any one asset class in isolation.
Imagine two assets, A and B, each with 20% volatility (a measure of how much prices swing up and down). If you put half your money in each, you might expect the portfolio to have 20% volatility, too — 50% from A and 50% from B. But that is not how portfolio risk works.
If the two assets typically move in opposite directions (for example, gold and equities), the portfolio can have much lower volatility — perhaps less than 14% instead of 20%.
When you combine different assets, the volatility of the portfolio can actually be lower than the volatility of the individual assets that make it up. When I first came across this a few years ago, I remember being very surprised. This is one of the important ideas from Harry Markowitz’s portfolio theory.
Today, the asset class testing our patience happens to be equity. At another point, it could be gold, or something else. But when you look at a portfolio that holds all of them, the picture changes.
There is something called the Callan Periodic Table of Investment Returns that makes this easy to see.
It shows how different asset classes have performed relative to each other over the years. The asset class that does well in one year can end up near the bottom in another, while something else takes its place at the top.
We don’t know which asset class will win next. But we can decide how much our portfolio depends on any one of them.
Which brings us back to the quote we started with:
“Life can only be understood backward, but it must be lived forwards.”
Looking backward gives us context. But to live forwards, perhaps the better approach is to look at the portfolio as a whole rather than trying to figure out what happens to a single asset class.

Say you want to invest in companies like Apple, Google, Nvidia, or Tesla. Or maybe you just want to buy foreign ETFs or funds that track global markets. If you are sitting in India, how do you do that?
One way is to open an account with a foreign broker, figure out how to transfer money abroad and buy the stocks/ETFs yourself. This route comes with LRS remittance, foreign-asset reporting, dividend withholding tax and capital gains calculations and estate tax planning (that is a tax some countries charge on the assets of an investor who passes away to transfer them over to heirs).
The only other option, with far less hassle, was Indian mutual funds with overseas exposure. For example, the Motilal Oswal S&P 500 Index Fund lets you invest in the 500 largest US companies. You just buy it like any other mutual fund. Everything is in rupees, you deal with an Indian AMC, and the fund house handles the foreign investing part on its own.
But you know the problem. RBI has set a cap on how much the entire mutual fund industry can collectively invest abroad. Once that cap was hit, most of these international funds stopped accepting new money. That is why many overseas funds are closed for new investments today.
So now there is a third route through funds, and that is what this newsletter is about.
A bunch of well-known Indian fund houses (DSP, Parag Parikh, Edelweiss, HDFC) have set up shop in GIFT City, an international financial centre in Gandhinagar, Gujarat, with some funds starting at a minimum investment of just $500 (roughly ₹48,000).
There are many types of funds in GIFT City. Some are “inbound” funds, where foreign investors put money into Indian markets. Others are “outbound” funds, where Indian investors send money to invest in global markets. This newsletter is only about the outbound retail schemes that are open to regular Indian investors like you and me.
See, GIFT City is physically located in Gandhinagar, Gujarat. Very much on Indian soil. But for all financial and regulatory purposes, GIFT City is treated as if it is outside India, in simplistic terms. When you send money to a fund sitting in GIFT City, it is treated as a foreign remittance, just like sending money to New York or London.
Because these fund houses are set up in GIFT City (a special financial zone), they can freely take money from Indian investors and invest it in global markets.
Also, they are not regulated by SEBI, which is the regulator for Indian capital markets.
GIFT City has its own separate regulator called IFSCA (International Financial Services Centres Authority). Just like SEBI makes the rules for Indian mutual funds, IFSCA makes the rules for everything inside GIFT City: the funds, the disclosures, the investor protection, all of it.
The terminology is also different. See this table for funds:
The products look and behave a lot like mutual funds. You invest, you get units, there is an NAV, you redeem when you want. But they live under a completely different legal and regulatory roof.
FAQ Part 1:
1. What funds can you actually invest in today?
These outbound funds cover different geographies. Parag Parikh focuses on the US (S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100). DSP goes wider with global equities. Edelweiss focuses on China. HDFC covers developed markets (US, Europe, Japan) and emerging markets (China, Taiwan, South Korea, Brazil).
They also come in different styles. Some are actively managed, where the fund manager picks foreign stocks based on her skill and judgement (like DSP).
Others are passive fund of funds (FoFs), where your GIFT City fund simply invests in an overseas ETF that tracks an index passively (no stock-picking).
Then there is a third kind, like Edelweiss FoF, where the GIFT City fund invests in another fund that is itself actively managed by JPMorgan.
With any FoF, you pay expenses at two levels: the GIFT City fund and the underlying fund.
2. Does investing in these funds eat into my LRS limit?
LRS stands for Liberalised Remittance Scheme. Whenever you transfer money abroad as an individual, it falls under LRS. This is the process that allows you to send up to $250,000 abroad per financial year for purposes like investing, travel, education, or gifts.
When you send money to a GIFT City fund, since it is considered a foreign remittance, it counts against this limit. Just to be clear: when you invest in a regular Indian mutual fund, you are sending money to the fund house in rupees, so your LRS limit is untouched. But when you send it to GIFT City, it is counted.
3. How does the tax work?
Pay extra attention to this one.
When you invest in an Indian mutual fund, it does not matter how many times the fund manager buys and sells stocks inside the fund. No capital gains tax is triggered on those transactions. The only thing that matters is when you, the investor, bought and sold your units. You pay tax on your gain.
With GIFT City funds, it works differently. Whatever you receive on redemption of units from the fund, there is no tax in your hands.
Sounds like music to your ears? Wait.
The taxation is at the scheme level. Every time the fund sells a security, tax is applicable on that transaction at the fund level. That too, at eye-watering rates. If the fund held that security for less than 24 months, the gain is taxed at a whopping 42.74%. If it held for more than 24 months, the rate is 14.95%.
This is especially important for an actively managed fund. More buying and selling of stocks means more short-term gains inside the fund, which means more tax at 42.74%, which eats into the fund returns that investors finally get. So a lot depends on how that active fund is managed.
[Check out an interesting take from PPFAS GIFT City on why the GIFT City route could actually be better on a post-tax returns basis compared to investing directly. We cover that in Part 2 ].
4. What is a “post-tax NAV”? And why can there be more than one?
In an Indian mutual fund, the NAV is broadly the value of the fund’s assets minus liabilities and expenses, divided by the number of units.
GIFT City funds are different because tax arises inside the fund. So the NAV you see is after providing for this tax. Hence “post-tax NAV.”
And there is not always just one NAV.
PPFAS, for example, has a Subscription NAV at which you buy units. When you redeem, there are two possible NAVs: a short-term Redemption NAV and a long-term Redemption NAV, depending on how long you held.
DSP also publishes a Subscription NAV and a Redemption NAV, but its calculation works differently.
As an investor, check which NAV you enter at, which one applies when you exit, and how that particular fund calculates it.
5. What about TCS?
TCS stands for Tax Collected at Source. It is basically the government’s way of collecting a portion of tax upfront at the time of certain transactions. When you buy a car above a certain value, the dealer collects TCS. When you send money abroad, your bank collects TCS.
So when you remit money to a GIFT City fund under LRS, your bank will collect TCS and deposit it with the government on your behalf. The first ₹10 lakh you send abroad in a financial year has no TCS, regardless of purpose. After that, TCS kicks in, and the rate depends on why you are sending the money. For investments, it is 20%. For education, medical, or travel purposes, it is much lower at 2%.
Note that this is not an additional tax. Think of it as an advance payment. You claim it back as a credit when you file your income tax return at the end of the year.
One useful tip from Hema Thakkar of PPFAS GIFT: if you plan to remit money for both investments and self-funded education in the same financial year, the order can matter for TCS. The first ₹10 lakh of aggregate LRS remittances attracts no TCS. Beyond that, investment remittances attract 20% TCS, while education remittances attract only 2%. So, purely from a cash-flow perspective, doing the investment remittance first can be more efficient.
6. Do I have to report this in Schedule FA?
When you hold foreign securities, the Income Tax department wants you to disclose them in your income tax return under Schedule FA (Foreign Assets). If you invest in Indian mutual funds with international exposure, you generally do not need to do this.
For GIFT City funds though, the answer is not very clear. There is no definitive ruling either way. In such cases, to sleep peacefully, it is better to just declare it.
7. What about estate or inheritance tax?
This was anyway never a concern with Indian mutual funds that invest internationally. But when you hold foreign stocks or ETFs directly through a foreign broker account, some countries like the US can charge estate tax on those assets if something happens to you. With GIFT City funds, you hold units of an Indian trust, not the foreign securities directly. So this risk does not arise. India itself has no inheritance or estate tax.
FAQ Part 2:
8. Do I need a foreign bank account? How does money reach the fund?
No. The funds are denominated in USD, but you start with rupees. Your bank converts and remits.
You subscribe to these funds through the fund house’s website directly, or through a distributor. Just like Indian mutual fund schemes, these come in Direct and Regular plans, with the Regular plan carrying a higher expense ratio.
Some fund houses have integrated the LRS remittance process with partner banks and made the process largely digital. If you have a savings account with a partner bank like HDFC Bank, ICICI, Axis, or IDFC, and you choose the digital route, everything is auto-populated, including Form A2 (the RBI form where you declare why you are sending money abroad). You do not need to separately reach out to your bank for the remittance; it is all handled within the subscription process itself. If you do not have a savings account with a partner bank, you may have to visit your bank branch to submit the forms that are available on the fund’s website.
9. Can I do an SIP?
Currently not available, as we understand.
10. What does it cost beyond the expense ratio?
Apart from the fund’s TER and the underlying fund’s expenses (in case of a FoF), there is the forex markup your bank charges when converting rupees to dollars. If you were to invest directly through a foreign broker, you would be doing this conversion on your own at whatever rate your bank offers. With GIFT City funds, because the fund entities have tied up with partner banks and negotiated, they may get you a more favourable exchange rate. That said, it depends on your relationship with your bank and the transaction amount. Do check before assuming.
11. What about KYC and redemption?
KYC is regular, nothing out of the ordinary. Redemption typically takes 7 business days. Money returns in USD and your bank converts to INR. You get daily NAV, quarterly portfolio disclosure, annual audited reports, and monthly account statements. There is no AMFI-style centralised database for all GIFT City schemes yet.
12. Why GIFT City could be better on a post-tax returns basis compared to investing directly
As Hema Thakkar of PPFAS GIFT City points out: “What most people do not realise is that when you invest directly through a foreign broker, your gains are taxed in rupee terms. That means you are taxed not just on the actual dollar gain your investment made, but also on the rupee depreciation over the years. With GIFT City funds, the tax is paid at the fund level in foreign currency. So the rupee depreciation effect is simply not taxed.”
Here is an example. You buy a US stock for $5,000 when the dollar is at ₹83. Seven years later, you sell at $8,000 when the dollar is at ₹95. Your dollar gain is $3,000. For tax calculation, you convert both purchase and sale price into rupees separately. Purchase cost: ₹4,15,000. Sale value: ₹7,60,000. Taxable gain: ₹3,45,000. The real dollar gain at the selling rate is only ₹2,85,000. The extra ₹60,000 is purely because the rupee fell, and you are paying tax on that too. In a GIFT City fund, this does not enter the picture. This view is from PPFAS GIFT while we couldn’t verify this claim independently.
One thing to keep in mind though: the way these funds are taxed today could be favourable, but tax laws can change. Do not assume this is permanent. Check with your CA.

When you land your first job and that first payslip hits your account, everyone has something to say.
Your parents say buy a home. An insurance uncle shows up and asks you to buy a policy that doubles your money in fifteen years.
Meanwhile, you come across a finance video that says start early, invest in the stock market, there’s nothing like it. Your cousin in the US says she goes all in on Bitcoin and asks you to do the same. You hear an inspiring story about a couple of friends who pooled their money, took the risk, and started something on their own. While your colleague might say YOLO, you’re only young once, just enjoy..
And this is not even counting the financial goals already lined up ahead of you.
There is a partial truth to everything above. But if there is one thing that is undeniably, indisputably, quantitatively proven amongst everything that everyone has ever said about money in your twenties, it is this: time is on your side.
The small amount of money that you invest now, for a long period of time, can build a massive difference. Because of that 8th wonder of the world - Compounding.
Really. In twenties, how much you invest matters far less than the fact that you invest. You may not believe that now because the amount feels tiny. But look at this:
The person who started a systematic investment plan (SIP), investing a fixed amount every month, at 25 ends up with over a crore. The one who started 10 years later would be left with astonishingly less. That’s what time does.
I am not here to ask you to save every last rupee.
I talk about five things you must definitely do. One thing you absolutely must not. And one thing you need to think really, really hard about before deciding.
Even before we get into that: if you have any education loan, start there. Prioritise repaying your loans. You don’t want to carry that weight throughout your journey. If you have any other borrowing and your parents are contributing, take ownership. Transfer the amount. Repay from your paycheck every month. Let your parents also have the chance to build their own retirement corpus, especially if they don’t have one.
Now, on to 5 must-dos:
1. Build an emergency fund
“Staying in the game is more important than winning any single hand.”
Think about it this way. Without an emergency fund, the moment something goes wrong, a medical bill, a sudden job loss, a family situation, you’re back to depending on your parents.
Or worse, in the case of emergencies, if you don’t have a cushion, you borrow at terrible interest rates, you sell investments at the worst possible time, you take the first job offer that comes your way because you can’t afford to wait. That’s not a position you want to be in after finally getting your independence.
Start with having at least six months of basic expenses as a separate FD. You don’t have to build it overnight. If it’s convenient, set up a recurring deposit in your bank that automatically deducts a certain amount every month and saves it as a separate deposit.
The best return an emergency fund gives you is the ability to say no to a bad decision.
So, build the damn foundation before you think of decorating the house.
2. Check if your parents are covered
“The best time to buy insurance is before you need it.”
There are two kinds of insurance: life and health.
Life insurance is for when you have dependents ; if something happens to you, they get the money. Health insurance covers medical costs on hospitalisation.
In your twenties, the risk for both is relatively low.
But the urgency is with your parents. Check if they are covered. Does your company’s group policy include them? What’s the overall sum insured and is it enough.
How much is enough? start with ₹5 lakhs, and then add another ₹5 lakhs for each of these factors — if your parents live in a metro, if they use chain hospitals, if they’re above 45, and have any medical issues, stack it up, and the ideal coverage can reach ₹25 lakhs.
If they are covered only under your corporate policy, try getting a separate family floater for your parents. Because, the day you lose your job or switch, corporate cover disappears. And your parents will be left uninsured exactly when they might need it the most.
Don’t do this next week. Call your parents today. Check your corporate policy. One hospitalisation can wipe years of savings. It is preventable. Prevent it.
3. Start saving for the habit
“In exercises, muscles build by tearing. Savings muscle works the same way.”
The money you can invest today may not make you rich. With time, potentially. But at least in the near future, the returns on a few thousand a month are not going to change your life.
But there are other benefits that comes with staying the course of investing, and they matter more than the money itself.
One, habit formation. We all know that humans are animals of habit, and it takes a lot of time to develop one. If you suddenly think of saving in your 30s, it may not work out. Trust me, I see this in my circle of folks and it’s hard. SIP is one of the best things that happened in the Indian financial industry to help us build that habit almost without thinking.
Two, when you invest in the markets, it takes time to get used to the ups and downs. The first time the market falls 20%, you may panic. The second time, you’ll think let me wait. The third time, you understand it’s just part of the game. It’s something you earn by staying invested through a few cycles.
“You need to build the infrastructure in your character to put up with it”: I read this somewhere and loved how it sounded.
So, start an SIP, an amount that you can put aside even if its as low as a few hundred bucks. If you don’t know where to invest, split equally across asset classes like equity (direct stocks/mutual funds), debt (like FD /PPF), and gold. There’s real research showing that simply dividing your money equally works surprisingly well. Don’t overthink where. Just begin with basic index fund.
But keep one thing in mind though. If you need money for near-term goals like wedding, car, travel, keep the money safe in FDs or liquid funds. For long-term goals, equity is proven to be good.
And you might want to bet on something like Bitcoin, or something that sounds very fancy but comes with a lot of risk; also, I am sure you will come across someone along your journey telling you “this is a once in a lifetime deal”. Even if you really, really want to invest, just try ten to twenty percent of your capital. Not more than that. Better to skip, though.
4. Invest in your skills and your health
“Before 30, follow somebody…Learn the passion. Learn to dream.” — Jack Ma
The return on your investments in your twenties will not make a dent compared to what your income growth will do. The single biggest thing you can do for your financial future right now is enhance your income.
Buy books. Attend conferences. Travel if you need to, to learn something new. Find a good mentor. A genuinely good mentor can change your entire trajectory. Even if it means sacrificing some salary to work with the right person, do it. And if you’ve been using AI already, you know what it can do. Learn more, buy a paid plan if you need to. Don’t be the person who ignored it :)
And your health. “Health is wealth” is a throwaway phrase until you price it. Good food costs money. Protein powder costs money. A decent gym costs money. Playing a sport costs money. Periodical check-ups cost money. Renting a place closer to work so you sleep an extra hour costs money.
The compounding on good health in your 20s is just as real as the compounding on your SIPs — except the dividends show up in your energy, your focus, and decades later, in medical bills you never have to pay.
5. Enjoy your money. Give some to the people who got you here.
“Memories are the real dividends.” — Bill Perkins
Whatever age you reach, the tussle between spending on something versus investing or saving will always be there, unless you give yourself the permission to enjoy what you earn.
In your twenties, your age and health are on your side right now. The energy, the curiosity, the ability to sleep on a bus and wake up fresh. That has a shelf life. Go on trips. Try that restaurant. The experiences you have at 25 give you a kind of joy that the same experiences at 55 simply cannot.
And look, even if you can’t save for retirement right now, it’s okay. But please keep a note in your head that you are betting on your future self to start investing aggressively later. There is a difference between consciously letting it go for now and just ignoring it altogether.
And finally, if giving some money to your parents makes them happy, just give it. Even if it’s a little, it means something to them in a way we don’t fully understand. We never get that time back.
The one thing not to do: for god’s sake, do not borrow for lifestyle
“Do you want it, or do you need it?”
Phone on EMI. Holiday on EMI. Clothes on EMI. Car upgrade on EMI. For god’s sake, please don’t. I am not saying don’t upgrade your life , of course you should when you start earning money.
But sometimes, especially when you’re living in a metro, spending creeps up without any intention. I notice it in myself. How differently I spend when I’m in hometown versus when I’m in the city. It just tends to happen. Be mindful of it.
See, there is a difference between productive debt and destructive debt. An education loan that improves your earning power ? Productive. A loan for a genuine business opportunity ? A bet worth taking.
But a phone because the new one has a slightly better camera? A holiday on a credit card? That’s destructive. And even for productive debt, don’t go overboard. If your total EMIs ever cross 40% of your take-home pay, you’re stretching yourself and might be one bad month away from being broke.
The one thing to think really, really hard about: buying a home
“Protect your optionality.”
I know. In India, the moment you start earning, people expect you to buy a house. Your parents will say it. Your cousin would have already bought one recently. The reasoning is always the same: “instead of paying rent, why not pay an EMI? At least you’ll have an asset.”
I understand the security a home gives. Especially the tangibility feature. I am not getting into ‘Buy vs Rent’ debate here, but a much broader point.
A home loan that comes with monthly mandatory obligation will take away your options, especially when your salary is still low.
If your organisation is toxic, can you leave? If you want to try a different career, can you? If an opportunity comes up in another city, can you say yes? If you just want to take a break, can you? Your twenties are the time to explore, to try, to figure out what you actually like. You may not know yet. And for that, you need flexibility. A home loan may take that away.
I know this is a hard opinion for a few. Because, expectations from family and the emotional needs can overpower. But go into this decision with your eyes open. If you still decide to buy, go ahead knowing exactly what you’re giving up.
To close
So that’s the whole thing. Emergency fund, parents’ health insurance, a monthly SIP for the habit, your own skills and health, and enough spending to enjoy the life you’re building. Don’t borrow for lifestyle. Think really hard before that home loan.
I know, fitting all of this inside a starting salary is not easy, too. But these must-dos are the basics to start with, to get the hang of managing money before taking the next step.
And if there’s one thing that will help you stick to this plan along the way, it is being financially literate. I’m not saying understand what hedge funds are doing. I’m saying know the basics: what your insurance covers, how your SIPs work, what to check before signing a policy. We put out these explainers on Varsity all the time. Stay updated. Along the way, you’ll understand that in finance, simplicity beats complexity every single time . So when someone comes selling an insurance that works as an investment as well, or someone else shows you a complex product promising guaranteed high returns, you will know how to walk away.
“Money just makes more of who you already are.” That’s a powerful place to be in. Before that, build the character that can carry the weight. Build the floor. Build the habits. Everything else follows.
Time will do its thing. Trust it. Let it.
P.S. If you're still with me till here, a small bonus. I reached out to Karthik Rangappa , who has been in the space of finance education for over a decade and in the markets even longer, asking what his financial advice for someone in their 20s would be, in one phrase. This is what he said:
"Time is on your side, so don't hesitate to take that risk."
His point is that it is far easier to take risks and experiment when you are young, with smaller amounts, than to attempt it when you are older.

Nirmala Sitharaman says India’s Debt-to-GDP ratio will fall to 50% by 2030-31. It’s likely to be at 55.6% in this financial year.
A line going down looks good. And finance ministers love this number because it’s a convenient and easy way to convince people that the government is financially disciplined.
It’s a great metric in that sense.
Except…it’s not.
Because as per some economists, the Debt-to-GDP ratio might be flawed.
I’ll explain.
Let’s start from the very top; with debt.
If I tell you that India’s total debt is ₹200 lakh crore, it gives you zero perspective. It is just a number. Albeit a very, very large number.
You know it is money that the government owes to people who’ve bought its bonds or money it has borrowed from foreign investors. But other than the fact that it looks significantly big, it tells you nothing.
You need something to compare it to at least.
So if I tell you that the US debt is $40 trillion (~₹4,000 lakh crore), you get a sense of how insignificant India’s debt might be.
But that’s still not good enough. The US is a far larger economy than ours. Maybe they have the capacity to deal with that level of debt. Maybe we don’t.
That’s where the Debt-to-GDP ratio comes in.
After all, GDP is the one number every country calculates. It gets published in the papers and it’s a stand-in for a country’s economic muscle. That makes it the easiest thing to divide debt by if you want to compare, say, the US to India to Japan.
The headline number of Debt-to-GDP is convenient.
Economists Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff published a paper in 2010 titled Growth in a Time of Debt highlighting the negative effects of high debt-to-GDP levels on economic growth.
So when I say India’s debt-to-GDP is ~55% and that the US is at 120%, the puzzle makes sense a bit more. You can compare, contrast, and you’ll come to the conclusion that India is in a much, much better place.
It’s a good headline.
But why do high levels of debt even matter?
The most obvious risk is that lenders get nervous. A high debt load makes a country look like a riskier bet, and when lenders fear they won’t be repaid, they either charge higher rates to compensate, or simply stop lending.
At some point, the people holding a country’s bonds might stop wanting to hold them. That creates a mismatch: more sellers than buyers for the country’s debt.
Which leaves the government with two bad options. Either raise interest rates to attract buyers back, which slows markets and the economy down. Or the central bank steps in and starts “printing money” to buy the debt itself, which could push inflation higher than it otherwise would’ve been.
Also, another thing you have to remember is that rising government borrowing has a knock-on effect.
The government might have to raise taxes just to cover the growing interest bill. And that is money which might come straight out of savings — mostly of individuals — who otherwise would’ve spent it in the economy and created a multiplier effect of consumption. Higher government borrowing could also crowd out private investment because it pushes interest rates higher. And it could reduce private capital formation that would’ve funded new factories and equipment too.
So, too much debt is bad. We all agree with that.
Now that we have got all of this cleared up, let’s go back to the fault in the Debt-to-GDP ratio.
See, debt is what economists call a stock — a snapshot, the total pile of money India owes on one specific day. Like the water sitting in a bathtub right now.
GDP is a flow — economic activity over an entire year. Like the rate at which water is flowing through the tap.
“Debt-to-GDP” is a stock divided by a flow.
Of course, it’s not meaningless and it does help in comparisons but it might not be the best way to judge a country.
For example, Japan’s Debt-to-GDP ratio is at 250% today and no one is losing sleep over the country defaulting. Meanwhile, when Argentina defaulted in 2001, it had a ratio in the 50s.
Economists (Reinhart and Rogoff again, along with Savastano) have a term for this — debt intolerance ( pdf ) . Some countries tend to have weak fiscal structures and weak financial systems. That’s something the debt-to-GDP ratio does not capture — the institutional credibility, the track record of the central bank and government etc.
And if you look at Japan, its debt is almost entirely owned by Japanese institutions, in yen, backed by a central bank nobody doubts.
That’s trust placed in the system.
So, which number should India actually be watching if it’s not Debt-to-GDP?
Well, some economists say that a “flow” variable has to be compared to a “flow” variable. So it’s not debt-to-GDP but interest payments-to-GDP that has to be monitored.
And where does India stand?
Well, India spends roughly 5% of GDP on interest alone. That’s about double the emerging-market average. And just by this ratio alone, we’re paying more than roughly three out of four comparable countries.
Source: NITI Aayog ( India’s Debt Dilemma by Eichengreen, Gupta, and Ahmed)
And it isn’t that India borrows at unusually expensive rates. Indian bond yields, around 7-8%, aren’t wildly out of line with peers. It’s just that India’s debt burden is significantly high enough to produce an outsized bill.
In short, we end up paying too much by way of interest.
A different flow to flow measure is interest payment-to-government revenue , since GDP isn’t money the government can actually spend.
Ray Dalio, the hedge fund billionaire, wrote a 5 minute summary of his book called “How Countries Go Broke.” There was a subsection in the summary titled “The US Government’s Situation in a Tiny Nutshell,” so I’m going to borrow that and make it about India.
The Indian Government’s Situation in a Tiny Nutshell
Now, imagine that you are running a big business called the Indian government ( pdf )…
This business is expected to earn total revenue (not including from borrowings) of about ₹36.5 lakh crore in FY27 while the total expenses is about ₹53.5 lakh crore, so there will be a budget shortfall of about ₹17 lakh crore. So, this year, your organisation’s spending will be about 46% more than it is taking in.
And there is very little ability to cut expenses because almost all the expenses are previously committed to or are essential expenses.
Because your organisation borrowed a lot over a long time, it has accumulated a big debt— nearly six times the amount that it is bringing in each year — of about ₹200 lakh crore, which equals about ₹6.7 lakh per household that you have to take care of (assuming roughly 30 crore households in India).
And the interest bill on the debt will be about ₹14 lakh crore, which is ~40% of everything your organisation earns, and 83% of this year’s budget shortfall (deficit) that you will have to borrow to fund.
But that ₹14 lakh crore is not all that you have to give your creditors because, in addition to the interest you have to pay on your debt, you have to pay back the principal that is coming due, which is around ₹5.5 lakh crore .
So, the debt service payments—in other words, the paying back of principal and interest that you have to do to not default—is about ₹19.5 lakh crore, which is about 55% of the money coming in.
That is the current situation.
And here’s the thing, even though the US debt of $40 trillion is always in the news these days, when you look at how much of the government revenue goes into paying interest, India is nearly 2 times more — for India, it’s 38% versus ~20% for America.
That is the number we need to keep an eye out on.
Now there is one more thing that you should know. Debt is not really a Union Government problem.
See, when we read headlines saying India will cut back the Debt-to-GDP ratio to 50%, here’s what most people reading the headline will miss — that is just based on the loans the union government has taken on; whereas the GDP is actually for the country as a whole.
State governments have debt too. They’ve issued bonds and raised money to fund their own infrastructure and expenses.
And if you tack that on, you’ll see that the Debt-to-GDP ratio is actually upwards of 80%.
That is something you need to be aware of.
So, the final question is — does India have a debt problem?
Well, considering everything I’ve said so far, let me also tell you about economist Olivier Blanchard’s thumb rule. He said that what matters is R , the interest rate the government pays, versus G , the growth rate of the economy. If R stays below G or R<G, a country can carry a large debt load and the economy simply outgrows it.
In India’s case, the nominal interest rate (R) is roughly 7% and the nominal growth rate (G) is 10%.
We may not be in a bad position then.
Sure, how much we pay out as interest is concerning because it’s money that could otherwise have gone towards education or healthcare or capex. But we’re not in the danger zone. It’s just that as the paper by Eichengreen, Gupta, and Ahmed highlighted, even though there is no immediate crisis, there is no easy path to a dramatically lower debt load either — not without raising more tax revenue, privatising assets, and reining in states that are on a borrowing binge.
Also, a declining debt-to-GDP trajectory, even an imperfect one, still matters as a signal. It supports investor confidence, keeps borrowing costs in check, and buys the government room to keep spending on infrastructure. The direction is good.
It’s just that we need to remember that’s not the only number we have to track. And the next time a “Debt-to-GDP” headline shows up, we have to do a little more digging.
