India’s IPO calendar for 2026 brings together an unusual mix of businesses, from hospitals and dairy products to financial services and logistics. Some have already begun trading, while others are preparing to offer their shares to the public. Many are familiar to investors through everyday life. Others are being discovered as their IPO plans make the news and circulate on social media.
Reaching those investors once involved considerably more paper. In 2008, Reliance Power distributed more than four crore printed application forms through banks and collection centres across India. Around 50 lakh investors applied, and the issue was subscribed 73 times.
Today, an investor might first hear about an IPO through a news headline, watch its valuation being discussed on YouTube and later receive a notification when applications open. Subscription updates follow through the same feeds, while applying can be as simple as placing a bid and approving a UPI mandate on a phone. The excitement is familiar. What has changed is how quickly it reaches investors, and how often they encounter it before making a decision.
Some of the biggest IPO stories of 2026 may still be ahead. NSE and Jio could bring large offers to the market, while familiar names such as Cult.fit, ACKO, OYO and PhonePe are at different stages of their listing plans. Together, they span businesses we encounter through payments, shopping, insurance, travel and fitness.
As these companies prepare to meet public investors, the ones that have already listed offer a useful starting point. Their journeys so far show how investors have responded and give us a glimpse of the market the next wave of IPOs will be entering.
India’s Two IPO Markets
An IPO is how a company offers its shares to the public for the first time. In India, companies can take two main routes. A mainboard IPO leads to a listing on the main platform of the NSE or BSE, generally used by larger businesses. An SME IPO , short for small and medium enterprises, leads to a listing on platforms designed for for smaller businesses: NSE Emerge or BSE SME. Both allow investors to buy a stake in a company, but the eligibility requirements, minimum investment and trading rules differ.
The difference in scale becomes clearer when we look at the size of their offers.
The image above shows some of the larger mainboard and SME IPOs from 2026. Among those shown, SBI Funds Management’s mainboard issue was close to ₹10,000 crore, while Q-Line Biotech’s SME issue was just over ₹200 crore. Even the smallest mainboard offer in this comparison, Juniper Green Energy at ₹1,800 crore, was more than eight times the largest SME offer shown.
After the Listing
The size of an IPO tells us how much investors were asked to put into the offer. What happens after listing tells us how their expectations hold up once trading begins. Even a strong debut can give way to a fall in the weeks that follow. Among the companies shown here, several climbed substantially, while others slipped below their first closing price.
The following charts track the ten mainboard companies and five of the SME companies from the offer-size comparison above. They measure returns from each stock’s listing-day closing price , excluding any gain or loss between the IPO offer price and that first close. Each stock starts on its own listing date, while the indices are measured from the start of the year. The index lines therefore provide market context; they do not establish whether a stock outperformed the index over the same holding period.
The chart above follows all ten mainboard companies from the earlier comparison. Shadowfax stands out, rising 120.9%, meaning its share price more than doubled from its listing-day close. Clean Max gained 52.4%, while Central Mine Planning & Design Institute, Indo-MIM and Dhoot Transmission each rose about 31%.
The largest offer in the earlier comparison, SBI Funds Management, had a different experience. Its shares fell 12.3% from their first closing price, while Fractal Analytics declined 11.3%. Juniper Green Energy was only slightly higher, gaining 2.2%. Raising a large amount through an IPO clearly did not ensure a strong run afterwards.
The SME companies show an even wider spread of outcomes.
The chart above tracks five SME companies from the offer-size comparison: Vivid Electromech, Q-Line Biotech, Anawil Wire & Engineering, Optimystix Entertainment and Clay Craft India. Vivid Electromech rose 213.5% from its listing-day close, taking its share price to more than three times that level. Q-Line Biotech gained 42.6%, and Anawil Wire & Engineering rose 24%.
That strength did not extend to every name. Optimystix Entertainment fell 20.6%, while Clay Craft India declined 31.1%. Even among this small group of larger SME offers, investors experienced everything from a price more than tripling to a fall of nearly a third.
Several of the IPOs shown have delivered strong gains since listing, while others have struggled to hold their ground. As investors follow those businesses through their first months on the exchange, another set of companies is preparing to join them.
The Next Names on the Calendar
Among the next arrivals is a business at the centre of India’s stock market itself. NSE’s IPO opens from 17 to 21 September, with a price band of ₹1,700–₹1,785. The ₹22,562 crore offer would allow investors to own a stake in the exchange, with its shares set to trade on rival BSE.
The calendar above brings together mainboard and SME offers with announced bidding dates, alongside companies whose plans are still taking shape. NSE has an application window on the calendar, while Jio, ACKO and OYO appear without confirmed dates.
Jio Platforms could bring one of India’s largest public issues, opening up direct ownership in a business familiar through mobile connections and home broadband. Other prospective listings extend that familiarity into insurance, travel and fitness, with ACKO, OYO and Cult.fit at different stages of preparing to go public.
For many investors, these businesses already have a place in everyday life. An IPO offers an opportunity to become a shareholder, but each business has its own reasons for coming to market. NSE’s offer, for example, would allow existing shareholders to sell part of their investment. That purpose shapes how the IPO is put together.
The Reasons Behind an IPO
NSE’s upcoming IPO is an offer for sale , or OFS. Existing shareholders, including SBI, New India Assurance, Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and Aranda Investments, are offering shares they already own. No new shares are created, and the proceeds go to the sellers, not NSE. They can cash out part of their investment without exiting completely.
NTPC Green Energy took a different route with its ₹10,000 crore IPO in 2024. It was entirely a fresh issue , meaning the company created new shares and received the money raised. Around ₹7,500 crore was earmarked for investment in its subsidiary, NTPC Renewable Energy, to repay borrowings. Fresh issues can also fund factories, acquisitions or expansion into new markets.
Swiggy’s 2024 IPO combined both. It offered roughly ₹4,500 crore of fresh shares alongside an OFS of ₹6,800 crore. Swiggy raised money for Instamart’s dark-store network, technology and marketing, while investors including Prosus and Accel sold part of their holdings.
In each case, public investors became part-owners of the business, whether they bought newly created shares or shares from an existing holder. For an individual applying through a broker, the journey begins in much the same way: choosing a bid and setting aside the money.
Between Applying and Owning
An IPO application is a request for shares. Unlike buying a listed stock, where an order becomes a trade when it matches a seller at an agreed price, applying for an IPO does not immediately make us shareholders. We first wait for bidding to close and allotment to determine how many shares we receive, if any.
That journey has five steps.
The bidding window opens. In a book-built IPO, investors choose a bid price within the announced band and apply in lots, or fixed bundles of shares. Eligible retail applicants can select “cut-off”, agreeing to pay the final issue price.
The money is blocked. The applicant approves a block through their bank or a UPI mandate. The money remains in the account but is temporarily unavailable to spend.
The price and allotment are decided. After bidding closes, the issuer and selling shareholders, as applicable, finalise the issue price in consultation with the lead managers. Eligible applications are considered for allotment. Investors may receive all, some or none of the shares requested.
Shares and money are settled. The cost of the allotted shares is debited, the remaining blocked money is released, and the shares reach the investor’s demat account.
Trading begins. Buyers and sellers on the exchange now determine the share price, which can move above or below the IPO price.
The image above puts that journey on a calendar. The NSE example shows bidding from 17 to 21 September, allotment on 22 September, and refund initiation and demat transfers on 23 September. Listing follows on 24 September. The ₹1,700–₹1,785 range is the price band per share. With eight shares in a lot, one lot at the upper end costs ₹14,280.
But the price band is rarely the only number being discussed while investors wait. Another figure circulates through websites, news reports and social media: GMP, or grey market premium .
GMP is the premium quoted for IPO shares in an unofficial market before exchange trading begins. For example, in the case of NSE, a reported GMP of ₹198 over an issue price of ₹1,785 would imply a price of ₹1,983. It reflects sentiment in that informal market, rather than a promised listing price. The GMP however keeps changing until the listing.
Retail investors usually find these quotes on IPO-tracking websites and financial news platforms. They come from informal dealer networks, so different sources can report different numbers. Seeing a quote does not necessarily mean someone can buy or sell at that price. These transactions also sit outside the normal exchange trading system.
But before an applicant can experience a listing gain or loss, they need to receive shares. GMP has no role in that decision. Allotment depends on the eligible applications competing for the available allocation.
The Numbers Behind Allotment
In a mainboard IPO, shares are allocated to separate investor categories. For individual applicants in the general offer, the application amount determines the category:
Retail: Applications up to ₹2 lakh.
Small HNI: Applications above ₹2 lakh and up to ₹10 lakh.
Big HNI: Applications above ₹10 lakh.
Institutional investors, such as mutual funds and insurance companies, apply through the Qualified Institutional Buyers (QIB) category.
In the application example above, 248 shares at ₹1,785 amount to ₹4,42,680, automatically placing the bid in the small HNI category. If allotment requires a lottery, the application competes with other eligible applicants in that category.
Each category has its own subscription figure. A category subscribed ten times has received bids for ten times the shares available. It does not necessarily have ten applicants competing for every available allotment, because each applicant can request a different quantity.
When a lottery is required, the relevant comparison is between valid applicants and the minimum allotments available. With 1,000 allotments and 5,000 equally eligible applicants, the chance would be roughly one in five. With the same allocation and 10,000 applicants, it would be one in ten.
In a heavily oversubscribed retail category, applying for six lots instead of one does not buy six tickets to the draw. Small HNI and big HNI categories can also require a lottery, although their allocation rules differ.
A smaller group placing large orders can therefore produce a high subscription multiple without having as many applicants competing for each available allotment. Moving into a higher category does not automatically improve the odds. Both the number of applicants and the allocation available in that category matter.
Closing Bell
In 2008, Reliance Power’s IPO reached investors through crores of printed application forms distributed across India. Today, the journey from hearing about an offer to placing a bid can happen on the same phone. A headline starts the conversation, a broker notification announces that bidding has opened, and a UPI mandate sets the money aside.
The stories travel faster now, accompanied by subscription updates, unofficial price estimates and the experiences of recent listings. Once trading begins, attention gradually shifts from subscription figures and listing expectations to the company’s actual performance. Its revenue, profits and ability to carry out its plans begin to influence what investors are willing to pay for its shares.
The paper form has given way to a screen, but the share still represents the same thing: ownership in a business.
For market education only, not investment advice.

9 months ago, I wrote an edition of this newsletter titled “Why is India’s GDP being questioned? Again”.
India had reported a GDP print of 8.2% for that quarter which was scarcely believable to many people. So I broke down why there were niggling issues with India’s GDP calculations back then.
Today, the debate is back.
Last week, India reported that the economy grew by 7.8% in the first quarter of FY27 (April-June). Just to be clear, this is when compared to the same period in the previous year. So, if India’s overall real GDP value was ₹100 during April-June 2025 and it is ₹107.8 during April-June 2026, then it’s a 7.8% growth.
We’ll get to what is “real” GDP in a bit, but let’s just say that this number beat a lot of expectations. Even the RBI had anticipated the economy to grow only 7%.
But this positive surprise also meant that people began to question the GDP numbers again. Subhash Chandra Garg , the former Finance Secretary of India, proclaimed that growth was only an abysmal 2.6%.
What’s the truth?
Well, here goes Round 2 of explaining India’s GDP and we’ll get to Mr Garg’s claim right at the end.
So, the most important thing you should be aware of is that in February 2026 , India took some big steps to clean up the way we calculate GDP. We made it better. Much better.
How, you ask?
Well, there are 3 things that have gone through a massive transformation.
Firstly, one big bone of contention was that the GDP used 2011-12 as the base year for calculations. Think of the base year as the starting point that helps us compare economic data over time – so the prices of goods and services in that base year are used as the reference. GDP in other years is calculated using base-year prices and that helps in isolating the effect of quantity changes rather than price changes.
For example, assume a country produces 100 units of a good in Year 1 that’s priced at ₹10; and 110 units in Year 2 that’s priced at ₹12:
Nominal GDP in Year 2 = 110 × ₹12 = ₹1,320
If we adjust this for the price inflation, we get,
Real GDP in Year 2 (using Year 1 prices as base) = 110 × ₹10 = ₹1,100
The real GDP figure shows growth is driven by increased output — 10 more units — and not rising prices.
This allows us to compare GDP figures meaningfully across time.
For a long time, India’s GDP calculation assumed 2011-12 as the base year. And the thing is that this whole method assumed that today’s economy looked pretty much the same as it did in 2011.
But that wasn’t true. The economy had changed. Drastically.
Think about it — e-commerce wasn’t even a big thing back then and today we have quick commerce for out shopping needs, services were big but they’re now over 50% of the economy, digital payments was non-existent and today that has changed how we consume stuff, and GST wasn’t in the picture and the economy had an even bigger share of the informal sector.
India knew this too. The statistics ministry had to make a tweak. And in February of 2026, the base year was updated — to 2022-23.
The base year change also led to using newer methods of gathering data— things like the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE), the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), GST filings, and corporate ministry (MCA) records, even sales values of cars from the e-Vahan portal.
Think of it as swapping out a sample of the economy taken 14 years ago for one taken now — capturing businesses, sectors, and consumption patterns that simply didn’t exist or didn’t matter back in 2011-12.
That’s for the better.
Another criticism used to be that India relied on the Wholesale Price Index (WPI) and not the Producer Price Index (PPI) for the deflator*.
But what is the deflator?
Okay, remember how we adjusted the nominal GDP to real GDP earlier?
That was a very crude adjustment. But to make that adjustment to real GDP, there’s something called the GDP deflator. It measures the overall price level of all goods and services produced in an economy in any given year. And it’s an inflation-adjustment mechanism.
But how does it matter whether it’s the WPI or the PPI that’s used as a deflator?
So the WPI looks at the ‘first’ price a manufacturer gets for their product that is sold in bulk. Usually in the wholesale market. It usually also includes taxes like GST that come into the picture. And it doesn’t take into account the service industry.
The PPI on the other hand, takes into account including sales to all buyer types. It could be sales to other businesses who then use the input to produce their own product — for example coal used for energy. It could be products sold directly to the consumer such as jewelry. And it strips out indirect taxes like GST to look at the net revenue that the producer makes. It even includes services such healthcare, travel, and insurance to ensure a more holistic picture.
Put simply, WPI looks at goods while PPI includes services as well.
And for a country like India where over 50% of the economy is driven by the service sector, we needed PPI to make better sense of our world.
Again, better data is being used to calculate the GDP today.
And thirdly, we moved from a single deflator method to the globally accepted double deflator method for manufacturing.
What this means is that India used to only look at the final product price and deflate that to get to the real value. It did not deflate the price of inputs.
For example, the price of a laptop might have gone up by 20%, but the chip used as an input might have experienced a 40% increase in price.
A single deflator would just look at the final laptop price for the calculation. But the new system would attach a deflator for inputs too. And that’s the double deflation method.
It’s more comprehensive.
Although I do have to point out that better data doesn’t equate to “perfect” data.
Pronab Sen , the former Chief Statistician of India says it’s easier getting data for the final product or output when compared to getting it for the countless number of inputs that go into everything.
“...goods used as inputs could be four to five times the number of final products. If those inputs are not deflated correctly, it could result in large approximations, and you do not know which direction the numbers will go.”
That’s something to keep in mind.
Anyway, after all this, the big question is how did Mr Garg arrive at 2.6% growth for India?
So, the stats office had calculated the nominal GDP or GDP at Current Prices in Q1 of FY27 to be ₹88.27 lakh crore. And compared it against ₹80.00 lakh crore in Q1 of FY26. Ergo, the nominal growth rate of 10.3% (7.8% was the real growth rate) .
But hold on, wouldn’t comparing it to last year be flawed because the way we calculate GDP changed just a few months ago?
Indeed.
Which is why, the nominal GDP was recalculated using the new method as well. It was ₹86.00 lakh crore under the old method (in Q1FY26) but then was revised downwards.
And when Mr Garg proclaimed growth was actually just 2.6%, he was comparing the Q1FY27 nominal GDP of Rs 88.27 lakh crore with a completely new methodology with the unrevised Q1FY26 figure of Rs 86 lakh crore.
It’s great for a news headline but doing that wouldn’t be an apple to apple comparison, would it?
To the final question — can we trust the GDP numbers?
Well, I’m not going to answer that myself but here’s what Mr Ananth Narayan, a former SEBI Whole Time Member, said in response to an audience question during one of our live Zerodha Varsity Bootcamps .
…I’ll tell you why I think the numbers are okay. I’ll give you two statistics.
One thing I track very closely, CMIE [Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy ] comes out with this CMIE Prowess, which tracks the listed companies space.
Look at the earnings growth of around 5,000 companies which CMIE provides. FY25 was not that great. FY26 was actually quite good earnings growth. It was about 14%, if I remember correctly, That wasn’t bad.
I’ll give you another statistic from CMIE.
CMIE is an entirely independent private body and not the government, right?
CMIE conducts this employment survey which is very well regarded. It is called the Consumer Pyramid [Household] Survey. And typically, like during the times of demonetization, GST implementation, it showed very poor employment data.
But the last two years, CMIE data shows remarkable growth in employment. And this is not the periodic labour force survey of the government. It is from the CMIE. In fact, the numbers seem to tally if you do some adjustments between the government and the CMIE data.
So, irrespective of what we think, actually employment data seems to be going up, again, buttressing the fact that maybe the GDP data is not that bad.
Of course you might have more questions regarding the GDP, so leave a comment and let us know.
And in the meanwhile, do check out the entire conversation with Mr Ananth Narayan on our YouTube channel.

There are thousands of companies listed in the stock market, but most of us tend to follow only a small set of familiar names.
Reliance, Infosys, TCS, ONGC, HDFC Bank and a few others keep appearing in the news, on social media and in everyday market conversations. Over time, these become the companies we naturally know and track.
But what about the thousands of companies outside this familiar circle?
Discovering a stock is harder than it sounds. A company usually needs some reason to first come onto our radar. It could be an IPO, a news article, another company we already follow, a sector we are exploring, or even a screen based on financial numbers.
And once a company enters our radar, we can decide whether it is worth spending more time understanding.
So before we get to analysing stocks, there is a question worth asking: how do investors discover stocks in the first place?
Curiosity: where stock discovery often begins
The most important source of information is often just curiosity.
In investing, curiosity can be as simple as noticing something changing around us and asking one more question. Why is this store suddenly everywhere? Why are we seeing more of this product? Who owns this brand? None of these questions begin as stock research, but they can often lead us there.
The famous investor Peter Lynch gives a well-known example in One Up on Wall Street . His wife, Carolyn, came across a women’s wear product called L’eggs while grocery shopping. What stood out was not just the product, but how it was being sold. Instead of relying mainly on department stores, it was available in supermarkets where customers shopped much more frequently.
That small observation made Lynch curious about the company behind it, Hanes. He did not begin with a balance sheet or an analyst report. He began with something noticed in everyday life and followed the trail.
On a similar note, I had noticed multiple Zudio stores opening across neighbouring localities in Bengaluru. That naturally made me curious about who owned the brand, which eventually led me to Trent, the listed company behind it.
The same thing can happen with everyday services. Instead of calling a local plumber, we may now book one through Urban Company. Instead of calling a restaurant directly, we may order through Swiggy/Zomato. Or we may simply notice far more Ather, Ola and other electric scooters on the road than a few years ago. Each of these can lead us to companies we may not have looked at otherwise.
None of this means the company is a good investment or that the stock will do well. These are simply clues that help us discover more companies.
And that brings us to one of the more obvious ways of discovering a company: IPOs. When a company comes to the stock market for the first time, it is often the first time many investors hear about it.
IPOs: when a company first enters our radar
One of the most obvious ways to discover a new company is through an IPO.
When a company comes to the market, it suddenly gets a lot more visibility. We may see its name in the news, hear people discussing the IPO, or simply notice it while looking at the list of ongoing and upcoming IPOs.
This screen, for example, shows companies currently raising money through IPOs, along with their dates, price bands and minimum application amounts. Even if we had never heard of names like Rentomojo, Prasol Chemicals, Glass Wall Systems or Kanohar Electricals before, they are now on our radar simply because they are coming to the market.
From here, we can start learning what the company does, which industry it operates in, who its competitors are, how the business has grown and why it is raising money. The IPO documents themselves also contain details about the business, financials, risks and how the money raised will be used.
And sometimes, learning about one IPO introduces us not just to a new company, but to an entire industry we had never looked at before.
News and themes: when a story leads us to a stock
News is another common way for us to discover stocks, especially when the same companies or industries keep appearing repeatedly.
A simple search for stock-market news, for example, can bring up several companies that may not already be on our radar. Names like RVNL, Mazagon Dock and Cochin Shipyard can appear alongside much more familiar companies.
Sometimes, one article introduces us to one company. At other times, the more interesting discovery is the theme behind several articles.
If we keep seeing stories about defence orders, railways, data centres, power demand or electronics manufacturing, we may eventually start asking which listed companies are connected to that trend.
So a piece of news that begins with one company can sometimes lead us to several others.And once we find a company or an industry that interests us, there is another fairly simple way to expand the list.
Peers and sectors: from one company to an entire industry
We can start with a sector we already understand and look at the other companies operating within it.
There are several peer and sector screeners that group similar businesses together and show information such as market capitalisation, sales, profits and other financial metrics.
This screen from Tijori , for example, shows companies in the automobile sector. Most investors would already recognise larger names like Maruti Suzuki, Tata Motors, Bajaj Auto and Hero MotoCorp. But the same list also brings up companies such as Ather Energy and Olectra Greentech, which may otherwise have escaped our radar.
If automobiles are a sector we are already familiar with and want to study further, a simple peer or sector screen can quickly expand the number of companies available for research.
The chart above shows why looking beyond the obvious names can be interesting. While several of the larger automobile stocks struggled, Ather Energy, an electric two-wheeler company, performed much better than the broader automobile sector.
But sectors are still only one way for us to filter the market. What if we do not care which industry a company belongs to?
Screeners: using ideas to find the companies
Sector screeners are something most of us are comfortable with because sectors are relatively easy to understand. If we want to look at automobile companies, we can simply filter for automobiles and see the companies that belong to it.
But what if we want to find companies where promoters are increasing their stake, businesses undertaking major expansions, companies with strong cash flows, or stocks seeing unusually high volumes?
This is where screeners become much more useful. Instead of starting with a sector, we can start with the characteristic we are interested in and let the screener find companies that match it.
This screen shows a few examples. We can look for companies where promoter holdings are increasing, businesses undertaking major expansions, small caps that have compounded consistently, or companies with strong cash flows. There are also technical screens for things like high volumes, oversold stocks or golden crossovers.
The useful part is that we do not need to know the company before we begin. We only need to know what we want to look for, and the screener can narrow thousands of listed stocks into a much smaller list.
There is another way to do something similar without setting any filters ourselves: looking at what professional investors already own.
Mutual funds: looking inside professional portfolios
Mutual fund portfolios can also be a useful way for us to discover stocks. One simple place to begin is by looking at a fund that is doing well and then asking what it owns.
This screen ranks some of the larger multi-cap mutual funds by their year-to-date returns. If a fund has held up well, it is natural for us to get curious about what is inside the portfolio and whether some of those holdings helped drive that performance.
Let’s take Mahindra Manulife Multi Cap Fund as an example and look at its stock composition below.
A quick look at the portfolio is quite revealing. Some names will be familiar, such as ICICI Bank, Adani Enterprises and Larsen & Toubro. But there are also companies such as MCX, Neuland Laboratories and APL Apollo Tubes, which may not be part of the usual set of names many investors track, yet still have meaningful weights in the fund.
These are exactly the sort of companies that may never have come onto our radar otherwise.
The chart above shows why this can matter. APL Apollo and Neuland Laboratories have both outperformed the Nifty Smallcap 250 so far this year. Separately, MCX has also done very well.
Looking inside a mutual fund therefore gives us another ready-made list of companies to explore. Individual investors can also provide a similar source of ideas.
Well-known investors: following disclosed holdings
Many investors also follow the publicly disclosed investments of well-known stock pickers. Names such as Mukul Agrawal, Radhakishan Damani and Vijay Kedia are regularly tracked to see which companies are entering or leaving their portfolios.
Rakesh Jhunjhunwala was perhaps the best-known example of this. Because of his stock-picking track record and the wealth created by some of his investments, people closely followed changes in his portfolio. News reports would often pick these up from company shareholding patterns, bulk and block deal disclosures, and other exchange filings.
A simple search like this can surface companies that may otherwise never have come onto our radar. Here, for example, Mukul Agrawal is linked to Arisinfra Solutions, Radhakishan Damani to Sundaram Finance and VST Industries, and Vijay Kedia to Eimco Elecon.
If an unfamiliar company appears in the portfolio of an investor we follow, that alone can be enough to make us curious about what the business does, how it makes money and what may have attracted the investor to it.
The closing bell
There is no single right way for us to discover stocks.
One company may come onto our radar because it is going public. Another may appear in a news article. A familiar company may lead us to its peers, a screener may surface a business we had never heard of, and a mutual fund or well-known investor’s portfolio may introduce us to yet another.
The common thread is that discovery comes before research .
All these methods help solve one problem: taking a market with thousands of listed companies and giving us a smaller set of names worth looking at.
But that is where their job ends.
A company appearing in a screener, a mutual fund portfolio, a famous investor’s holdings or a fast-growing theme does not tell us whether it is a good investment today. It only tells us where to look next. From there, we still need to understand the business, its financials, valuation and risks, or study the price and technical setup if that is how we invest.
The art of discovering stocks, then, is not about finding the next winner instantly. It is about expanding the set of companies we know and giving ourselves better places to begin our research.
And there are probably hundreds of other ways to discover stocks beyond the ones we have covered here.
For me, one of those clues was simply noticing Zudio stores popping up around where I live. I’m curious if you’ve had something similar: a product you suddenly started seeing everywhere, a store that always seemed crowded, or a service everyone around you began using.
Let us know the most unexpected way a stock first came onto your radar.

Liquidity is about flow. It tells us how easily something we own can be converted into the form we need, without losing too much value in the process. Cash in a bank account is already ready to use. A house may be valuable, but selling it can take months. If the owner needs money immediately, they may have to accept a much lower price.
The same idea applies at a much larger scale. A company may own factories and machinery but still struggle to pay salaries if it does not have enough cash. A country may own land, gold and natural resources, but it still needs widely accepted currencies such as the US dollar to pay for imports and foreign debt. If it cannot obtain these currencies when required, trade and payments can be disrupted, confidence can fall and pressure can build on its own currency.
The smoother this conversion, the better the flow of money through a market or an economy. Problems begin when that flow becomes uneven. Something may appear valuable on paper, but there may be no buyer for it at the required time or at a reasonable price. In global markets, this can appear as a country struggling to access foreign currency. In financial markets, it becomes visible when an investor struggles to sell a stock without pushing its price sharply lower.
Liquidity is therefore not simply about whether something can be sold. Almost anything can be sold if the price is reduced enough. The real question is whether it can be converted quickly, in the required quantity and without giving up too much value.
Liquidity in Financial Markets
In financial markets, liquidity is created by investors, traders and institutions placing buy and sell orders at different prices. When enough orders are available, even large trades can take place without moving prices very much. But when buyers or sellers disappear, the flow becomes uneven and even a small order can move the price sharply.
We can understand this liquidity through three measures: the bid-ask spread , market depth and trading volume . Let us begin with the bid-ask spread.
The Bid-Ask Spread
A couple of years ago I was very bullish on Power Grid, good results and a stock making highs. I wanted to go long on it and decided to buy a call option, a contract that gains sharply in value if the Power Grid stock were to rise. The rally did happen and my option showed a profit. But when I exited, much of that profit disappeared. My first thought was that the broker had cheated me. :)
The problem was something I had ignored: the bid-ask spread. The bid is the highest price a buyer is offering, while the ask is the lowest price a seller will accept. The difference between the two is the spread. My option had very few active buyers. The price on my screen showed where the last trade had happened, not what someone would pay me now. When I sold, my order matched with a much lower buying price.
Let us look at another example. The image below shows four United Spirits call options, each in its own grid, with the five highest buying prices in blue and the five lowest selling prices in red, along with the orders and quantities waiting at each price. The stock itself is trading at ₹1,398.10. For call options, a strike price above the stock price is “out-of-the-money”, one close to it is “at-the-money”, and one below it is “in-the-money”. So the ₹1,500 call is out-of-the-money, ₹1,400 is almost at-the-money, and ₹1,360 and ₹1,200 are in-the-money.
For each of these, the spread is simply the difference between the ask and the bid. As a rule, the smaller that difference, the more liquid the contract.
Each box shows the five highest buying prices in blue and the five lowest selling prices in red, along with the orders and quantities at each price. For the at-the-money ₹1,400 call, the highest buying price is ₹19.40 and the lowest selling price is ₹19.70, a spread of just ₹0.30. For the in-the-money ₹1,360 call, the spread widens to ₹10.75. And for the deepest in-the-money call shown, at ₹1,200, buyers offer ₹194.55 while sellers ask ₹214.25, a gap of ₹19.70.
Buy at ₹214.25 and immediately sell at ₹194.55, and you lose ₹19.70 per unit, even if the stock price has not changed. With fewer participants competing, spreads can widen. This is why the last traded price alone is not enough. When we want to sell, what matters is the price buyers are offering and the quantity they are willing to buy.
Market Depth
The spread tells us the best buying and selling prices, but not how much we can trade at those prices. For that, we need market depth, which shows the quantities available at different prices.
This becomes especially important for large investors. A market order seeks to trade immediately at the available prices, but does not guarantee one price for the entire quantity. A large sell order can use up the nearest buy orders and move down to buyers offering progressively lower prices.
The image below shows what market depth looks like. Most brokers show five levels by default, and this snapshot from Zerodha has been expanded to twenty, listing the top twenty buy orders and the top twenty sell orders waiting in Page Industries. The more levels we can see, the better we can judge how far a large order would have to travel.
In this snapshot, buyers want just 3 shares at ₹35,495, another 9 at ₹35,490 and 8 at ₹35,485. Assuming these orders remain unchanged, selling 20 shares through a market order would use all three levels. A larger sale could reach further down the list, where buyers are offering ₹35,400.
The price difference here is relatively small. But in a stock with fewer buy orders and larger gaps between prices, a large sale can push the price down sharply. A large purchase can do the opposite. This is why liquidity depends not just on the stock, but also on the size of your order.
Trading Volume
The orders visible in market depth can change or disappear before a trade happens. A spread that looks tight can widen in milliseconds, and the quantities waiting at each price are only a promise until someone acts on them. Volume is different. It counts the shares that actually changed hands during a period, so nothing about it can be withdrawn.
The clearest way to see volume working as a measure of liquidity is to hold everything else constant. Let us take two companies from the same industry, TCS and 3i Infotech, on the same trading session, and watch how differently they trade.
TCS is shown at the top and 3i Infotech below. Each candle shows the price movement over five minutes, while the bar beneath it shows how many shares traded during that interval. The volume panels use different scales, so the numbers matter more than the height of the bars.
By 2:55 PM, around 45 lakh TCS shares had traded, compared with around 3.7 lakh shares of 3i Infotech. TCS shows regular activity throughout the session. In 3i Infotech, trading is concentrated in a few bursts, with quieter periods of little to no trading activity in between.
Now imagine trying to buy or sell a large quantity during one of those quiet periods. There may not be enough buyers or sellers at your preferred price. You might have to wait, pay more to buy, or accept less to sell. This is why consistently low volume can indicate lower liquidity and make entry and exit more difficult.
One session alone cannot establish this pattern, so it helps to look across several days. Consistently active trading generally makes transactions easier, but volume still tells us what has already happened. The spread and market depth help us understand what prices and quantities are available now.
The River Beneath the Economy
Earlier we looked at liquidity inside a market and inside a single trade. The same question applies to an entire country.
India buys more from the world than it sells to it, and the largest single thing it buys is crude oil. Almost all of it is paid for in US dollars. India has plenty of rupees. It cannot use them to buy oil.
The reason is not a rule written down anywhere. The company selling the oil has little use for rupees. It pays its staff and its suppliers in other currencies, so any rupees it took would have to be swapped first, and how easily that swap happens is the question we have been asking all along.
The chart above shows each currency’s turnover, or in simple terms how much trading activity is happening in that currency globally. Currency trading is just the swapping of one country’s money for another’s, and a large turnover is usually proof that a currency is liquid, which makes it easier for countries and companies everywhere to settle their transactions in it.
Every swap involves two currencies, so each trade is counted twice, once under each side. Counted that way, eighty nine of every hundred trades have the US dollar on one side. Twenty nine have the euro and seventeen the yen. A dollar for euro trade sits in both counts, which is why the numbers overlap rather than divide. The rupee is on one side of about two trades in a hundred, eleventh on the list.
This is volume again, applied to money instead of a stock. A currency traded that heavily can be swapped in size, at short notice, without the exchange rate moving much while you do it. Rupees can be swapped too, but in smaller amounts and at a worse price, and a foreign seller who takes them builds that conversion cost into the deal.
So India keeps a stock of what the world already trades, ready to spend. That stock is the foreign exchange reserves held by the RBI.
The chart above shows India’s foreign exchange reserves, the stock of foreign currency the RBI holds. Every country watches this number, and the usual way to read it is not the size of the pile but its cover, which is how many months of imports it could pay for if every inflow of foreign money suddenly stopped.
That scenario sounds remote. It is not. In 1991, India’s cover fell to under two weeks, and the country came close enough to defaulting on its foreign debt that it had to physically fly gold abroad and pledge it as security for an emergency loan.
Today that cover is about eleven months.
It is arithmetic a household already runs. A bank balance means nothing on its own. What matters is how it sits against the EMIs due next month.
By that measure India has never been better placed, with reserves at $786 billion in early September 2026, the highest ever recorded, giving the RBI a wide margin to steady the rupee when oil prices or foreign investors turn against it.
Closing Bell
A few years ago I was convinced my broker had cheated me. The stock had moved the way I expected, the option showed a profit, and most of it disappeared the moment I tried to leave.
Nobody cheated me. The river simply ran thin where I was standing. That option barely traded, so when I went to sell, the best bid waiting for me sat well below the price on my screen. I had assumed those two were the same thing.
That assumption runs through everything here.
The bid-ask spread tells us what it costs to leave right now. Market depth tells us how much we can sell before the price starts moving against us. Volume tells us whether anyone was trading in the first place. And at the scale of a country, the reserves tell us how much of the world’s currency India holds, while the cover tells us how long it would last.
Different scales, same question.
Almost anything can be sold if the price is cut far enough. Liquidity is simply the measure of how large that cut has to be.

Every few weeks, the same headline comes back.
Foreign investors have sold Indian stocks. Then, a few weeks later, foreign investors are buying again.
The amounts being bought and sold are often large, running into thousands of crores. And because FII flows are tracked so closely, it is easy to feel like foreign investors have an outsized say in where Indian markets go.
They certainly matter, but they are only one part of a much larger market.
Think of markets like a city’s transport system. A city has metros, buses, cars, autos and pedestrians. They all use the same network, but for different journeys and at different speeds. No single mode is necessarily better than the other. Together, they make the system useful for different needs.
Markets work in a similar way.
A retail investor may hold a stock for years. A mutual fund may slowly build a position over weeks or months. A proprietary trading firm may buy and sell within seconds. These participants operate very differently, but together they help improve liquidity and price discovery.
FIIs are an important part of this mix. These are investors and institutions based outside India that invest in Indian stocks and bonds. Today, they are usually referred to as Foreign Portfolio Investors, or FPIs , although the term FII is still commonly used.
And their activity in Indian markets in 2026 has been particularly interesting. Before looking at where exactly their money moved, it helps to first see what was happening to the Indian market as a whole.
What was happening to the broader market?
Indian markets themselves have had a difficult 2026. The chart below compares weekly FPI equity flows with the performance of the Nifty 50 and Sensex through the year.
The blue and orange lines show the returns of the Nifty 50 and Sensex from the beginning of the year, while the bars show weekly FPI equity flows. Green represents net buying and red represents net selling.
The first few months stand out. Both indices fell sharply through February and March, and by late March were down around 14–15% from the start of the year. This was also a period of some of the heaviest FPI selling, with large outflows appearing through January, March and parts of April.
The picture started to improve later. The Nifty 50 and Sensex recovered some of their losses, while the intensity of FPI selling reduced. By July and August, green bars became more common as foreign investors started buying Indian equities again. Even then, by the end of August the Nifty 50 remained down around 8% for the year, while the Sensex was down roughly 10%.
One thing the chart makes clear is that the heaviest FPI selling did not happen while the market was rising strongly. It came during a period when the broader market itself was weak. As the indices recovered, the selling reduced and eventually turned into buying in several weeks.
That does not mean FPI selling caused the market to fall, or that renewed buying caused it to recover. Markets move for many reasons. But it does show that FPI behaviour was also changing alongside the opportunity they saw in Indian equities.
And looking only at the Nifty or Sensex still hides a lot. Different parts of the market performed very differently, and FIIs were not buying or selling every sector in the same way. To understand that, we need to go one level deeper.
Which parts of the market FIIs preferred
FIIs have several choices when they decide to invest in India. They can buy stocks across sectors such as banking, IT, automobiles and healthcare. They can also invest in Indian government securities.
Instead of tracking hundreds of individual stocks, we can group their buying and selling by sector. The heatmap below does exactly that. Each column represents a fortnight in 2026. Green means FIIs were net buyers, while red means they were net sellers. The Sovereign row represents their investments in government securities.
The first thing that stands out is how red the first half of the year was. FIIs were selling across large parts of the market, with some of the sharpest outflows coming in February and March.
Financial Services saw some of the biggest selling. FIIs pulled out around ₹33,000 crore in the first half of March and another ₹29,000 crore in the second half. By mid-August, the sector had still seen around ₹1.05 lakh crore of net selling for the year. Other large sectors were hit too, with Automobiles seeing around ₹31,000 crore of outflows, while IT, Telecom and FMCG each saw roughly ₹28,000 crore leave.
But the right side of the heatmap starts to look different. From the end of June, the large red blocks become less common and more green begins to appear. Healthcare saw inflows in each of the last three fortnights, Consumer Services also saw buying, and IT moved from heavy selling earlier in the year to inflows in July and August. Even Financial Services, which had seen some of the largest outflows, received around ₹20,000 crore since June second half.
This does not mean FIIs suddenly started buying everything again. But the intensity of the selling clearly reduced, and money began returning to some parts of the market. One row, however, tells a very different story. While FIIs were selling equities, their investments in Indian government securities remained largely positive, adding up to around ₹78,000 crore for the year.
So FII money was not simply leaving India. In many cases, it was also moving between different parts of the Indian market. Now that we know where the money has been moving, the next step is to see how those sectors have performed.
Did FII flows translate into better returns?
We have seen where FII money moved through the year. The next question is whether sectors that received more foreign buying actually performed better. Let us first look at how different sectors have performed through 2026.
Looking at the full year, sector returns have been very different. Capital Goods is up around 18%, Healthcare 16%, while Power and Telecom are up around 14%. Metals have gained around 12% and Consumer Durables around 9%. At the other end, IT is down around 20%, Oil & Gas around 9% and FMCG around 8%, while Financial Services is also down around 4%.
Some of this lines up with FII activity. IT and Financial Services, for instance, saw heavy foreign selling and were also weak during the year. But the relationship does not hold everywhere. Capital Goods has been one of the strongest sectors despite relatively modest FII buying, while Telecom is up around 14% even though FIIs have been net sellers.
The picture becomes more interesting if we shorten the period and look only from mid-June, around the time the intensity of FII selling began to reduce.
Since mid-June, Realty has been the strongest performer, gaining around 14%. Consumer Durables and Automobiles are up around 9%, while IT and Healthcare have gained around 8%. IT is particularly interesting. It remains the weakest sector for the year, but has recovered around 8% since mid-June, around the same time FII selling reduced and eventually turned into buying.
Still, FII flows alone do not decide sector returns. Realty has been the strongest performer since mid-June despite receiving relatively small FII inflows, while Financial Services gained only around 2% even as foreign buying improved. So FII flows tell us where foreign investors are finding opportunities, but those investments do not always translate into immediate market returns. FIIs are ultimately trying to find the opportunities that can give them the best returns going forward.
And for an FII, that comparison does not stop at one Indian sector versus another. India itself is competing with markets and assets around the world for the same money.
What drives FII investment decisions
Foreign investors have many choices when deciding where to put their money. Large global investors are constantly comparing opportunities across countries, from the US and Japan to India and other emerging markets. So when they invest in India, they are also asking a simple question: will my money do better here than somewhere else?
A few things influence that decision. The first is the return they expect to make. If Indian companies are growing, valuations look attractive and markets offer good opportunities, India becomes more interesting.
Tax matters too. This became particularly relevant in 2026, when India exempted FPIs from tax on interest and capital gains earned from government securities from April 1. Equity investments, however, do not receive the same exemption.
But there is another factor that can significantly change what a foreign investor actually earns: the currency .
The blue line shows the USDINR exchange rate, while the bars show weekly FPI equity inflows and outflows. Through 2025 and 2026, the rupee weakened from around ₹86 to more than ₹95 against the dollar. An interesting pattern shows up in the chart. Periods when the rupee was relatively stable often saw stronger FPI inflows, while sharper periods of rupee depreciation were accompanied by larger outflows. The relationship is not perfect, since several other factors also influence FPI decisions, but it shows why currency movements matter.
Take early 2026 as an example. Suppose an FPI invested $100 when USDINR was around 90. That would give them ₹9,000 to invest.
If their Indian investments returned 5%, the value would rise to ₹9,450.
But by August, if USDINR had moved to around 95.5, converting ₹9,450 back into dollars would leave them with only about $99.
So even though the investment earned 5% in rupee terms, the return in dollar terms would be slightly negative. And that is before accounting for taxes and other costs. This is why currency movements matter so much for foreign investors. Indian stocks may deliver positive returns, but FPIs ultimately care about the return they take home in dollars, and how that compares with what the same money could have earned elsewhere.
Closing Bell
Put all of this together, and the FII story in 2026 becomes easier to understand. Foreign investors sold heavily through the first half, partly because of broader global conditions, but also because Indian markets were weak and the rupee continued to depreciate.
That combination matters. If stock prices are struggling and the rupee is weakening at the same time, the return a foreign investor earns after converting back into dollars can look much worse than the return seen in rupee terms. At the same time, they are comparing India with other markets and assets where the risk and return may look more attractive.
But the second half of the year has started to look different. Selling has reduced, money has returned to a few sectors, and some of the sectors that were weak earlier have begun to recover. So when we see headlines saying “FIIs are selling India” or “FIIs are back,” the more useful question is not just how much money moved. It is what changed in the market, what happened to the currency, which opportunities became more attractive, and which sectors foreign investors now prefer.

In 2019, Stephen Colbert asked Keanu Reeves a question you don’t usually hear on a late-night comedy show: “What do you think happens when we die?” Keanu paused for a moment and said, “I know that the ones who love us will miss us.” For a few seconds, the studio went silent.
The pain of losing someone can’t be replaced, and no amount of planning changes that. What good planning can do is spare the family a second kind of pain: going from pillar to post, between the bank, the broker, a lawyer, and sometimes a court, just to claim the money legally theirs.
Two documents decide whether the family has to go through that at all: a nomination and a will.
We often put them off, only to have our families discover their importance the hard way.
So here’s what it’s like not having them.
In this edition, I’ll stick to just a few forms of investments: demat holdings (stocks, mutual fund units, bonds) and mutual fund holdings in non-demat form, as well as bank deposits (savings accounts and FDs).
What happens if there is no nominee?
When you name a nominee, you are telling your bank or broker whom to hand the assets to after you.
But when there is no nominee, the bank, mutual fund company or broker can’t just transfer the assets to whoever walks in and says, “I’m the son” or “I’m the daughter”.
The intermediary doesn’t know who all the legal heirs are. So before handing over the money, the family needs to prove who is entitled to claim it. The larger the amount, the more proof it may ask for.
If the holdings in a demat account are worth up to ₹30 lakh , legal heirs can usually claim them with simpler paperwork. They may still need documents like the death certificate, an indemnity bond, and a no-objection certificate from the other heirs (see glossary at the end).
Once the value crosses ₹30 lakh , the process usually becomes more demanding. Families are often asked for stronger proof, including court-issued documents such as a succession certificate, probate or letters of administration (see glossary at the end). SEBI does allow some non-court alternatives, too, but the paperwork is still involved.
So, this ₹30 lakh is essentially the threshold for the simpler paperwork route for securities held in demat form.
For mutual funds held outside a demat account, that threshold is at ₹10 lakh per fund house. Banks, meanwhile, follow their own limits rather than a single industry-wide number. SBI and Axis, for example, use ₹15 lakh . Above these limits, court-issued certificates, indemnities, NOCs and sureties (see glossary at the end) may be needed.
hmm…I hope you’re still with me after all that document jargon.
You know what? Much of this hassle can be avoided by adding a nominee , a simple process that hardly takes 5–10 minutes to fill out. Upon the investor’s death, the nominee typically submits a few basic documents , and in a straightforward case, the assets will usually be transferred within a few weeks.
What happens if there is no will?
So, let’s say the nominee or the family members finally jump through all the hurdles, and the assets land in their account. You can breathe a sigh of relief, right?
Well, the job is only halfway done.
Whether you received the money smoothly through a nomination form or painfully through a court certificate, getting the money doesn’t mean it’s yours . In the eyes of the law. The person who receives the assets is merely “a trustee holding them on behalf of the actual legal heirs”.
What does that mean? Let’s say Ram was the registered nominee on his father’s account, so the bank handed the funds over to him. But, his father’s Will explicitly states that his mother gets 50%, Ram gets 25%, and a charitable trust gets the remaining 25%. Even though Ram received the money from the bank, it is now his legal responsibility to distribute it exactly as the Will dictates.
To put it simply: a nomination decides who receives the asset, but a will decides who owns it.
But what if there is no will at all? Then, who-gets-what has to be decided by a mutual family settlement or the country’s succession laws.
The family settlement
The easier route is for all the legal heirs to just agree among themselves. They decide who gets what, put it in writing, and everyone signs. If someone chooses to walk away from their share, they simply sign a No Objection Certificate (NOC) or a relinquishment deed. And if real estate is involved, this settlement agreement may need to be officially registered.
Interestingly, the final split doesn’t even have to match what the law prescribes, as long as every single heir agrees to it. When families get along, this works well.
When the family doesn’t agree: succession law
If even one heir refuses to sign, the settlement route closes and succession law decides, often with a court involved. And once trust breaks down, things get ugly fast.
And unfortunately, this happens a lot more often than you and I can expect.
And do you know what makes this even trickier? India doesn’t have one succession law. Which one applies depends on your religion, and sometimes on your gender and how you got married.
For Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs, the Hindu Succession Act generally applies. If a Hindu man dies without a will, his mother, wife and children, among the Class I heirs, usually share the estate. For a Hindu woman, the rules are different and can also depend on where the property came from. Christians are largely governed by the Indian Succession Act, which has separate provisions for Parsis. Muslims follow their personal law, where the rules can differ between Sunni and Shia schools. Even with a will, generally only up to one-third of the estate can be given away freely.
Ultimately, all of this legal dilemma can be avoided if you simply have a will in place, preferably one that clearly explains why you are splitting the estate the way you are, which leaves less room for arguments. Sure, a will can still be contested; there is no denying that. But deciding not to make one just because someone might challenge it is a classic case of letting perfect be the enemy of good. :)
Bringing it together
To put it simply, the nomination helps move the assets. The will makes clear who should ultimately own them. Without them, what should be a simple handover can quickly turn into paperwork, delays and family disputes.
1. Keep your nominee and beneficiary aligned
Wherever possible, name the same person as the nominee and the beneficiary in your will. That way, the person who collects the asset is also the person meant to keep it. Scope for disputes would be low.
2. Joint ownership can make things easier
For bank accounts and FDs with an “either or survivor” instruction, the surviving holder can continue without the usual claim process. Demat accounts can also be held jointly, making transmission simpler.
3. Writing a will is not rocket science
You don’t need stamp paper, a notary or registration. Just clearly state what you own and who should get it, sign the will, and have two witnesses sign it too.
If you need help getting started, here is our step-by-step guide to writing a will .
4. Change how you have “the conversation”
Asking your parents to write a will can feel like you are counting their days or being money-minded.
A lawyer once told me: Don’t just ask them to do it. Do it together.
Sit down as a family, write your own will alongside theirs, and check everyone’s nominations too. It feels less overwhelming.
So, set aside an evening. Check your nominations, write that will, keep it somewhere accessible, and make sure someone you trust knows where it is.
Keanu was right, the ones who love us will miss us. The least we can do is make sure that missing us is the only thing they have to deal with.
What each document means
Let’s take Ravi. Under the Hindu Succession Act, his father’s legal heirs are his mother, Ravi himself, and his sister Meena. His father’s own mother passed away years ago. Here is what each document means in this case.
Affidavit: Ravi makes a sworn statement saying that the facts he has given, such as who the legal heirs are, are true.
NOC: His mother and Meena sign, saying they have no objection to Ravi making the claim and collecting the assets.
Bond of indemnity: Ravi promises to compensate the institution if it suffers a loss because his claim turns out to be wrong or another rightful claimant appears later.
Legal heir certificate: A competent government authority certifies who the legal heirs of Ravi’s father are.
Succession certificate: This comes from a court and is mainly used for debts and securities . It allows Ravi to collect those assets. An FD can count as a debt because the bank owes that money to his father.
Letters of administration: If there is no will, the court can appoint Ravi, or someone else, to manage the whole estate (not just debt and securities).
Probate: If there is a will, probate is the court confirming that the will is genuine and can be acted upon. It is no longer compulsory in the old cases where it was once mandatory, though it can still come up when stronger proof of the will is needed.
Surety: Another person stands behind Ravi’s claim and agrees to pay the institution if Ravi cannot honor his indemnity.

In 2001, a Goldman Sachs economist named Jim O’Neill wrote a research note to describe what he believed would be the economies that could shape global growth over the following decades. The countries he picked were Brazil, Russia, India, and China. In no particular order other than when the first letters were arranged in order, you’d get a nice sounding acronym — BRIC.
That’s the whole origin story.
It wasn’t a case of the countries coming together and deciding to join hands. It was a report by an investment bank that led to someone sitting in Delhi, Moscow, Beijing, or Brasilia to pick up the phone, get on a conference call and say, “Hey, I think we should all get together and formalise this bloc.”
So the first summit happened in 2009. And barely a year later, the group decided to invite South Africa to join; turning BRIC into BRICS.
The acronym sounded even better!
Now let’s cut to today.
Because if you look at this one chart from Reuters , you’d think, “Wow, BRICS countries are really cooperating and trading with each other in a big way.”
The trade in goods among BRICS countries has expanded at a faster pace than world trade and even trade among certain emerging economies (what is known as the South-South trade ).
It’s doing exactly what an economic bloc is supposed to do.
Source: Reuters
And if these countries are trading with each other that much, you’d assume more of it is settling in local currencies too and less in the dollar. That’s certainly the rhetoric. As Brazil’s president, Lula da Silva, said a couple of years ago, “Every night, [I ask myself] why all countries have to base their trade on the dollar.”
That’s the entire point of de-dollarization — when countries reduce their reliance on the US dollar for trade, financial transactions, and forex reserves.
But here’s the problem. The one thing I can say is that there isn’t much to prove de-dollarization is happening when it comes to trade at least.
One of the most comprehensive invoicing-currency trackers ( pdf ), covering 120-plus countries, shows that as of 2023, the US dollar still accounts for ~40% of global trade invoicing. Another 40% is invoiced in the Euro. That split has held at those levels for decades now.
Source: European Central Bank
When the researchers tested whether countries drifting geopolitically away from the US were also abandoning dollar invoicing, the relationship was quite weak. And if you removed Russia, Belarus, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and the rest of the world’s invoicing habits barely moved away from the dollar and the euro.
Russia moved, or was forced to move, after the sanctions imposed on it after the Ukraine war. Not because of a real de-dollarization wave.
So now you’ve got two true things sitting side by side. Intra-BRICS trade is genuinely growing exponentially. But the currency the world actually prices its trade in is barely moving even though blocs like the BRICS have aimed to dethrone it.
What explains this?
Part of that answer is scale. Intra-BRICS trade is still only about 4-5% of total world trade, even after all that growth, because it started from almost nothing and because BRICS as a whole still trades mostly with everyone else in the world.
Another part of the answer is trade deficits. .
Here’s a chart created by my colleagues behind The Daily Brief newsletter. India’s goods trade with BRICS has more than doubled since FY21, but imports have grown far faster than exports. And that has left India with the bloc’s largest trade deficit — roughly $226 billion, of which China alone accounts for around 41%.
Will India settle its trade with China in the yuan?
No.
And will the other counterparty be willing to settle in Indian rupees?
Well, the Russia-India oil trade is a prime example. Despite all the noise around settling transactions using a rupee-rouble mechanism, it never took off. And that’s to do with this trade imbalance — Russia will end up earning rupees by selling oil to India, but if it isn’t importing a similar amount worth of goods or services from India, how will it end up spending those rupees? It becomes a giant pile of currency it has no use for.
Which means, the dollar remains entrenched in trade invoicing. At least for now because of the
As David Lubin of Chatham House put it ,
The distribution of global currency power changes very, very slowly because of what economists call ‘network effects.’ The more widely the dollar is used – the bigger its network – the more entrenched it becomes and the more costly it is for anyone to operate without it.
The dollar is to international finance what the English language is to international communication. That status is reinforced by the reliability of the US legal system, the depth and liquidity of its capital markets, and its global cultural appeal.
Another decisive factor that keeps the dollar on top is its ready convertibility into other currencies, which makes it exceptionally easy to use internationally.
In short, dollar dominance exists because everyone uses it and that itself makes it more useful.
But the deeper answer as to why the growth in intra-BRICS trade may not have amounted to much, at least in terms of de-dollarization, is that BRICS was never built to move as one unit in the first place. Because if you look at the group again, it raises a question worth actually asking: what is a “bloc,” if it isn’t built on geography?
Look at how the blocs we’re used to actually formed.
The EU grew out of a coal-and-steel pact between six neighbouring countries trying to make another war too expensive to fight. The goal was to run their coal and steel industries under a common management so that one single country wouldn’t be able to make the weapons of war to turn against others.
ASEAN formed among Southeast Asian nations that already shared supply chains, tourism, migration…a region.
In both cases, “bloc” was just the natural word for what proximity had already built.
BRICS didn’t have that.
For starters, there’s the origin story. It’s a group born out of an economic prediction rather than real shared interests.
Then there’s the intra-BRICS growth. China is the behemoth of the group. And there is India’s economic prowess. The rest are some ways behind. And when the gap between members widens, it’s the biggies who actually get to call the shots.
Finally — and this might be the big one — put India and China in the same room and they don’t agree on much. They’re two countries that are both founding members of the same club and, mostly rivals.
The bloc came first and the reasons to actually act work together as one came later.
And you can see some of this “force-fittedness” play out.
A few years ago, they thought about launching a common BRICS currency but that fell flat.
And now, the mechanism getting the most attention was BRICS Pay — an attempt to stitch together India’s UPI, China’s CIPS, and Russia’s SPFS into one interoperable layer, so payments could clear among members without routing through SWIFT (SWIFT is a global messaging system for payments). This way, each country keeps full control of its own money and the systems just talk to each other.
But even that’s not going to be easy.
India has already blocked the integration of China-linked Alipay+ and has also clearly said that it is not interested in building a settlement system that hands China the reins.
So, can BRICS actually push de-dollarization?
Well, in pieces, yes. Russia and China have shifted real volumes of bilateral trade into local currencies. India and the UAE have a working rupee-dirham corridor. BRICS Pay is a genuinely serious infrastructure project that will find some traction.
But as a coordinated, bloc-wide push, it seems quite improbable. Despite the intra-BRICS trade chart telling you otherwise.
What do you think?
PS: If you’re wondering why the illustration of the flags on a brick wall have a lot more countries, it’s because the membership has expanded even if the name hasn’t.
Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE are now full member countries.
Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam are called Partner Countries.
