Markets are down. Screens are red, and foreign investors are selling. For someone who began investing recently, it can feel as though this is what the market always does.
An investor who started at the beginning of 2020 has seen a very different journey. The Nifty 50 fell about 39% during the COVID crash, then climbed to a level roughly 115% above where it began 2020 by September 2024. That investor has seen both a frightening fall and a long rise. But someone who started near the end of 2024 arrived after that long rise. Nearly two years later, waiting for the market to make clear progress can feel like an eternity.
This, too, is part of passive investing. Buying a Nifty 50 or Nifty 500 fund means following the broader market through years when it rises and years when it barely moves. But even when the broader market is sideways, the stocks within it do not all move together. Some groups rise, others fall, and last year’s winners may stop doing well.
Today, passive investors have more choices than funds tracking the Nifty 50, Sensex or Nifty 500. A search for index funds and ETFs also brings up names such as Momentum, Value, Quality, Alpha and Low Volatility. The names may sound complicated, but these are indices that follow different rules to choose stocks. Many also have index funds or ETFs through which people can invest.
These are called factor strategies. Instead of simply owning a broad basket of the market, each focuses on certain kinds of stocks that may do better in different market conditions. So how do these strategies work, which ones have done well, and how can investors access them?
The strategy behind each factor index
The image below shows some of these factor strategies and how their indices are built. Most start with the Nifty 500, which covers 500 large, mid and small companies. Nifty Alpha 50 starts with a different group: companies ranked among the top 300 by both market value available for trading and trading activity. Each strategy then follows its own rules to decide which stocks to include.
The first two rows show how much the weight of a stock matters. The Nifty 500 gives bigger companies more weight, so their price movements have more effect on the index. Nifty500 Equal Weight holds the same 500 companies but gives each roughly the same weight.
The other strategies change which stocks are selected. Momentum looks for stocks that have risen strongly in recent months. Value looks for stocks that appear relatively cheap compared with measures such as their earnings. Quality looks for financially stronger companies, while Low Volatility looks for stocks whose prices have fluctuated less. Alpha looks for stocks that have performed strongly relative to the broader market.
The rules stay the same, but the stocks in these indices can change. They are reviewed regularly, and companies can enter or leave as their scores change. The name describes the approach an index follows, rather than a fixed list of companies.
That leads to the interesting question: which approach performed best, and did the winner stay the same every year?
The winner keeps changing
In the image above, each column is a year. The strategies are ranked from the highest return at the top to the lowest at the bottom, with the return shown inside each box. The colours help track the same strategy across years. The last column shows 2026 so far , rather than a full year.
The top row keeps changing. Momentum led in 2017, 2019 and 2021. Value came first in 2016, 2022, 2023 and 2025. Alpha led in 2020 and 2024, and is at the top so far in 2026.
The moves lower down the chart are just as telling. Alpha returned about 67% in 2017, then fell about 15% in 2018. It led in 2024 with a return of about 33%, but finished last in 2025 with a loss of about 11%. Low Volatility was second in 2025, yet sits at the bottom so far in 2026.
The broader Nifty 500 also changes position. In 2022, when several strategies lost money, it gained about 3%. Value did much better that year, returning about 19%.
No factor stays at the top. A strong trend may help Momentum, while a period when cheaper stocks recover may help Value. The chart also shows why buying whichever factor won last year is risky. It shows what worked in the past, not what will work next.
A closer look at 2026
The yearly rankings show where each strategy stands, but they hide the path it took to get there. The chart below follows the same indices from the first trading day of 2026, with every line starting at 0%. That makes their movements easier to compare.
In the image above, Alpha is the red line. It pulled ahead during the second half of the year and is up about 7% at the point shown, while the broader Nifty 500 is down about 7%. Equal Weight and Momentum are close to where they started. Low Volatility, which was near the top of the yearly rankings in 2025, is among the weakest in 2026.
Alpha’s lead is striking, but the red line also shows that it gave up some gains after reaching a higher point in September. A return at one date tells only part of the story. The falls along the way and the way a strategy behaves in different kinds of markets matter too.
There is one more distinction before looking for a way to invest: these charts show index returns, not the returns of funds that track those indices.
From factor indices to ETFs
Each index is a set of rules for choosing and weighting stocks. Its rules, factsheet and constituent list can be found on the NSE Indices strategy page . An investor could follow the list, buy the stocks in the same weights and update the portfolio whenever the index changes. An exchange-traded fund, or ETF, offers a simpler route: it holds a basket of stocks designed to track an index, and its units can be bought and sold on the exchange.
The image below shows what appears when terms such as Momentum, Value, Nifty 500 and Alpha are searched on the market watch on Kite.
The search results make these strategies feel more accessible, but a matching name is only a starting point. For example, the Alpha search shows ETFs linked to different indices, including Nifty Alpha 50 and Nifty200 Alpha 30. Before choosing a fund, the key check is its underlying index : does it follow the exact strategy being considered? The fund’s costs and how closely its returns have followed that index matter as well.
Liquidity matters because an ETF trades on the exchange like a stock. If the best available buying price is ₹101 and the best selling price is ₹100, the ₹1 gap is a cost to someone who needs to trade immediately. A wider gap, or too few units available at the quoted price, can make it harder to enter or exit at a fair price. Choosing a strategy is therefore only one part of choosing an ETF.
Matching an ETF to the right index
The NSE’s Exchange Traded Funds page provides a useful way to narrow the search. It lists ETFs traded on the exchange, including their symbols, prices and trading volumes. Its Sub-category column shows the index or market segment associated with each fund.
The screenshot shows why the full index name matters. The ETF in the first row is linked to Nifty 100 Low Volatility 30 . That is different from Nifty500 Low Volatility 50 , even though both names contain “Low Volatility”. Starting with the intended strategy index and then checking an ETF’s benchmark helps narrow the list to funds that follow the right approach.
Price and volume offer a quick first look at trading activity. Before placing an order, the available buying and selling prices and the number of units offered at those prices are worth checking too. The journey from a factor idea to an investment has two choices: the index whose rules make sense, and the fund that follows it.
The closing bell
Passive investing once felt straightforward: buy a Nifty 50 or Nifty 500 fund and let the broader market do the work. For investors who started near the end of 2024, that approach has tested their patience as the market has struggled to make progress.
But the broad indices are not the only way to invest through an index. Factor indices use set rules to select or weight stocks differently. As the charts show, some of these strategies have done better than the Nifty 500 this year, while others have done worse. The winner has changed from one year to the next.
The Nifty 50 and Nifty 500 remain useful measures of how the market is doing. They just do not tell the whole story. Even when the broader market is struggling, a different way of selecting stocks can produce a very different result.

1 out of every 12 Health Insurance claims in India gets rejected!

This can be easily avoided by keeping just a few things in mind.

1. The Room Rent Clause:

If you have an Insurance of 5 Lakh rupees and the Insurance document says “Room Rent Limit capped at 1% of insured amount” you can basically take a room that has a rent of 5,000 per day. But in case you wish to upgrade yourself to a better room of 10k, chances are only 50% of your claim would be accepted.

When you exceed the room rent limit, ‘proportionate deduction kicks in’. Since the Insurance only covered 50% of the room rent you actually paid, your expenses like Doctor Consultation Fees, Surgeon Fees, Diagnostics Fees etc would proportionately be adjusted and only 50% of such expenses would be accepted for the claim.

Ideally you should opt for an Insurance that does not have a Room Rent Limit and in case your existing insurance has this cap, you should keep the proportionate deduction factor in Mind.

2. The Waiting Period Clause.

Every Insurance policy has a waiting period of certain months for different diseases. For example certain Insurance might not cover Hypertension for 24 months. Knowing this becomes important specially if you are buying this for your parents or elderly.

3. Mis Statement of Facts.

This is one of the most common and the most avoidable reasons for claim rejection. Hiding facts related to lifestyle like smoking or drinking habits, age or pre existing medical conditions can lead to complete rejection of claims if the Insurance company finds out these facts at the time of claim approval.

People generally hide these things fearing high premiums or issues at the time of receiving the claim, but it is best for you to be completely honest and disclose every material fact so that your insurance can help you smoothly at the time of emergency.

💡 KEY EPISODE TAKEAWAYS

- Banks Are for Banking Only: Use banks strictly to hold deposits, clear transactions, or issue simple FDs. Avoid buying wealth products, insurance, or investment plans directly inside a branch.   

- Separate Insurance from Investment: ULIPs and Endowment plans provide inadequate life cover while yielding returns worse than simple benchmark index funds. Buy pure term insurance separately and put investment capital into low-cost index funds.   

- The "Hotel California" Trap: ULIPs carry high upfront commissions (4% to 10%) and exit penalties that move your money into 4% discontinuation funds if you stop early.   

- No Mandatory Home Loan Insurance: RBI rules strictly prohibit banks from bundling home loans with mandatory internal insurance policies. Demanding written confirmation to submit to the Banking Ombudsman stops forced sales instantly.   

- RM Accountability Deficit: Unlike SEBI-registered RIAs or MFDs, bank Relationship Managers carry no individual regulatory license, allowing them to mis-sell without personal legal liability.

India’s Irrigation Revolution: From Dams to Groundwater
India’s irrigation system has transformed dramatically since Independence. Large dams and canal networks initially drove irrigation and food security, but gaps in last-mile delivery, rising costs and repeated droughts pushed India towards groundwater and tubewells. This shift helped make India more resilient to monsoon shocks and a net grain exporter, but it also created serious challenges around groundwater depletion, subsidised electricity and inefficient water use.
The story also looks at how underground pipelines, drip irrigation and sprinkler systems have improved the efficiency of delivering water to farms — while pointing out why better irrigation technology alone cannot solve the problem of groundwater over-extraction.

We’ll cover:
●From dams to tubewells: How India moved from large public irrigation projects to decentralised groundwater irrigation.
●The groundwater–power link: How subsidised electricity encouraged groundwater extraction and created financial stress for state power utilities.
●The next irrigation challenge: Why groundwater depletion remains a problem despite micro-irrigation, drip systems and improved water-delivery infrastructure.

Is there really such a thing as "free money" in the markets? And if covered calls are one of the most popular option strategies ever sold to investors, why was the man who co-created the Black-Scholes formula not convinced?

We start with how covered calls are pitched to investors, as a way to earn "free money" on stocks you already own, and why even Fischer Black, co-creator of the Black-Scholes formula, was skeptical of the idea.

We then look at the history of the strategy, how it was sold by brokers over the decades, and what a behavioral study on Dutch investors revealed about why people find it attractive in theory but less so when they actually see the payoff.

The episode breaks down the mechanics of a covered call with real numbers, what happens when the stock falls, stays flat, or rallies, and why the strategy has a capped upside but nearly full downside.

Finally, we run a backtest on 10 of the most liquid large-cap Indian stocks from January 2022 onward, selling a 5% out-of-the-money call every month, and compare the results stock by stock to see whether covered calls actually add value to a buy-and-hold portfolio in India.

Welcome to The Long and The Short, a show where you can expect an honest take on trading and investing, something you won't hear elsewhere.

I'm your host, Sandeep Rao (SEBI Registered Research Analyst - INH000013059).

Planning a wedding involves much more than choosing the venue, food, outfits and guest list. For many families, a wedding is also one of the biggest financial commitments they will make.

But what happens if, just days before the wedding, something unexpected forces you to cancel or postpone the event?

A large amount of money may already have been paid to hotels, vendors, decorators, photographers and other service providers and depending on their cancellation and refund policies, you may not be able to recover all of it.

This is where Insurance can become relevant.

The Wedding Insurance can potentially cover you from: 

• Event cancellation or postponement 
• Damage to wedding-related property
• Accidents or medical emergencies

But Wedding Insurance does not mean every wedding-related loss is automatically covered.

There can be exclusions for things such as normal wear and tear, damage caused by negligence and other circumstances specifically excluded by the policy. The exact coverage, exclusions, deductibles and claim conditions vary between insurers and policies.

A wedding is an emotional milestone, but it is also a significant financial commitment. Planning for the unexpected can help prevent an unforeseen event from turning into a major financial setback.
